Have you seen a window where the glass moves vertically up and down at the touch of a button?

This is a Motorized Guillotine Window, also known as a Motorized Vertical Sliding Glass Window.

Unlike conventional sliding windows, which move horizontally, a guillotine window operates vertically using a motorized lifting mechanism.

🔹 How does it work?

The system typically consists of:

• Motor and gearbox
• Vertical guide channels
• Lifting mechanism such as belt, cable or chain
• Rollers/carriers
• Counterbalance or load-support mechanism
• Safety sensors and control system
• Glass panels and aluminium framing

When the system is activated, the motor drives the lifting mechanism, allowing the glass panels to move upward or downward smoothly.

⬆️ Glass moves up → Opening closes
⬇️ Glass moves down → Opening opens

Why is it useful?

✅ Maximizes the usable opening
✅ Convenient one-touch operation
✅ Clean and modern architectural appearance
✅ Suitable for large openings
✅ Can be integrated with smart-home/automation systems
✅ Useful for restaurants, balconies, terraces and commercial spaces

The real engineering challenge isn't simply making the glass move. The motor, glass weight, balancing system, guides, safety protection and structural design all need to work together reliably.

For large motorized glass systems, proper consideration of glass weight, wind load, motor capacity, safety sensors and maintenance access is essential.

Technology is changing the way architectural openings are designed — and motorized guillotine windows are a great example of this evolution.

One sentence in JPMorgan's 2025 Annual Report changed how I looked at the entire company.

It wasn't a revenue number.

It wasn't net income.

It wasn't ROTCE.

It was this:

“We need to maximize the benefits of our scale and scope, which are necessary to our largest institutional and government clients, while minimizing their considerable negatives.”

At first glance, it sounds like ordinary corporate language.

I don't think it is.

That sentence captures one of JPMorgan's biggest strategic contradictions.

Scale is JPMorgan's moat.

But scale is also one of its problems.

Being enormous gives JPMorgan:

• Massive client relationships
• Global infrastructure
• Huge technology budgets
• Data advantages
• Capital strength
• Ability to serve complex institutional clients

But the same scale can create:

• Bureaucracy
• Complexity
• Slower decision-making
• Higher costs
• Organizational inertia

And management knows it.

In fact, the 2025 shareholder letter explicitly says size can become a business disadvantage because it can bring complexity, bureaucracy and complacency.

That's why this sentence matters.

JPMorgan doesn't simply need to become bigger.

It needs to become more effective at being big.

And that's a very different challenge.

This also connects directly with the company's AI and technology strategy.

If technology can make a giant organization faster, more automated and more intelligent, then JPMorgan's scale becomes an even bigger competitive advantage.

But if technology simply adds another layer of complexity?

The advantage becomes less obvious.

My takeaway:

The most important question for JPMorgan may not be:

“How big can it become?”

It may be:

“Can JPMorgan remain fast while operating at enormous scale?”

Because if the answer is yes, its moat gets wider.

If the answer is no, its biggest strength could gradually become its biggest weakness.

That's the kind of sentence I look for in an MD&A.

A sentence that sounds simple.

But underneath it contains the entire strategic problem.

YOUR MIND IS POWERFUL—BUT IT IS NOT ALWAYS RIGHT. 🧠

1️⃣ MIND IS BLIND — It doesn’t always see reality; it sees reality through your beliefs, fears, and past experiences.

2️⃣ MIND LOVES COMFORT — It will often choose what feels safe over what helps you grow.

3️⃣ MIND FOLLOWS PATTERNS — Repeat a thought long enough, and your mind starts treating it like truth.

4️⃣ MIND CREATES CONFLICT — One part of you wants growth, while another part screams, “Stay safe!”

5️⃣ THE REAL PROBLEM? — We often obey our thoughts without questioning them.

6️⃣ THE SOLUTION: S.T.O.P. FRAMEWORK 🛑

S — SEE  the thought.
T — TEST  the thought.
O — OBSERVE  the pattern.
P — PICK your response.

7️⃣ Before saying, “I can’t,” ask: Is this a fact—or simply a familiar thought?

8️⃣ Before choosing comfort, ask: “Will this decision help my future self?”

9️⃣ Remember: A thought is not a fact. A feeling is not a command. Comfort is not always growth.

🔟 MASTER YOUR MIND → CHANGE YOUR CHOICES → CHANGE YOUR FUTURE.

You don’t have to control every thought.
You have to control which thoughts get to control you.

AI is creating jobs. But will those jobs last?
 
A recent Print report from Noida and Gurugram highlights the rise of AI data-annotation jobs people helping AI learn by labelling images, text, audio and video, checking AI responses and preparing training data.
 
The interesting part?
 
Many of these jobs are repetitive and relatively low-paid, and some could themselves be automated as AI improves.
 
This is an important lesson for students and parents.
 
Instead of asking:
 
Which degree will get me a job?
 
Start asking:
 
Which combination of skills will remain valuable as jobs change?
 
Students can explore:
 
 Biology + AI , Medical AI, Bioinformatics 
 Psychology + AI . Human-AI Interaction, Behavioural Research 
 Finance + AI . FinTech, Risk & Data Analytics 
 Law + AI , AI Governance & Compliance 
 Design + AI , AI Product & UX 
 Computer Science + AI , Data Science, ML, Computer Vision, NLP 
 
Data annotation may be an entry point but domain knowledge plus AI skills could be the bigger opportunity.
 
The future of careers may not be about choosing one job for life.
 
It may be about building the ability to learn, adapt and work with technology.
 
Career counselling needs to move from career selection to career adaptability.

Thanks to #print to publish such inspiring post and pushing students and parents to think beyond traditional career approach.

On June 27th, I made a decision that felt small at the time but changed how I show up professionally.
I decided to actually use LinkedIn. Not just have a profile — use it.
At that point, I had 29 followers. Most of them were people I already knew personally. My profile views were sitting around 5 a week. I wasn't sure anyone outside my own circle would care what a court administrator from Faisalabad had to say.
I started posting anyway. Sharing my 20+ years of admin experience. Writing about my freelancing journey. Commenting genuinely on posts instead of scrolling past them.
Today, that number is 235 followers. My connections have grown to 174. Profile views are up nearly 10x from where I started.
One post — sharing that I type 70 WPM — ended up getting over 700 impressions. A number I never expected for something so simple.
None of this happened overnight, and I know by many standards, these numbers are still small. But that's not really the point.
The point is that a couple of months ago, I didn't believe my experience was something worth sharing publicly. Today, I show up here every single day because I've learned that consistency, not perfection, is what actually builds visibility.
If you're sitting on 20+ years of experience wondering if anyone would care to hear about it — they will, if you show up long enough to let them.
What's one small decision you made that ended up changing more than you expected?

From a late-night conversation to a room of 17 people.

That was STEM Innovators Conference 2024.

No big team. No long list of partners. No impressive track record. 

Just an idea, a lot of uncertainty, and a willingness to try.

Then came 2025.

17 to 45+ attendees.
0 to 4 partners.
1 to 6 sponsors.
3 to 4 speakers.
0 to 3 video responses.

These numbers may look small from the outside, but to me, every number carries a story, every person who showed up, every organization that said yes, every speaker who gave their time, every sponsor who trusted an idea that was still growing, and every teammate who stayed and kept building.

STEM Innovators  did not start from a place of experience.

It started with a girl and a question:

“Why can’t young people in STEM in Cameroon have more than what classrooms could offer?”

I didn't have any clear answer or even know exactly what STEM Innovators would become.

But I couldn't ignore the question.

So a question became conversations.
Conversations became a bold reach for guidance.
And those conversations became something we could build.

August 30th 2026 marked two years of STEM Innovators.

What started with one initiative has grown into:

💙  STEM Innovators Conference-  our flagship initiative
💙 World Connect- our video outreach
💙 STEM Innovators Community- our official community
💙 Empathy-Centered Design Challenge- our hybrid bootcamp and innovation challenge
💙  STEM Innovators Konnect-  our community podcast
💙 STEM Impact Magazine- Spotlighting people shaping the future of STEM in Cameroon 

From 0 to 300+ LinkedIn followers
From 0 to 120+ Facebook followers 
From 0 to 20+ Instagram followers 
Yes, from 40 to 380+ community members 

Every milestone means more to me than I can properly explain. 

At the success of every initiative, my heart swells and I sometimes have to hold back my tears. 

Because I remember the uncertainty, the limited resources, the moments things didn't go as planned, infact I never planned on coming this far.

A girl in the dark still chose to move forward. No experience, just question she couldn't let go of.

Today, hundreds of young people have encountered that same call- to ask questions, build, learn and create opportunities beyond what already exists.

And that means more to me than any number could capture.

My heart is filled with so much gratitude.

To my teammates, mentors, organizers, speakers, sponsors, partners and our incredible community, thank you for believing, showing up, and building with us💙🫂

And to everyone who has ever encouraged us, volunteered, shared our work, or simply said “Keep going”  thank you.

Happy anniversary, STEM Innovators 💙

Motorized Guillotine Window – A Smart Solution for Modern Openings

Have you seen a window where the glass moves vertically up and down at the touch of a button?

This is a Motorized Guillotine Window, also known as a Motorized Vertical Sliding Glass Window.

Unlike conventional sliding windows, which move horizontally, a guillotine window operates vertically using a motorized lifting mechanism.

🔹 How does it work?

The system typically consists of:

• Motor and gearbox
• Vertical guide channels
• Lifting mechanism such as belt, cable or chain
• Rollers/carriers
• Counterbalance or load-support mechanism
• Safety sensors and control system
• Glass panels and aluminium framing

When the system is activated, the motor drives the lifting mechanism, allowing the glass panels to move upward or downward smoothly.

⬆️ Glass moves up → Opening closes
⬇️ Glass moves down → Opening opens

Why is it useful?

✅ Maximizes the usable opening
✅ Convenient one-touch operation
✅ Clean and modern architectural appearance
✅ Suitable for large openings
✅ Can be integrated with smart-home/automation systems
✅ Useful for restaurants, balconies, terraces and commercial spaces

The real engineering challenge isn't simply making the glass move. The motor, glass weight, balancing system, guides, safety protection and structural design all need to work together reliably.

For large motorized glass systems, proper consideration of glass weight, wind load, motor capacity, safety sensors and maintenance access is essential.

Technology is changing the way architectural openings are designed — and motorized guillotine windows are a great example of this evolution.

One sentence in JPMorgan's 2025 Annual Report changed how I looked at the entire company.

It wasn't a revenue number.

It wasn't net income.

It wasn't ROTCE.

It was this:

“We need to maximize the benefits of our scale and scope, which are necessary to our largest institutional and government clients, while minimizing their considerable negatives.”

At first glance, it sounds like ordinary corporate language.

I don't think it is.

That sentence captures one of JPMorgan's biggest strategic contradictions.

Scale is JPMorgan's moat.

But scale is also one of its problems.

Being enormous gives JPMorgan:

• Massive client relationships
• Global infrastructure
• Huge technology budgets
• Data advantages
• Capital strength
• Ability to serve complex institutional clients

But the same scale can create:

• Bureaucracy
• Complexity
• Slower decision-making
• Higher costs
• Organizational inertia

And management knows it.

In fact, the 2025 shareholder letter explicitly says size can become a business disadvantage because it can bring complexity, bureaucracy and complacency.

That's why this sentence matters.

JPMorgan doesn't simply need to become bigger.

It needs to become more effective at being big.

And that's a very different challenge.

This also connects directly with the company's AI and technology strategy.

If technology can make a giant organization faster, more automated and more intelligent, then JPMorgan's scale becomes an even bigger competitive advantage.

But if technology simply adds another layer of complexity?

The advantage becomes less obvious.

My takeaway:

The most important question for JPMorgan may not be:

“How big can it become?”

It may be:

“Can JPMorgan remain fast while operating at enormous scale?”

Because if the answer is yes, its moat gets wider.

If the answer is no, its biggest strength could gradually become its biggest weakness.

That's the kind of sentence I look for in an MD&A.

A sentence that sounds simple.

But underneath it contains the entire strategic problem.

YOUR MIND IS POWERFUL—BUT IT IS NOT ALWAYS RIGHT. 🧠

1️⃣ MIND IS BLIND — It doesn’t always see reality; it sees reality through your beliefs, fears, and past experiences.

2️⃣ MIND LOVES COMFORT — It will often choose what feels safe over what helps you grow.

3️⃣ MIND FOLLOWS PATTERNS — Repeat a thought long enough, and your mind starts treating it like truth.

4️⃣ MIND CREATES CONFLICT — One part of you wants growth, while another part screams, “Stay safe!”

5️⃣ THE REAL PROBLEM? — We often obey our thoughts without questioning them.

6️⃣ THE SOLUTION: S.T.O.P. FRAMEWORK 🛑

S — SEE  the thought.
T — TEST  the thought.
O — OBSERVE  the pattern.
P — PICK your response.

7️⃣ Before saying, “I can’t,” ask: Is this a fact—or simply a familiar thought?

8️⃣ Before choosing comfort, ask: “Will this decision help my future self?”

9️⃣ Remember: A thought is not a fact. A feeling is not a command. Comfort is not always growth.

🔟 MASTER YOUR MIND → CHANGE YOUR CHOICES → CHANGE YOUR FUTURE.

You don’t have to control every thought.
You have to control which thoughts get to control you.

AI is creating jobs. But will those jobs last?
 
A recent Print report from Noida and Gurugram highlights the rise of AI data-annotation jobs people helping AI learn by labelling images, text, audio and video, checking AI responses and preparing training data.
 
The interesting part?
 
Many of these jobs are repetitive and relatively low-paid, and some could themselves be automated as AI improves.
 
This is an important lesson for students and parents.
 
Instead of asking:
 
Which degree will get me a job?
 
Start asking:
 
Which combination of skills will remain valuable as jobs change?
 
Students can explore:
 
 Biology + AI , Medical AI, Bioinformatics 
 Psychology + AI . Human-AI Interaction, Behavioural Research 
 Finance + AI . FinTech, Risk & Data Analytics 
 Law + AI , AI Governance & Compliance 
 Design + AI , AI Product & UX 
 Computer Science + AI , Data Science, ML, Computer Vision, NLP 
 
Data annotation may be an entry point but domain knowledge plus AI skills could be the bigger opportunity.
 
The future of careers may not be about choosing one job for life.
 
It may be about building the ability to learn, adapt and work with technology.
 
Career counselling needs to move from career selection to career adaptability.

Thanks to #print to publish such inspiring post and pushing students and parents to think beyond traditional career approach.

Semester 1 & 2 (Fase Adaptasi & Eksplorasi):

Selama masa perkuliahan, apabila memiliki kesempatan, saya juga ingin mengikuti berbagai kegiatan di luar kampus, seminar, pelatihan, volunteer, maupun pengalaman kerja yang dapat menambah wawasan, relasi, dan pengalaman saya.

On June 27th, I made a decision that felt small at the time but changed how I show up professionally.
I decided to actually use LinkedIn. Not just have a profile — use it.
At that point, I had 29 followers. Most of them were people I already knew personally. My profile views were sitting around 5 a week. I wasn't sure anyone outside my own circle would care what a court administrator from Faisalabad had to say.
I started posting anyway. Sharing my 20+ years of admin experience. Writing about my freelancing journey. Commenting genuinely on posts instead of scrolling past them.
Today, that number is 235 followers. My connections have grown to 174. Profile views are up nearly 10x from where I started.
One post — sharing that I type 70 WPM — ended up getting over 700 impressions. A number I never expected for something so simple.
None of this happened overnight, and I know by many standards, these numbers are still small. But that's not really the point.
The point is that a couple of months ago, I didn't believe my experience was something worth sharing publicly. Today, I show up here every single day because I've learned that consistency, not perfection, is what actually builds visibility.
If you're sitting on 20+ years of experience wondering if anyone would care to hear about it — they will, if you show up long enough to let them.
What's one small decision you made that ended up changing more than you expected?

From a late-night conversation to a room of 17 people.

That was STEM Innovators Conference 2024.

No big team. No long list of partners. No impressive track record. 

Just an idea, a lot of uncertainty, and a willingness to try.

Then came 2025.

17 to 45+ attendees.
0 to 4 partners.
1 to 6 sponsors.
3 to 4 speakers.
0 to 3 video responses.

These numbers may look small from the outside, but to me, every number carries a story, every person who showed up, every organization that said yes, every speaker who gave their time, every sponsor who trusted an idea that was still growing, and every teammate who stayed and kept building.

STEM Innovators  did not start from a place of experience.

It started with a girl and a question:

“Why can’t young people in STEM in Cameroon have more than what classrooms could offer?”

I didn't have any clear answer or even know exactly what STEM Innovators would become.

But I couldn't ignore the question.

So a question became conversations.
Conversations became a bold reach for guidance.
And those conversations became something we could build.

August 30th 2026 marked two years of STEM Innovators.

What started with one initiative has grown into:

💙  STEM Innovators Conference-  our flagship initiative
💙 World Connect- our video outreach
💙 STEM Innovators Community- our official community
💙 Empathy-Centered Design Challenge- our hybrid bootcamp and innovation challenge
💙  STEM Innovators Konnect-  our community podcast
💙 STEM Impact Magazine- Spotlighting people shaping the future of STEM in Cameroon 

From 0 to 300+ LinkedIn followers
From 0 to 120+ Facebook followers 
From 0 to 20+ Instagram followers 
Yes, from 40 to 380+ community members 

Every milestone means more to me than I can properly explain. 

At the success of every initiative, my heart swells and I sometimes have to hold back my tears. 

Because I remember the uncertainty, the limited resources, the moments things didn't go as planned, infact I never planned on coming this far.

A girl in the dark still chose to move forward. No experience, just question she couldn't let go of.

Today, hundreds of young people have encountered that same call- to ask questions, build, learn and create opportunities beyond what already exists.

And that means more to me than any number could capture.

My heart is filled with so much gratitude.

To my teammates, mentors, organizers, speakers, sponsors, partners and our incredible community, thank you for believing, showing up, and building with us💙🫂

And to everyone who has ever encouraged us, volunteered, shared our work, or simply said “Keep going”  thank you.

Happy anniversary, STEM Innovators 💙

This White Paper is based on an online survey of risk managers at leading global companies, combined with insights gathered through seminars with hundreds of Japanese global companies.
It takes a fresh and unprecedented perspective on the gap between top-tier global practices and current market realities.

Core message is:
the purpose of risk management is not simply to manage risk, but to connect risk to business strategy.
Identifying risks through ERM is not enough to create enterprise value. Only when residual risk is quantified, decisions are made based on risk appetite regarding retention, transfer, and mitigation, and the outcomes are linked to strategy, capital allocation, and business growth, can risk management truly contribute to value creation.

今年、ルネサスは発足から15周年という節目を迎えました。この15 年間、私たちは変化を恐れず挑戦を続け、真のグローバル企業としての土台を築いてきました。 

この大切な節目を記念し、そしてこれからのルネサスの姿を社員みんなで共有したいという思いから、社内の壁をキャンバスにするアートプロジェクトをスタートしました。 
今回の壁画制作には、芸術大学に通う学生のみなさんにご協力いただきました。世界に挑み続けるルネサスの姿勢と、未来へ向かって努力を惜しまない学生たちの情熱には、どこか共通するものを感じました。その想いが結びつき、今回のコラボレーションが生まれました。 
この取り組みが学生アーティストのみなさんにとって成長のきっかけになると同時に、オフィスに新しいエネルギーが生まれることを願っています。私自身、完成した壁画がオフィスの雰囲気を明るくし、社員のウェルビーイングを支え、クリエイティブなアイディアが自然に生まれる場になっていることを実感しています。 
こうした変化は、私たちが推進する「Back‑to‑Office」 の取り組みにも、大きな力を与えてくれます。 
中村さん、赤佐さん、素敵なアートでオフィスを彩ってくださり、本当にありがとうございました。

「HRは次のR&Dになる（HR is the next R&D）」
AIという強力な波が押し寄せる中で、HRは単に制度やオペレーションを運用する機能ではなく、「人とテクノロジーを掛け合わせ、未来の働き方を実験し続ける“研究開発部門”」へと変わりつつある

AI時代のリーダーに求められるマインドセットは、好奇心・謙虚さ・判断力・信頼の4つ

「スーパー・ワーカー（Super Worker）」 AIを活用しながら複数のタスクやプロジェクトを横断的に担い、自律的に価値を生み出す人材——それが、AI時代の“仕事の単位”の中心になる
チームの働き方を再設計できる“スーパー・マネジャー（Super Manager）” AIと人の協働モデルをデザインし、学習と実験の文化を支え、チームの生産性を新しい水準に引き上げるリーダー

今後のHRは4つの領域で大きく再編されていく
①Employee Self-Service（セルフサービス化）
②Digital HRBP
③Agentic Recruiting、
④L&D再構築

“効率化のためのAI”ではなく、“人間性を拡張するためのAI”

AI導入は単なるITプロジェクトではなく、「業務プロセスと組織文化の再設計」

小さく始め、早く学ぶ
AIを「人の代わり」ではなく「特定スキルを提供する仕組み」として設計する
業務プロセスを整えたうえでAIを乗せ、成功を称えながら文化として根づかせる

「HRの仕事とは、制度を整えることでも、ルールを守らせることでもない。
それは、人が自分のパーパスを生きられる環境をつくることなのです。」

A small habit, an unexpected insight

Closing my eyes while listening is a habit I’ve had for a long time—even during Teams calls or meetings. My intention is simple: to focus more deeply on what the other person is saying.

Recently, I had an interesting experience that became an “aha” moment for me. During a Teams call, I did this as usual. After a moment, a person asked, “Are you okay?” She was concerned that I might not be feeling well or disengaged.

It surprised me.

This behavior, which feels natural—perhaps even culturally familiar from a Japanese perspective—was interpreted very differently in a global, remote setting. It reminded me of something important: In today’s environment, where we work across countries and cultures, it’s not always easy to understand how our actions are perceived. 

I took away two reflections from this: First, I need to be more mindful of how my behaviors might be interpreted by others—and avoid unintentionally creating confusion. Second, I truly appreciated that the person chose to ask directly. She didn’t make assumptions—she checked her understanding. That simple clarification prevented a potential misunderstanding.

To me, this is a great example of inclusive communication in action. Curious to hear your thoughts—have you had similar moments where intention and perception didn’t quite align?

Have a great weekend!

A small cultural note that makes a big difference

In working with colleagues in Japan, one small detail can go a long way: the use of “-san.” Using “-san” isn’t just a linguistic habit — it’s a simple expression of respect, professionalism, and equality. While it’s perfectly fine to call someone by their first name without “-san,” using a last name without any honorific (for example, calling someone just “Yamada”) can come across as disrespectful.

From my own experience, being addressed by last name only usually happened in very specific contexts — school, among close friends, or in highly hierarchical environments. Even then, I personally avoided addressing others that way.

If someone calls me “Sugita (my last name)” without an honorific, I usually ask them to use “Kats (my first name)” or “Sugita‑san,” regardless of our relationship. Not because of formality — but because respect matters, and it’s often conveyed through small, thoughtful actions.

Being mindful of these nuances helps build trust and makes cross‑cultural collaboration smoother for everyone.

Unleashing Potential with Yoshuku: Visualizing Success Before It Happens

Like everyone else, I also have good days and bad days. Running is my best way to refresh my mind. During a run today, an idea suddenly came back to me: Yoshuku.

A few years ago, a professional Yoshuku practitioner was invited to our Tokyo headquarters, and around 30–40 people joined the session. I was one of them. At that time, I didn’t fully realize how deeply this concept connects with both our culture and modern business thinking. Yoshuku is a Japanese tradition of celebrating success in advance. Originally linked to prayers for a good harvest, it can be seen today as a form of success-oriented mental simulation. 

If we constantly imagine failure, our actions often follow that direction. But when we create concrete and detailed images of success, we begin to see what really matters—key actions, potential pitfalls, and risks we should avoid.

Inspired by this, I’ve decided to restart a personal Yoshuku routine every Monday—a moment to clearly and positively visualize success before it happens. I’m curious to see how this mindset will influence my thinking and actions over time, and I hope to share some good progress with you in the future.

• Clap twice: a way to open your heart and express sincerity.
• Bow once again: a gesture of gratitude and closure.

Ekiden: A Lesson in Shared Purpose, Resilience—and Grace in Defeat

Every January, millions in Japan tune in to watch the Hakone Ekiden, a two-day, 217 km (135 mile) university relay race. It’s more than a sporting event—it’s a living example of leadership, teamwork, and character. The word Ekiden means “station to station,” rooted in an ancient courier system. Today, the sash (tasuki) symbolizes trust, responsibility, and continuity. Each runner pushes beyond personal limits, not for individual glory, but to honor the team and the shared goal. 

Sometimes, we witness something even more inspiring: grace in defeat.
I’ll never forget a team captain who gave a heartfelt speech after his team—expected to win after dominating two prior races—fell short. He thanked his general managers and teammates, made humble reflection of the race and then shouted, “I love my team!” despite the loss. Finally, he promised that his successors would win next year.
Moments like these remind us:
• We cannot always enjoy great business outcomes.
• Being a good loser—and learning from setbacks—is just as important as winning.
He embodied that spirit.

Ekiden is true teamwork:
• Success is a relay of effort, trust, and adaptability.
• Passing the baton—knowledge, responsibility, encouragement—is as critical as running your leg.
• Leadership means creating conditions where every runner feels their role is vital.

Every year, I cheer the runners in person. It’s my New Year ritual, and their determination gives me incredible energy. If you’re in Japan, I highly recommend experiencing it in person—or at least watching it on TV. You’ll gain a deeper understanding of Japanese culture and its emphasis on collective purpose: valuing the team over the individual, prioritizing endurance over speed, and cherishing the act of “passing on” responsibility. These principles are deeply woven into how Japanese organizations operate.

As we start a new year, let’s ask ourselves: “How can we design our teams to run like an Ekiden—aligned, resilient, and inspired by a common purpose?”

Great slides aren’t decoration—they’re strategy.

Too often we see the same deck used for a team update, an executive decision meeting, and a broad town hall. The result? Dense slides, tiny fonts, and audiences who can’t engage.

For me, slide design is both Inclusion and Business Effectiveness:
• Inclusion: Design for everyone in the room (and on the call). Use clear hierarchy, large readable fonts, high contrast, minimal jargon, and one message per slide. If people can’t read it, they can’t contribute.
• Plain Language for Global Audiences: Global leaders avoid overly sophisticated word choices because many listeners are non‑native English speakers. I appreciate that almost all Astellas senior leaders are mindful of this and consistently communicate so everyone can follow and contribute.
• Business Effectiveness: Tailor to the occasion. Executives need a crisp story and a clear “ask.” Broad communications need simplicity and clarity. Fewer, sharper slides improve decision velocity and alignment.

As leaders, our responsibility is to communicate accessibly and decide decisively. Let’s choose readability over density and clarity over completeness—and get better outcomes for our people and our business.

Inclusion at Astellas: business discipline that creates VALUE for patients
Inclusion at Astellas isn’t a slogan—it’s the way we turn innovative science into real‑world outcomes for patients. When we all stay relentlessly business‑oriented, inclusion becomes practical and measurable: we learn what the business needs, and we co‑create solutions that move the business.
To keep that discipline, our meetings run on a one‑page proposal. On a single page we capture:
• Topic
• Why now (why this deserves the meeting)
• Options (viable solutions)
• Today’s recommendation & why
• Timeline
• Cost proposal
Charts or a table can be attached, but only the one‑pager is presented on the day—because clarity invites diverse voices, focuses debate on decisions, and accelerates execution. At Astellas, if a proposal is not presented as a one‑pager, it will not be tabled for discussion or approval.
Inclusion is also imagination. It asks: What do they need? How can I support them? Without imagination, we cannot work well in any organization. Imagination helps us anticipate needs, design better options, and include perspectives that might otherwise be missed.
From my experience as CPO at Astellas, initiatives go well when we follow this guideline. When we don’t, even high‑quality proposals face challenges. The difference is business‑side buy‑in and understanding the audience—without those, HR initiatives risk becoming self‑satisfaction rather than business impact.
HR experts often default to technical explanations, but what the business truly needs is a clear line of sight to how the proposal drives our business—pipeline impact, operational efficiency, and patient outcomes. HR is part of the business, not adjacent to it. Thinking from that point of view is critical.
When we combine diverse perspectives with business rigor, we make faster, smarter decisions—and that’s how we win for patients and for Astellas.

Impact-Focused: Prioritizing What Truly Matters
Many people find it essential to prioritize and focus on what really matters. As Kobe Bryant once said that he had given full priority to everything he could do to become the best basketball player. It can be difficult to say in front of a crowd that you want to be the best CEO or marketer in the world. It's easy to say that in the world of sports, but in the business world, it's a bit hesitant. 
Then how about another way to say this? "If you were to die tomorrow or next week, what would you like to accomplish today or this week?" "How do I really want to spend my day today?" That's the question. It means that we should put our effort into believing that it really matters, rather than reacting to feeling urgent. Our lives are shorter than we think. 
In professional life, it's easy to get caught up in tasks that need to be addressed immediately, and it's easy to neglect long-term goals that are important but not urgent. Many people tend to focus their energy on important and urgent things, and then turn to unimportant but urgent things. It is quite difficult to pay proper attention to important matters that do not require immediate action if you are not aware of it. 
To be honest, I'm good at troubleshooting and day-to-day problem-solving, but I'm not very good at strategic thinking. This is because in my career, I have prioritized urgent and less important tasks for my internal clients. My advice to the next generation is to focus enough on strategic priorities rather than focusing too much on the wants of our internal and external customers. If we want to accomplish something important, we should not seek recognition or admiration from others.

Before having a dog, my weekend time management was more relaxed. But now, with this routine, I can get a lot done in the mornings on Saturdays and Sundays. I can go for a long-distance run, catch up on reading, and spend quality time with my wife discussing various topics. This sense of accomplishment and the extra energy it brings is quite rewarding.

Globish – empathy and customer service quality. 
 
I have often emphasized that at Astellas, our business language is not simply English, but "global English": clear and easy-to-follow communication that supports understanding for all colleagues. 
Recently, I noticed a contrast during my travels on an airplane and at the airport. While announcements in these international settings were delivered at a very fast pace, which can make it challenging for non-native English speakers to follow, Japanese airlines and airports tend to make announcements that are clear, deliberate, and accessible to everyone. For example, in Tokyo, announcements are paced thoughtfully, allowing all passengers to understand the important information being shared.
This distinction highlights what I see as a difference in empathy and customer service. In some environments, the priority seems to be completing tasks quickly, while in others, there is a clear focus on ensuring every customer feels included and informed. I appreciate how Japan emphasizes clarity and service, though I also recognize the challenges faced by staff making announcements in busy, multilingual international airports. Each approach has its own strengths, and these observations have made me reflect on the value of empathy in global communication.
I'm grateful that at Astellas we prioritize clear communication as part of our commitment to inclusivity and customer service. I welcome your thoughts on how we can further encourage empathy and effective communication across global settings. Please let me know if you have specific ideas or experiences to share.

Mind the Gap - Employee Engagement is a key for our business success.
 
 Today, I wanted to share some thoughts on the importance of engagement surveys and the significant role they play in shaping our organization. Engagement surveys are more than just diagnostic tools—they symbolize our commitment to our teams. I firmly believe that the real work begins after the survey closes. All of us can find some unexpected gaps in the surveys always, which is the benefit of having them. 
Sharing results openly with the team demonstrates respect for every voice, building trust and setting the foundation for collaboration. Only after that, can we move to action taking stage. And then, tracking and communicating progress of the actions is equally important. Timely updates reinforce accountability and show that feedback drives action. 
Over the years, I’ve searched for a magic solution, but I’ve come to realize there’s no single formula. The key lies in open sharing and action taking, then diligently tracking those actions and sharing progress. Leaders who embrace this approach consistently see the best results.

What is a short-term assignment in Astellas? It really works well! 

I wanted to share some exciting news regarding the progress we've made with "short-term assignments" in Astellas. For those who might not be familiar, a short-term assignment is a 1-6 month stint in a different country. During this period, employees maintain their original responsibilities while also taking on some project-type initiatives at the new location.
 
The rationale behind these assignments is straightforward. Long-term assignments, such as those lasting 2-3 years, can sometimes be unfeasible for individuals due to family or other personal reasons. However, short-term assignments offer a more manageable alternative. While some may argue that a short duration isn't sufficient, I believe that any exposure is better than none. Of course, a longer period of 2-3 years or more would be ideal for in-depth learning, but short-term assignments can still provide valuable experiences and growth opportunities. Additionally, participating in a short-term assignment can pave the way for long-term assignments if needed later.
 
I've seen many individuals benefit immensely from these short-term assignments. Although there isn't an official program for short-term assignments, it's essentially an extended business trip, making it relatively easy to initiate. All it takes is a career conversation with our supervisor to identify the best opportunities for our development. Ideally, our expertise and experience will contribute to the success of the new location, creating a win-win situation for everyone involved.
 
I recently learned that some regions have 10-15 short-term assignees, which is fantastic! I believe we can achieve even more. I encourage our people to have career discussions with their supervisors and make their dreams a reality.

How to get control of our time

I recently came across a message that resonated with me, and I wanted to share it with all of you as I believe it could significantly enhance our workflow and communication. The message stated: "If I do not receive any response from you prior to [specified deadline], I will assume you have no edits to this latest draft, and I will proceed."
 
I think this approach is fantastic for maintaining a sense of urgency and ensuring that projects move forward without unnecessary delays. It is both polite and effective, and it fosters accountability. By not responding, you are essentially signaling trust and delegation, which can be very empowering.
 
Many years ago, I had the experience of working with a great supervisor who was in a different country. Despite their many strengths, their response speed was a weak point that often slowed down my work. This situation led to frustration and a realization that I needed a better way to manage communication. My mentor recommended the same proactive communication technique “if I don’t receive…”, and it dramatically changed my professional life.
 
By using this approach, I was able to control my work and plan my timing more effectively. It required me to be outcome-focused and accountable for the results, but it also provided a sense of empowerment and control over my schedule. I highly recommend this method to all of you. It allows you to plan your actions and manage your timing independently, leading to improved efficiency and productivity. It will increase your white space, definitely.

Integrity Comes First, In Every Decision We Make

Earlier this year, we launched our Organizational Values & Behaviors, with Integrity intentionally placed first.

For me, this is more than symbolic as everything we do starts with doing the right thing. It’s the foundation of trust, and the basis for how we work together as One Astellas. Two recent milestones show how we are putting this into action.

The first is the launch of our updated Code of Conduct. Originally introduced in 2016, it has now been completely redesigned to be clearer, more practical, and more relevant to the realities of our work today. It’s a guide to help all of us make sound decisions, collaborate across borders, and speak up when something doesn’t feel right. I’m proud that over 100 colleagues contributed to shaping the new Code, which makes it something we all own together.

The second is the success of our Ethical Leadership workshops, delivered jointly by Ethics & Compliance and HR. 500 senior leaders and managers from every region have already participated and the feedback has been very encouraging. Every single participant said the workshop deepened their understanding of the role leaders play in modelling Integrity, and almost all said they feel more confident building trust and transparency in their teams.

For me, Integrity is not a policy, it’s a daily practice. It’s how we lead when no one is watching, how we support each other, and how we build a culture where everyone feels safe to speak up and do the right thing. It’s no mistake this is the first of our three Values: Integrity; Innovation and Impact.

As leaders, it starts with us. The Code and the workshops are important tools, but what matters most is the consistency of our actions, big and small, every day.

Let’s Break the Silence Around Menopause at Work

For too long, menopause has been treated as a private issue, when it is clearly a workplace one too. Our global Menopause Experience and Attitudes Study, covering 13,800 respondents across six countries, shows just how widespread the impact is:
- Over a third of people going through menopause experience some kind of negative impact at work.
- 1 in 20 believe they’ve lost out on promotions or pay rises.
- Many feel unable to talk to colleagues or managers.

This is a reality we can and must change.

That’s why I’m proud to support Astellas’ Pledge to Champion a Menopause-Inclusive Workplace. Through education, training, and open dialogue, we aim to create a culture where no one feels they have to suffer in silence.

This is about health, inclusion, and respect.

It’s also a reminder that leadership means listening, even when the topic is uncomfortable. It is especially important we listen then.

As I mentioned the other day, business leadership is essential for the realization of HR measures. In this article, I would like to introduce specific success stories.

Four years ago, I wanted to update the company's values and code of conduct for the first time in 15 years right, and I proposed it to a few executives, but at that time the time was not ripe, so I smashed it brilliantly. However, two years ago, there were organizational and operational process changes in large business units, and it was time for a major change in mindset and behavior. We have been in discussions with business leaders since April last year and introduced a new Values & Behaviors (V&B) in April this year. We have conducted more than 100 versions of the discussion to get to this point, thoroughly reflecting the opinions of business leaders.

The main point of this introduction was that we were able to make the business side feel the need for this initiative. Business leaders talked about V&B themselves, and we human resources also went to various places to explain and ask questions, and we worked on a company-wide approach. We also researched 66 leadership models around the world and decided to retire all of them in favor of the V&B. 

In addition, we fully integrated V&B into our recognition, performance management, hiring, and promotion criteria, which we also incorporated into our PR tools and engagement surveys. This area of arrangement is usually what human resources are good at. I feel that the key to the success of this initiative is that it was not led by human resources, but was led by business leaders and proceeded with business needs. 

In fact, when I was thanked for human resources at a management meeting, I was truly happy that an executive said, "This is not what HR did, we are the main actor." I find it very rewarding that HR measures have been driven and successfully driven by business leaders. This is also thanks to the cooperation of fellow leaders and HR members.

先日お話しした通り、人事施策の実現にはビジネスリーダーのオーナーシップが欠かせません。今回は、その具体的な成功事例をご紹介したいと思います。

4年前、私は会社の価値観と行動規範を15年ぶりにアップデートしたいと考え、数名の役員に提案しましたが、その時は機が熟していなかったため、見事に玉砕しました。しかし、2年前から大きなビジネス部門での組織と業務プロセス変更があり、マインドセットと行動面の大きな改革が求められる時期が来ました。この波を捉え、昨年4月からビジネスリーダーと何度も議論を重ね、今年4月から新しいValues & Behaviors（V&B）を導入しました。これに至るまでに100バージョン以上の議論を行い、ビジネスリーダーの意見を徹底的に反映しました。

今回の導入では、ビジネスサイドにこの取り組みの必要性を感じてもらうことができたのが大きなポイントでした。ビジネスリーダーが自らV&Bについて語り、我々人事も各地へ赴き説明やQ&Aを行うなど、全社的に取り組みました。また、導入に際して世界中の66個のリーダーシップモデルを調査し、全てを廃止してV&Bに集中することを決めました。

さらに、表彰、評価や採用、昇進の基準にV&Bをフルに統合し、PRツールやエンゲージメントサーベイにも反映させました。この辺の段取りは、通常、人事が得意とするところです。今回の取り組みは、人事主導ではなく、ビジネスリーダーが主体となって、ビジネス上のニーズありきで進められたことが成功の鍵だと感じています。

実際に、ある経営会議の場面で人事に対する感謝のコメントがあったとき、ある役員が「これは人事がやったことではない、我々が主体だ」と言ってくれたことが心の底から嬉しかったです。人事の施策がビジネスリーダーによって推進され、成功を収めたことに大きなやりがいを感じています。これもひとえに同僚のリーダーや人事メンバーの協力のおかげです。

今年も雲一つない晴天に恵まれ、森田社長と社員のご家族の皆さんとのタウンホールミーティングなど、昨年以上にパワーアップしたイベントになりました。笑顔で手を振って家路につかれていくご家族の皆さんを見て、主催側も大いに元気をもらい、私自身もあたたかな気持ちになりました。日々会社を支えてくれている社員とご家族の皆さんありがとうございます。

For a long time, the traditional org chart made sense. It gave us clear accountability for business outcomes and a structure that scaled. But as AI changes how work gets done, that same model started to slow decisions, filtering context through layers rather than the people closest to the problem being in the room.
  
To move with speed, we had to recognize that this structure wasn't serving us anymore. So we are leaning into the same shift we're asking of our teams: be willing to unlearn what got you here. For us, that means moving beyond the org chart and building teams around the work.
  
We're testing different models and intentionally keeping them nimble, shifting based on the problem in front of us, the way a startup does. Doing that inside a company of our scale requires being intentional about what we simplify, what we flatten, and where we hold structure.
  
Some of what we're testing:
• Spinning squads up around specific challenges. We're tightening how decisions get made through smaller cohorts that run fast, have direct access to accountable leaders, and use short, consistent feedback loops so ideas get tested, measured, and acted on quickly.

•  Moving from static roles to more fluid ways of contributing. We're experimenting with models where some talent flows to where it's needed, while some roles stay anchored to a product or problem. 

• Opening up larger forums where individual contributors (engineers, builders, and customer-facing teams) share what they're seeing and help disseminate AI-first ways of working more broadly.
  
Some of our most impactful people are already working well beyond their formal reporting lines. Because who you report to doesn't define where you do your best work and shouldn't determine how quickly your ideas can move.

Charles Lamanna just made this concrete. His engineering org rebuilt itself around the work, using small super teams organized around agentic coding, and moved products like Copilot Cowork and Microsoft Scout from concept to launch in months. Charles shared that he’s started treating the evolution of his teams and structures as his main work product as a leader. His article is worth a read: https://lnkd.in/e8eub4mE
  
I'm curious how others are thinking about this. Are you making the move from org charts to work charts? If not, how are you redesigning the way your teams actually work together?

We often talk about AI in terms of productivity and time saved. Here, its impact shows up differently.

AI is helping all of us work differently. And in this case, it's also helping us better understand and care for the world around us.

I had the joy of hosting Frances Frei, Harvard Business School professor and one of the clearest voices anywhere on trust and change, as part of Microsoft's Outside In series.
  
Here are learnings I keep coming back to: 
• Trust is something we can actually work on. The thing I love about Frances' work is that she turns trust from an abstract idea into something you can actually improve. "Every single time trust exists, there is authenticity, logic, and empathy. Every single time trust is broken, we can trace it back to one of these three things."

• We don’t have to choose between speed and trust. I used to think slowing down to build trust was the tax you paid for bringing people along. Frances pushed that when      trust is high, teams move faster because they're not spending the back half fixing what broke along the way. 

• Empathy, or the lack of it, shows up everywhere- even in how we run our meetings. Most organizations spend about 50% more time in meetings than they need to, and      Frances argues that a bloated meeting culture is actually an empathy breakdown. One of the simplest ways to show people you care is to respect their time.

• Match your confidence to your competence. "Don't let your circle get outside your      square." In this analogy, the square is what you know well. The circle is what you speak about with confidence. We earn trust when our confidence matches what we actually know.

• Not all failure is created equal. New failure is worth celebrating, you just learned a      way not to do it. The same failure over and over means it's time to change something. "Make sure you wring out every ounce of insight that came from getting it wrong. That's how we honor failure."

• The art of the apology. The room reacted immediately when Frances said most apologies fall short because we treat "I'm sorry" like a period instead of a comma, and then quietly start judging people for not accepting it. Frances pushes that we have to share what we’re sorry for, "in exquisite detail” so the person harmed feels seen, valued, and secure.
  
Thank you, Frances Frei and Anne Morriss for a conversation I'll be thinking about for a long time.

We can’t ask people to work in new ways, and then measure, reward, and manage them like nothing has changed. 
 
The 2026 Microsoft Work Trend Index puts data behind a conversation I’m hearing everywhere, something we’re calling the Transformation Paradox. 
 
People feel real urgency to move fast with AI.  
Yet many still default to what feels safe.

Rahul Jindal's latest paper on “Organizational Metabolism” is a masterclass in shifting our focus from AI adoption to AI absorption. His core thesis? The real differentiator in 2026 isn't your technology budget—it’s your "Metabolic Rate."
The framework’s biggest win is the concept of Workflow Debt. We are often layering AI on top of legacy processes instead of retiring them. As Rahul puts it: "Low-metabolism organizations accumulate experiments. High-metabolism organizations retire workflows."
The one piece I think we still need to solve for: The Emotional Metabolism.
While the structural roadmap is brilliant, we can’t ignore the "human immune system." Retiring a workflow can feel like retiring an identity. For an organization to truly become "Adaptive," we have to figure out how to build the psychological safety that allows teams to dismantle their own processes without fearing for their future.

The agentic enterprise is here! 🚀

What stays with me in moments like this isn’t the policy change. It’s the people behind it.
 
In too many rural communities, health care can feel stretched thin with limited resources, complex processes and real pressure on the people delivering care.
 
Care teams are often small, but deeply rooted in the places they serve. They’re not just providers — they’re neighbors, lifelines and a source of stability when everything else feels far away.
 
That’s why reducing administrative burden and speeding up payments matters. It’s giving time back to a nurse covering two roles. It’s helping a physician focus on a patient instead of paperwork. It’s helping rural hospitals stay strong for the communities that depend on them, while easing some of the financial pressure they face.
 
Because supporting the people who deliver care is how we make health care work better. Especially in the places that need it most.

Some of the most meaningful conversations I’ve had as a leader have been with mothers sharing what they needed, and too often didn’t receive, during pregnancy and childbirth.
 
For many families, this experience can feel overwhelming and difficult to navigate. For Black mothers, those challenges are too often compounded by real and persistent disparities. #BlackMaternalHealthWeek is a time to listen, reflect and act.
 
I've heard from women who wanted something simple but powerful: to feel supported, to be understood and to have someone by their side advocating for them.
 
Expanding access to doula support is one way we are working to make care more personal and more connected — helping mothers feel seen and supported before, during and after childbirth. This work is part of a bigger responsibility we have: to help make health care easier to navigate, more equitable and more affordable for the people we serve.
 
We know there is more work ahead. But listening, and turning what we hear into action, is how progress happens. Every mother deserves that support. Every family deserves a healthier start.

As Women’s History Month comes to a close, I’ve been taking a moment to reflect—not just on the month itself, but on the legacy we carry forward every day.
 
We stand on the shoulders of extraordinary women. Women like Marie Curie, who pushed the boundaries of science. Amelia Earhart, who redefined courage. Rosa Parks, who showed the quiet power of conviction. Katherine Johnson, whose brilliance helped launch humanity into space. Florence Nightingale, who transformed care through compassion and discipline. Mother Teresa, who embodied service. Jane Goodall, who taught us to listen more closely to the world around us.
 
And for me, this reflection is also deeply personal. I think about my mom—her resilience, her strength, and the example she set long before I understood what leadership really meant.
 
What connects all of these women isn’t just what they accomplished—it’s how they led. With purpose. With persistence. With a willingness to challenge what is and imagine what could be.
 
As leaders today, our responsibility is to carry that forward. To create space. To lift others. To lead in ways that make it easier for the next generation to rise even higher.
 
Women’s History Month may be ending, but the work—and the opportunity—continues.
 
Let’s keep going.

Wishing you the happiest of holidays! 

With gratitude,

Every year as part of our Standout program, we bring some of the most talented university students from across North America to Procter & Gamble for an immersive look at our business, culture and people.

When I met with this year's group, I shared something I believe deeply: Developing leaders is not something that happens years into a career. It starts on Day 1.

At P&G, leadership development starts on Day 1. We give people meaningful responsibility early and intentionally place them in roles that stretch them. When I look at students in programs like Standout, I don't just see candidates for today's openings. I see future function leaders, business leaders and, potentially, future CEOs. Our ambition for our people is higher than even their ambition for themselves.

As we celebrate the 10th anniversary of Learn. Develop. Perform. (LDP) Week at AbbVie, I had the honor of sitting down with Adam Grant to discuss the importance of “unlearning” to accelerate change. Our conversation explored how discomfort can fuel learning and challenged us to be less afraid of change, and more afraid of not changing. This insight underscores why programs like LDP are so impactful. When we focus on learning and sharing ideas, we challenge our own thinking, adapt and innovate so we can grow as the pace of change continues to accelerate. Thank you to the HR team members, leaders and expert speakers like Adam who have helped AbbVie deliver more than 1,300 LDP learning events over the past 10 years to empower employees to build future-ready skills and grow in their careers.

Last week at our first All-HR meeting of the year, HR colleagues came together to listen and learn from Scott D. Anthony about thriving during times of change. Thank you, Scott, for challenging us to think beyond reacting to change and instead build the muscle to be truly change-ready: leading with curiosity, clarity, courage and a willingness to work differently, not harder. A key takeaway for me was that managing change starts by looking inward, getting comfortable with discomfort, staying clear on the “why,” and focusing on the impact we’re trying to create. With accelerating change one of our company’s culture priorities, it’s critical that we keep building the mindset and behaviors that help us adapt faster and more effectively.

HR professionals are not only navigating change ourselves, but guiding leaders to move through it in ways that unlock innovation, strengthen culture and prepare us for what’s next. What’s one mindset shift or leadership behavior you believe is most important for staying change ready right now?

I've been thinking...about context.
  
As AI becomes increasingly capable of delivering information, I've found myself reflecting on one leadership skill I believe is becoming even more valuable to every organization's success: providing context.
  
Information has never been more accessible. Context has never been more important.
  
Context lives in the space between the data and the decision. It's understanding the history behind an issue before determining the next step, recognizing when a team's reaction is influenced more by previous experiences than the current situation, hearing what isn't being said in a meeting, and knowing when to ask one more question.
  
Recently, my team was reviewing a data trend that seemed to tell a very clear story. Without context, we could have over-indexed on the wrong solution and distracted our businesses from delivering the life-changing work our customers depend on.
  
Once we layered in organizational history and understood what had changed, the data told a very different story.
  
The numbers hadn't changed – our understanding had. That's the power of context.
  
AI will continue to get better at generating information. It will summarize, analyze, and identify patterns faster than ever before. But context still requires experience, judgment, curiosity and an understanding of people.
  
In a world where information is becoming abundant, context may become a leader's greatest contribution – perhaps one of the most uniquely human forms of leadership.
  
What do you think will become more – not less – uniquely human about leadership in the age of AI?

In a recent conversation with one of our Business Resource Groups, I was asked about strategies for moving into #leadership roles and it made me reflect on the important distinction between being managed and being mentored.

Both are essential – managers help us succeed where we are, mentors help us prepare for what’s next.

Great managers build performance. They set clear goals, coach through challenges, hold people accountable and remove barriers to team success. 

Great mentors build perspective. They help you zoom out – think strategically about your growth, test ideas, and explore what’s next. A strong mentor challenges your assumptions and helps you see possibilities you might not see yourself. 

If you are aspiring to lead, or even just accelerate your own development, here’s where you can start:

– Find a mentor who checks the right boxes.
 □ Has the skills, judgment or influence you want to build
 □ Is known for developing others and consistently leading high-performing teams
 □ Will offer honest feedback, including the tough truths to push and support you
 □ Sits outside your reporting line to allow more freedom for curiosity and candid exploration

– Use the time with your mentor to discuss lessons learned from their experiences, both successes and setbacks, as well as what you’re currently experiencing. 

– Engage your manager in open conversation about your goals and how to create stretch opportunities.

– Pair your mentor’s perspective with your manager’s coaching for greatest impact.

And if you already lead, be both – a strong manager who develops people today, and a mentor who invests in the leaders of tomorrow. Results always matter, but the greatest legacy is leaving behind those truly ready to lead.

– Put the Wrench Down: Why ROI Starts with People – 
  
There’s a fine line between what we can do and what we should do. I learned that the hard way—not in the office, but under my kitchen sink on a Saturday morning.

With a wrench in hand and YouTube at my side, I was determined to fix a stubborn hot water valve. But I realized something: sure, I could try. But at what cost? A flooded kitchen? Hours wasted? Instead, I called a plumber.

That small moment reminded me of something far bigger—the curse of competence. Just because we’re capable doesn’t mean it’s the best use of our time, energy or expertise.

In #HR, this shows up everywhere. We tell ourselves, “It’s easier if I just do it myself.” 

But real impact comes when we invest in the right skills, empower others and align work where it belongs—whether that’s business partners driving outcomes, specialized experts elevating the function or colleague self-service.

Over my 30+ years in HR, I’ve seen our profession transform from administrators to business enablers. The greatest #ROI isn’t in doing everything ourselves—it’s in unlocking the potential of people and maximizing efficiency.

Sometimes the smartest move is to put the wrench down. Because when we stop trying to do it all, we create space for growth, innovation and real returns—on skills, on people and on business results.

#strategicHR #HReffectiveness

September always feels like a reset – a reminder that none of us are ever too senior, too experienced or too established to keep learning. One of the most powerful, and sometimes overlooked, ways to grow is through #apprenticeship. 

At Thermo Fisher Scientific, we view apprenticeship as more than mentoring. It’s a two-way exchange between expert and learner, where both are developing, not just delivering. It’s a mutual investment built on trust, feedback and real-time collaboration.

—  For the expert, apprenticeship means sharing your thought process, creating scaffolds that empower independence, and coaching through real challenges – knowing when to step back so others can step up.
—  For the apprentice, it’s about watching closely, asking questions, articulating your reasoning and taking ownership of your growth. Over time, that practice builds both confidence and capability.

When done well, apprenticeship doesn’t just shape individuals – it builds a culture where learning is continuous, feedback is natural and teaching is everyone’s responsibility. That’s the kind of culture I want to be part of.

Looking back, I’ve been fortunate to experience both sides. I’ve learned the mechanics of a balance sheet from a former CFO and the basics of plumbing from my dad. Both shaped how I think, work and lead. And in turn, being able to teach others those same lessons has been one of the most rewarding experiences of my career – and my life.

As this new season begins, I invite you to reflect: What are you learning? Who are you teaching? And how can we each show up as both expert and apprentice?

Here’s to learning, always – together.

Today marks #WorldCancerDay, a day that hits close to home for me.

Cancer has affected my life in very personal ways—my dad fought prostate cancer for more than 17 years and my mom faced stage 3b breast cancer. And just last year, one of my routine screenings came back with an irregular result. Like so many people who face this type of unexpected news during their preventive screenings, my first reaction was fear. Thanks to Merck’s comprehensive benefits, I was able to quickly get follow-up testing and a biopsy — and fortunately, everything came back clear.

These tough moments remind me of how much access and support matter. That’s why I am so proud of the progress our company has made in support of cancer prevention and early detection. In under a year, we have expanded access to WHO-recommended screenings (breast, cervical, colorectal), HPV-related cancer vaccinations, and the time and flexibility to use these services—now reaching more than 96% of employees and their families across 71 countries. The team continues the hard work to extend these benefits where they are not yet available.  

I’m so grateful to everyone at Merck who made this possible and to all those working tirelessly to advance cancer prevention, early detection and care.

A new IBM Institute for Business Value global study highlights a growing disconnect many business leaders are seeing. Nearly two-thirds of executives say AI is reshaping roles and workflows yet most organizations have not redesigned the people systems needed to support that shift. 
 
The result? A widening gap between how leaders report AI progress and how employees actually experience it. 
 
A few findings stood out: 
➡️ Permission: 70% cite unclear authority is causing issues in AI projects. 
➡️ Practice: 93% say AI-enabled work is harder to evaluate. 
➡️ Proof: 81% of executives believe employees are rewarded for AI skills, but only 64% reward employees who challenge AI outputs. 

The takeaway isn’t that AI strategies are failing. It’s that organizational change hasn’t kept pace with technological change. 
 
The organizations that succeed won’t simply deploy AI faster. They’ll help employees understand how work is changing, what skills are becoming more valuable and where new opportunities are emerging. More importantly, they’ll make employees active participants in shaping the future of work. Because the people best positioned to redesign work are often the ones doing it every day.

One of the biggest mistakes in HR transformation isn’t choosing the wrong AI model or platform.
 
It’s conceptual failure.
 
Many leaders in HR (and other disciplines, honestly) still think of AI as a distinct program or initiative. But AI isn't a program – it’s a permanent shift in how work gets done. That means cascading changes to everything from talent, to skills, to (entry-level) hiring.
 
I wrote about this for Fortune, below. #AI #HR #Transformation
 
P.S. You often hear that AI will automate rote tasks and unlock “higher-value work.” How do you define that higher-value work?

Thank you, Chip Cutter, for the conversation about HR and AI last week. (And congratulations to WSJ Leadership Institute on the inaugural CPO Council Summit!)
 
CPOs and CHROs are under intense pressure to undergo AI transformation. But what does success look like? We discussed how:
 
1. AI-powered productivity is the means, not the end. Growth is the end goal. Couple that extra time with talent for true results. This is why IBM is tripling entry-level hiring.
 
2. Value can be measured in (many) more ways than one, from time saved to downstream growth. On the flip side, remember: AI usage isn't free. Every query comes with a cost. 
 
3. No matter how sophisticated the technology becomes, HR leaders always need to prioritize the employee experience. Tech *in service of* the experience.
 
4. Please, please, please: Don't put agents on org charts. Especially if that technology isn't actually an agent.

What does AI mean for your talent strategy? How do you prepare for it?

Huge thanks to Paulo Carvao, former IBMer and Senior Fellow at Harvard University, for this great article in Forbes about how AI is redefining the future of work.

Here are my top three insights:

1️⃣ Economic growth through human-AI collaboration
AI delivers its greatest value when it augments, not replaces, human capabilities. Organizations that design work to combine human judgment with AI efficiency will see productivity gains that help fuel long-term growth.

2️⃣ Skills are the new competitive advantage
The rate and pace of technological change demand continuous learning. Both employees and employers alike must do their part to invest in the skills development necessary for future success.

3️⃣ Productivity with purpose
AI can automate tasks, but the real opportunity lies in freeing up employees to focus on the more strategic work that involves creativity, innovation and problem-solving, which drives differentiation and engagement.

How are you rethinking skills development and redesigning work in the AI Era? I’d love to hear your perspective. #AI #GenAI #skills

During a recent fireside chat with our Pfizer Futures interns, I was asked, "What's your advice for finding a mentor?" I shared that the most meaningful mentoring relationships in my career weren't found; they were built.

Looking back, the mentors who had the greatest impact on my career weren't necessarily the most senior people. They were the ones who got to know me personally and professionally, understood my strengths, challenged my thinking, and cheered me on every step of the way.
 
The best mentoring relationships develop through trust, shared experiences, and showing up consistently for one another. Over time, someone begins to understand not just what you do, but who you are, what motivates you, and where they can help you grow. That kind of investment takes time and rarely happens after a single conversation.
 
To our interns, thank you for your curiosity and for the conversations we've shared this summer. Each of you is incredibly talented, and I encourage you to find mentors who believe in your potential, sometimes even before you fully believe in it yourself. Those relationships have made all the difference in my own career, and I hope they do the same for yours.

Last week, we hosted a global broadcast at Pfizer on becoming an AI-fluent organization. The session came on the heels of launching our “AI Foundational Essentials” course to every colleague across the company, an important step in building the skills needed to thrive in an AI-powered future.

We were joined by two leading researchers, Kate Niederhoffer & Jeff Hancock, who study how AI is reshaping the way we work. Their message was clear: tools and training matter, but they are only the hard wiring. Successful AI adoption highly depends on the soft wiring, or the mindset, we bring.

Kate and Jeff described the difference between Pilots and Passengers. Pilots approach AI with curiosity, optimism, and a sense of agency, using it as a tool to challenge their thinking and explore different perspectives. The research shows these are the individuals most likely to unlock new ideas, accelerate execution, and help organizations realize the potential of AI.

Passengers, on the contrary, tend to hand tasks over to AI and let it do the thinking for them. While that can improve efficiency, it often misses the critical opportunities for reflection and creativity that drive innovation. 
 
Building a Pilot mindset across the organization is as much about how we work together as it is about the tools we put in people's hands. As Kate and Jeff put it, "AI is not a single-player game." 
 
For organizations striving to become AI-fluent, the goal is not simply greater adoption, it’s creating more Pilots.

Thank you to Kate, Jeff, Albert Bourla and BetterUp for a fantastic conversation, and to our colleagues who continue to embrace this evolution with openness and curiosity.

This week, we hosted a global broadcast at Pfizer for Mental Health Awareness Month, and I was honored to be joined by the incredible Arianna Huffington for a conversation on all things mental health. We covered topics like the science of sleep, brain health, the power of physical connection, and how AI can help us reconnect with what makes us human.

Here are my top takeaways:

▪️ Stress is inevitable, but cumulative stress is avoidable. In as little as 60 seconds of conscious breathing, or focusing on something that brings you joy, you can interrupt the stress cycle. Small, consistent micro-steps will outlast big, unsustainable resolutions.
▪️ You can't pour from an empty cup. Whether you're a caregiver, a leader, or both, taking care of yourself isn't selfish — it's how you show up fully for the people who need you.
▪️ As AI becomes more capable, being human becomes more valuable. Resilience, empathy, creativity, and connection aren't soft skills anymore. They're the skills that matter most when intelligence alone is no longer a differentiator.

Thank you, Arianna, for a conversation that was both grounded in science and full of heart - you never fail to leave us with a renewed sense of optimism. And thank you to everyone who tuned in! 

#MentalHealthAwarenessMonth

Geoff makes an important point: AI readiness should be measured not only by technological capability, but by workforce capability as well. Realizing AI's full potential starts with the outcome in mind, redesigning work to achieve it, and building the capabilities of the people who make it possible.
 
At Medtronic, we're focused on helping our people build the skills and capabilities needed to lead in an AI-powered future. That means creating an environment where people can learn, adapt, and embrace new opportunities as technology continues to evolve.
 
I’m optimistic about what’s possible when technology and workforce readiness advance together - helping us accelerate innovation, strengthen performance, and ultimately advance our Mission for patients.

The skills people bring to a role aren’t always captured by a degree or traditional career path. As the needs of our workforce evolve, the way we think about talent must evolve with them.

At Medtronic, we’re taking a more skills-first approach, looking beyond traditional credentials and creating more pathways for people to build and apply their skills.

We’re seeing encouraging results: more than 500 roles no longer require a degree, and through Medtronic Advancement Pathways and Skill-building (MAPS), delivered in partnership with InStride, 4,700 employees have participated and 47% have advanced into new roles.

These stories bring that approach to life, highlighting employees who are growing their careers and pursuing new opportunities through MAPS and our Multiple Pathways Initiative.

The future of work will require organizations to think differently about talent. For us, that means focusing on skills, expanding opportunity, and helping people build meaningful careers while continuing to deliver for patients.

Meaningful early-career experiences should work both ways. We want our interns to learn from us, and we need to be just as willing to learn from them.

Great reflections from Geoff on the energy, perspective, and ideas this year’s intern class brought to Medtronic. Thank you to everyone who helped make this summer such a valuable experience, and to our interns for challenging us to see new possibilities.

At Medtronic, growth is about our people and the impact we can have for patients. Programs like MAPS bring that to life.
	 
MAPS (Medtronic Advancement Pathways and Skill-Building) offers flexible learning options - including undergraduate degrees, certificates, and courses - with 100% upfront tuition coverage for qualifying programs. It’s a benefit we’re proud of because it removes barriers and helps employees build skills while continuing to do their jobs.
	 
Today, we’re recognizing colleagues who completed their studies through MAPS. It’s no small accomplishment.
	 
As one graduate shared, “Completing my degree through MAPS has been one of the proudest achievements of my life… I’m deeply grateful for the investment in my growth.” Another reflected that it was a reminder that “you’re never too old to learn, grow, or take on something new.”
	 
Congratulations to our recent graduates and thank you for showing what’s possible when people are supported to grow.

Proud to recognize the first 100 recipients of the Medtronic Spark Scholarship - an important milestone for a program that’s just getting started.

The Medtronic Spark Scholarship is designed to do more than help students get to college. It’s about helping them succeed through financial support, mentorship, career-building experiences, and resources to navigate unexpected challenges along the way. When students have that kind of support, it changes outcomes.

For me, this work is personal. The future of health tech depends on the next generation of talent, and these students represent that future.

We’re excited to be part of their journeys and to learn from them along the way. Learn more about the initiative and each recipient at MedtronicSpark.com.

The culture.  Even with so much transformation in the business over the last few years, the teams and people still have an appetite to do more and to evolve, for the right reasons, in the right way. The most productive thing you can do today? Embrace JOMO. We’ve all been raised on FOMO (Fear Of Missing Out), but in the corporate world, FOMO is just a polite term for a bottleneck.

If you feel the need to be in every 30-person meeting to "stay aligned," you aren't leading; you’re hovering. If you need to be CC'd on every email thread to "feel informed," you aren't empowering; you’re slowing the engine.

At Verizon, we are architecting an AI-enabled ecosystem to eliminate "the mundane". But tech alone won't give us speed. We need a cultural pivot from "Agreeable to Accountable".

JOMO - The Joy of Missing Out —is the ultimate leadership flex. * It’s the joy of trusting your team to take "Total Ownership" of the talent lifecycle without you in the room.

When we stop trying to be everywhere, we finally give our leaders the space to be innovative and quick. Speed doesn't come from more eyes on a project; it comes from fewer, more decisive ones.

Let’s stop rewarding "presence" and start rewarding "impact."
Who’s brave enough to decline that 4:00 PM "update" meeting and trust the team to handle it? That’s the BOLD standard.

#Leadership #JOMO

It shifts when we change the systems behind it — when leaders take risks, make different choices, and model through action and accountability what those values truly look like.

At Verizon, we often say our values guide everything we do. But that only happens when each of us practices them — in how we show up for our customers and communities, and in how we care for one another.

That’s exactly what our Culture OS is about. It’s not a campaign or a checklist — it’s how we build our values into the way we work every day. It’s how we make our culture real and lasting.

Because culture isn’t something we communicate.

It’s something we practice and live — in every decision, every interaction, every day.
