I never recycle my Post-its, but this one just hits home. Last year, a familiar fury friend asked a simple question that sparked a significant response, highlighting the importance of self-care and self-reflection.

You all know I believe kindness is the ultimate superpower — but too often, we see it only as something we give to others, not something we extend to ourselves.

It’s time to change that.

We need to check in — not just on each other, but on ourselves.

The truth is, many of us are carrying more than we let on. The pace, the pressure, the constant waves of everything happening in the world — it adds up and it can be a HEAVY load to shoulder. And if we don’t take time to pause, breathe and acknowledge how we’re really doing, it catches up with us.

Checking in with ourselves shouldn’t feel like a rare act of care. It should be part of how we work, lead and live. Because emotional resilience starts with awareness — noticing when we’re stretched thin, speaking up when we need help, and making it safe for others to do the same.

If you lead a team, make check-ins part of your rhythm and rituals. Ask how people really are — and be ready to listen. Create the space, model the behaviors and show that care isn’t a policy — it’s an essential practice.

When we care for ourselves and each other, we build stronger teams, deepen trust and deliver better results. Because people who feel seen and supported bring their best — to work and to life.

So let’s make “How are you doing?” more than a greeting. Let’s make it a habit.

Most importantly, let’s do this together. 💞

Over the past few months, I’ve been having a lot of conversations about what really drives success at work. And time and again, it comes back to this: soft skills aren’t soft at all—they’re the foundation. And my career is living proof. 

When I was a new leader, I was handed a project that was well beyond my comfort zone. I didn’t have all the answers (far from it), but what made the difference wasn’t the technical playbook—it was leaning on soft skills. Listening. Asking the right questions. Building trust with people who knew more than I did. Staying calm when things didn’t go as planned.

That experience taught me something I’ve carried ever since: it’s not just what you know, it’s how you show up.

Soft skills—things like communication, empathy, adaptability, critical thinking—aren’t “extras.” They’re essential. They’re what allow us to navigate change, lead through uncertainty, and create the kind of environments where people can do their best work.

In today’s world, where technology and tools evolve faster than any of us can keep up, it’s these human skills that stand the test of time. They’re what make us resilient. They’re what help us grow into leaders. And they’re what ultimately set us apart.

As we think about developing our teams—and ourselves—it’s worth remembering: technical knowledge might get you started, but it’s your soft skills that will carry you forward.

The start of the school year always takes me back. I can still remember the excitement and waves of nerves on that first day—walking into class with brand-new notebooks, wondering what the year would bring, and feeling like the slate had been wiped clean.

I’ve realized that same feeling doesn’t have to end when we graduate. In our careers, we get the same opportunities to start fresh—whether it’s raising a hand for a new project, learning a new skill or simply shifting our perspective.

This season is a reminder to stay curious, to keep seeking out what’s next, and to embrace the discomfort that comes with growth and change. Because just like those first days of school, the things that feel unfamiliar often turn out to be the ones that shape us the most.

So as the school year kicks off, ask yourself:

✨ What new opportunities can I lean into?
✨ Where do I want to challenge myself?
✨ What skills am I ready to build next?

Above all, let’s keep pushing each other. It’s much easier to stay curious and embrace the unknown when you surround yourself with people who want to see you rise and thrive. 

And to my fellow parents out there — good luck with the start of the school. Give yourself grace to settle back into your routines and give your little ones (or not-so-little ones) extra hugs as they step into this next chapter. I am still wrapping my head around the fact that I have a 6th grader, but I couldn’t be more excited to see what this school year brings for both of us. 

We got this! 💪 💪

Motorized Guillotine Window – A Smart Solution for Modern Openings

Have you seen a window where the glass moves vertically up and down at the touch of a button?

This is a Motorized Guillotine Window, also known as a Motorized Vertical Sliding Glass Window.

Unlike conventional sliding windows, which move horizontally, a guillotine window operates vertically using a motorized lifting mechanism.

🔹 How does it work?

The system typically consists of:

• Motor and gearbox
• Vertical guide channels
• Lifting mechanism such as belt, cable or chain
• Rollers/carriers
• Counterbalance or load-support mechanism
• Safety sensors and control system
• Glass panels and aluminium framing

When the system is activated, the motor drives the lifting mechanism, allowing the glass panels to move upward or downward smoothly.

⬆️ Glass moves up → Opening closes
⬇️ Glass moves down → Opening opens

Why is it useful?

✅ Maximizes the usable opening
✅ Convenient one-touch operation
✅ Clean and modern architectural appearance
✅ Suitable for large openings
✅ Can be integrated with smart-home/automation systems
✅ Useful for restaurants, balconies, terraces and commercial spaces

The real engineering challenge isn't simply making the glass move. The motor, glass weight, balancing system, guides, safety protection and structural design all need to work together reliably.

For large motorized glass systems, proper consideration of glass weight, wind load, motor capacity, safety sensors and maintenance access is essential.

Technology is changing the way architectural openings are designed — and motorized guillotine windows are a great example of this evolution.

One sentence in JPMorgan's 2025 Annual Report changed how I looked at the entire company.

It wasn't a revenue number.

It wasn't net income.

It wasn't ROTCE.

It was this:

“We need to maximize the benefits of our scale and scope, which are necessary to our largest institutional and government clients, while minimizing their considerable negatives.”

At first glance, it sounds like ordinary corporate language.

I don't think it is.

That sentence captures one of JPMorgan's biggest strategic contradictions.

Scale is JPMorgan's moat.

But scale is also one of its problems.

Being enormous gives JPMorgan:

• Massive client relationships
• Global infrastructure
• Huge technology budgets
• Data advantages
• Capital strength
• Ability to serve complex institutional clients

But the same scale can create:

• Bureaucracy
• Complexity
• Slower decision-making
• Higher costs
• Organizational inertia

And management knows it.

In fact, the 2025 shareholder letter explicitly says size can become a business disadvantage because it can bring complexity, bureaucracy and complacency.

That's why this sentence matters.

JPMorgan doesn't simply need to become bigger.

It needs to become more effective at being big.

And that's a very different challenge.

This also connects directly with the company's AI and technology strategy.

If technology can make a giant organization faster, more automated and more intelligent, then JPMorgan's scale becomes an even bigger competitive advantage.

But if technology simply adds another layer of complexity?

The advantage becomes less obvious.

My takeaway:

The most important question for JPMorgan may not be:

“How big can it become?”

It may be:

“Can JPMorgan remain fast while operating at enormous scale?”

Because if the answer is yes, its moat gets wider.

If the answer is no, its biggest strength could gradually become its biggest weakness.

That's the kind of sentence I look for in an MD&A.

A sentence that sounds simple.

But underneath it contains the entire strategic problem.

YOUR MIND IS POWERFUL—BUT IT IS NOT ALWAYS RIGHT. 🧠

2️⃣ MIND LOVES COMFORT — It will often choose what feels safe over what helps you grow.

3️⃣ MIND FOLLOWS PATTERNS — Repeat a thought long enough, and your mind starts treating it like truth.

4️⃣ MIND CREATES CONFLICT — One part of you wants growth, while another part screams, “Stay safe!”

5️⃣ THE REAL PROBLEM? — We often obey our thoughts without questioning them.

6️⃣ THE SOLUTION: S.T.O.P. FRAMEWORK 🛑

S — SEE  the thought.
T — TEST  the thought.
O — OBSERVE  the pattern.
P — PICK your response.

7️⃣ Before saying, “I can’t,” ask: Is this a fact—or simply a familiar thought?

8️⃣ Before choosing comfort, ask: “Will this decision help my future self?”

9️⃣ Remember: A thought is not a fact. A feeling is not a command. Comfort is not always growth.

🔟 MASTER YOUR MIND → CHANGE YOUR CHOICES → CHANGE YOUR FUTURE.

You don’t have to control every thought.
You have to control which thoughts get to control you.

AI is creating jobs. But will those jobs last?
 
A recent Print report from Noida and Gurugram highlights the rise of AI data-annotation jobs people helping AI learn by labelling images, text, audio and video, checking AI responses and preparing training data.
 
The interesting part?
 
Many of these jobs are repetitive and relatively low-paid, and some could themselves be automated as AI improves.
 
This is an important lesson for students and parents.
 
Instead of asking:
 
Which degree will get me a job?
 
Start asking:
 
Which combination of skills will remain valuable as jobs change?
 
Students can explore:
 
 Biology + AI , Medical AI, Bioinformatics 
 Psychology + AI . Human-AI Interaction, Behavioural Research 
 Finance + AI . FinTech, Risk & Data Analytics 
 Law + AI , AI Governance & Compliance 
 Design + AI , AI Product & UX 
 Computer Science + AI , Data Science, ML, Computer Vision, NLP 
 
Data annotation may be an entry point but domain knowledge plus AI skills could be the bigger opportunity.
 
The future of careers may not be about choosing one job for life.
 
It may be about building the ability to learn, adapt and work with technology.
 
Career counselling needs to move from career selection to career adaptability.

Thanks to #print to publish such inspiring post and pushing students and parents to think beyond traditional career approach.

I decided to actually use LinkedIn. Not just have a profile — use it.
At that point, I had 29 followers. Most of them were people I already knew personally. My profile views were sitting around 5 a week. I wasn't sure anyone outside my own circle would care what a court administrator from Faisalabad had to say.
I started posting anyway. Sharing my 20+ years of admin experience. Writing about my freelancing journey. Commenting genuinely on posts instead of scrolling past them.

Motorized Guillotine Window – A Smart Solution for Modern Openings

Have you seen a window where the glass moves vertically up and down at the touch of a button?

This is a Motorized Guillotine Window, also known as a Motorized Vertical Sliding Glass Window.

Unlike conventional sliding windows, which move horizontally, a guillotine window operates vertically using a motorized lifting mechanism.

🔹 How does it work?

The system typically consists of:

• Motor and gearbox
• Vertical guide channels
• Lifting mechanism such as belt, cable or chain
• Rollers/carriers
• Counterbalance or load-support mechanism
• Safety sensors and control system
• Glass panels and aluminium framing

When the system is activated, the motor drives the lifting mechanism, allowing the glass panels to move upward or downward smoothly.

⬆️ Glass moves up → Opening closes
⬇️ Glass moves down → Opening opens

Why is it useful?

✅ Maximizes the usable opening
✅ Convenient one-touch operation
✅ Clean and modern architectural appearance
✅ Suitable for large openings
✅ Can be integrated with smart-home/automation systems
✅ Useful for restaurants, balconies, terraces and commercial spaces

The real engineering challenge isn't simply making the glass move. The motor, glass weight, balancing system, guides, safety protection and structural design all need to work together reliably.

For large motorized glass systems, proper consideration of glass weight, wind load, motor capacity, safety sensors and maintenance access is essential.

Technology is changing the way architectural openings are designed — and motorized guillotine windows are a great example of this evolution.

One sentence in JPMorgan's 2025 Annual Report changed how I looked at the entire company.

It wasn't a revenue number.

It wasn't net income.

It wasn't ROTCE.

It was this:

“We need to maximize the benefits of our scale and scope, which are necessary to our largest institutional and government clients, while minimizing their considerable negatives.”

At first glance, it sounds like ordinary corporate language.

I don't think it is.

That sentence captures one of JPMorgan's biggest strategic contradictions.

Scale is JPMorgan's moat.

But scale is also one of its problems.

Being enormous gives JPMorgan:

• Massive client relationships
• Global infrastructure
• Huge technology budgets
• Data advantages
• Capital strength
• Ability to serve complex institutional clients

But the same scale can create:

• Bureaucracy
• Complexity
• Slower decision-making
• Higher costs
• Organizational inertia

And management knows it.

In fact, the 2025 shareholder letter explicitly says size can become a business disadvantage because it can bring complexity, bureaucracy and complacency.

That's why this sentence matters.

JPMorgan doesn't simply need to become bigger.

It needs to become more effective at being big.

And that's a very different challenge.

This also connects directly with the company's AI and technology strategy.

If technology can make a giant organization faster, more automated and more intelligent, then JPMorgan's scale becomes an even bigger competitive advantage.

But if technology simply adds another layer of complexity?

The advantage becomes less obvious.

My takeaway:

The most important question for JPMorgan may not be:

“How big can it become?”

It may be:

“Can JPMorgan remain fast while operating at enormous scale?”

Because if the answer is yes, its moat gets wider.

If the answer is no, its biggest strength could gradually become its biggest weakness.

That's the kind of sentence I look for in an MD&A.

A sentence that sounds simple.

But underneath it contains the entire strategic problem.

YOUR MIND IS POWERFUL—BUT IT IS NOT ALWAYS RIGHT. 🧠

1️⃣ MIND IS BLIND — It doesn’t always see reality; it sees reality through your beliefs, fears, and past experiences.

2️⃣ MIND LOVES COMFORT — It will often choose what feels safe over what helps you grow.

3️⃣ MIND FOLLOWS PATTERNS — Repeat a thought long enough, and your mind starts treating it like truth.

4️⃣ MIND CREATES CONFLICT — One part of you wants growth, while another part screams, “Stay safe!”

5️⃣ THE REAL PROBLEM? — We often obey our thoughts without questioning them.

6️⃣ THE SOLUTION: S.T.O.P. FRAMEWORK 🛑

S — SEE  the thought.
T — TEST  the thought.
O — OBSERVE  the pattern.
P — PICK your response.

7️⃣ Before saying, “I can’t,” ask: Is this a fact—or simply a familiar thought?

8️⃣ Before choosing comfort, ask: “Will this decision help my future self?”

9️⃣ Remember: A thought is not a fact. A feeling is not a command. Comfort is not always growth.

🔟 MASTER YOUR MIND → CHANGE YOUR CHOICES → CHANGE YOUR FUTURE.

You don’t have to control every thought.
You have to control which thoughts get to control you.

AI is creating jobs. But will those jobs last?
 
A recent Print report from Noida and Gurugram highlights the rise of AI data-annotation jobs people helping AI learn by labelling images, text, audio and video, checking AI responses and preparing training data.
 
The interesting part?
 
Many of these jobs are repetitive and relatively low-paid, and some could themselves be automated as AI improves.
 
This is an important lesson for students and parents.
 
Instead of asking:
 
Which degree will get me a job?
 
Start asking:
 
Which combination of skills will remain valuable as jobs change?
 
Students can explore:
 
 Biology + AI , Medical AI, Bioinformatics 
 Psychology + AI . Human-AI Interaction, Behavioural Research 
 Finance + AI . FinTech, Risk & Data Analytics 
 Law + AI , AI Governance & Compliance 
 Design + AI , AI Product & UX 
 Computer Science + AI , Data Science, ML, Computer Vision, NLP 
 
Data annotation may be an entry point but domain knowledge plus AI skills could be the bigger opportunity.
 
The future of careers may not be about choosing one job for life.
 
It may be about building the ability to learn, adapt and work with technology.
 
Career counselling needs to move from career selection to career adaptability.

Thanks to #print to publish such inspiring post and pushing students and parents to think beyond traditional career approach.

Sejak lama, saya memiliki ketertarikan terhadap dunia komunikasi, public speaking, media, kreativitas, serta bagaimana sebuah pesan dapat disampaikan dan diterima dengan baik oleh orang lain. Semester 1 & 2 (Fase Adaptasi & Eksplorasi):

Semester 3 & 4 (Fase Pengembangan Diri & Organisasi):
Saya berencana mulai aktif mengikuti organisasi, UKM, kepanitiaan, maupun kegiatan kampus yang dapat membantu meningkatkan kemampuan komunikasi dan kerja sama tim. Semester 7 & 8 (Fase Tugas Akhir & Profesional):
Fokus saya adalah menyelesaikan tugas akhir dengan sebaik mungkin serta mempersiapkan diri untuk memasuki dunia profesional. Saya ingin membawa pengalaman dan keterampilan yang telah saya dapatkan selama kuliah sebagai bekal untuk menghadapi dunia kerja.

Selama masa perkuliahan, apabila memiliki kesempatan, saya juga ingin mengikuti berbagai kegiatan di luar kampus, seminar, pelatihan, volunteer, maupun pengalaman kerja yang dapat menambah wawasan, relasi, dan pengalaman saya.

On June 27th, I made a decision that felt small at the time but changed how I show up professionally.
I decided to actually use LinkedIn. Not just have a profile — use it.
At that point, I had 29 followers. Most of them were people I already knew personally. My profile views were sitting around 5 a week. I wasn't sure anyone outside my own circle would care what a court administrator from Faisalabad had to say.
I started posting anyway. Sharing my 20+ years of admin experience. Writing about my freelancing journey. Commenting genuinely on posts instead of scrolling past them.
Today, that number is 235 followers. My connections have grown to 174. Profile views are up nearly 10x from where I started.
One post — sharing that I type 70 WPM — ended up getting over 700 impressions. A number I never expected for something so simple.
None of this happened overnight, and I know by many standards, these numbers are still small. But that's not really the point.
The point is that a couple of months ago, I didn't believe my experience was something worth sharing publicly. Today, I show up here every single day because I've learned that consistency, not perfection, is what actually builds visibility.
If you're sitting on 20+ years of experience wondering if anyone would care to hear about it — they will, if you show up long enough to let them.
What's one small decision you made that ended up changing more than you expected?

From a late-night conversation to a room of 17 people.

That was STEM Innovators Conference 2024.

No big team. No long list of partners. No impressive track record. 

Just an idea, a lot of uncertainty, and a willingness to try.

Then came 2025.

17 to 45+ attendees.
0 to 4 partners.
1 to 6 sponsors.
3 to 4 speakers.
0 to 3 video responses.

These numbers may look small from the outside, but to me, every number carries a story, every person who showed up, every organization that said yes, every speaker who gave their time, every sponsor who trusted an idea that was still growing, and every teammate who stayed and kept building.

STEM Innovators  did not start from a place of experience.

It started with a girl and a question:

“Why can’t young people in STEM in Cameroon have more than what classrooms could offer?”

I didn't have any clear answer or even know exactly what STEM Innovators would become.

But I couldn't ignore the question.

So a question became conversations.
Conversations became a bold reach for guidance.
And those conversations became something we could build.

August 30th 2026 marked two years of STEM Innovators.

What started with one initiative has grown into:

💙  STEM Innovators Conference-  our flagship initiative
💙 World Connect- our video outreach
💙 STEM Innovators Community- our official community
💙 Empathy-Centered Design Challenge- our hybrid bootcamp and innovation challenge
💙  STEM Innovators Konnect-  our community podcast
💙 STEM Impact Magazine- Spotlighting people shaping the future of STEM in Cameroon 

From 0 to 300+ LinkedIn followers
From 0 to 120+ Facebook followers 
From 0 to 20+ Instagram followers 
Yes, from 40 to 380+ community members 

Every milestone means more to me than I can properly explain. 

At the success of every initiative, my heart swells and I sometimes have to hold back my tears. 

Because I remember the uncertainty, the limited resources, the moments things didn't go as planned, infact I never planned on coming this far.

A girl in the dark still chose to move forward. No experience, just question she couldn't let go of.

Today, hundreds of young people have encountered that same call- to ask questions, build, learn and create opportunities beyond what already exists.

And that means more to me than any number could capture.

My heart is filled with so much gratitude.

To my teammates, mentors, organizers, speakers, sponsors, partners and our incredible community, thank you for believing, showing up, and building with us💙🫂

And to everyone who has ever encouraged us, volunteered, shared our work, or simply said “Keep going”  thank you.

Happy anniversary, STEM Innovators 💙

AI ambition is everywhere, but how do organizations turn it into real results? 

For me, the answer is clear - invest in people as much as technology.

That was the focus of my discussion last Monday at London Tech Week with Matt Prebble, CEO of Accenture UK & Ireland, and Patricia Clarke, Tech Editor at The Observer, discussing how bp is reshaping for growth. 

My biggest takeaway is that AI adoption is not primarily a technology challenge. It’s also a people challenge. 

AI is not new to bp, we have used it for years to help improve safety, performance and efficiency. What has changed is the pace and scale, and this changes the skills conversation completely.

At bp, we are investing in building those capabilities from the c-suite to the frontline, helping people use AI to challenge, redesign and improve how work gets done every day. We are building a simpler, more valuable bp and the more skills we put into the hands of our people, the more effective and efficient we become.

As these tools become more powerful, the human skills matter more, not less. Critical and strategic thinking, adaptability, real-world experience and judgement turn AI capability into delivery. The organizations that perform best will be those where people feel confident to stay curious, try new things, challenge outputs and keep learning. 
 
Because if we can help people learn faster, we can adapt faster. And in a world moving at this pace, that is what will turn AI ambition into real business value.

This year’s Social Mobility Day theme #StoriesMatter speaks to me.
 
My route into work was through an apprenticeship. It wasn’t obvious, and it wasn’t always easy. What made the difference were people who took a chance on me, guided me, and helped me see beyond where I started. Many of them are still in my life today.

That’s why stories matter.

Across bp, colleagues have been sharing theirs - from teams in the UK, Kuala Lumpur, Pune and the US, as well as students visiting our offices for Social Mobility Day. It’s been a powerful reminder that there is no single path.

We often make assumptions about how people got to where they are. Those assumptions can hold people back. When we share our stories - and really listen - we start to break those barriers. We help others see what might be possible. And we create space for voices that might otherwise go unheard, because not everyone asks for help.

For me, social mobility is about more than access - it’s about belonging. It’s about being able to say, “I belong on the other side,” and having the confidence to include yourself in spaces where you might not initially see people like you.

I believe deeply that where you start should not define where you end up. Talent is everywhere - opportunity is not.

I’m proud of the work we’re doing at bp, including our Social Mobility business resource group, which has brought colleagues together today across the company. But there is more to do. We need to widen access, notice those who may not speak up, and continue to create space for every voice.

#thisismenow

Tough times have a way of sharpening your perspective and reshaping how you think about resilience.

This was me, living with breast cancer in 2020. Having since recovered, I realised it was never about speed - and neither was reaching Everest Base Camp. Both were journeys where mindset mattered and where the harder moments called for focus and resolve.

Treatment taught me to slow down, respect my limits, and keep moving when progress felt uncertain. Training for the trek felt much the same. Some days were strong. Others were simply about showing up and putting one foot in front of the other.

What stayed with me was how similar recovery and the climb really are. Resilience isn’t about pushing nonstop. It’s about good judgement, staying clear on what matters, and keeping things moving when the road gets harder.

I’m deeply grateful to my family, especially my son, Finlay, who joined the trek, and to the friends and volunteers who supported me along the way. None of this is ever done alone.

For me, resilience shows up in how I lead day to day. Staying grounded. Making thoughtful choices. And sometimes, when the moment comes, resilience is about finishing strong.

Curiosity doesn’t fade with experience. If anything, it becomes more important over time. I had a really thoughtful conversation this week about careers, curiosity and what actually keeps people motivated – and it left me reflecting on a few things.

Curiosity still matters: probably more than ever. 

Not curiosity for curiosity’s sake, but that instinct to ask questions, look beyond your own role, and really understand people, context and what’s changing around you. Especially now, when AI can take on so much of the “task” work.

Purpose is what gets people out of bed – and keeps them coming back.

People don’t come to work just for tasks or titles. They come for learning, connection and to feel part of something that matters. If organisations want the next generation to show up, stay curious and keep growing, we have to create cultures that don’t knock that instinct out of them.

Careers aren’t neat.

They’re built on a mix of hard work, capability and opportunity – and having the confidence to say yes, or ask the question. If you don’t ask, you don’t get. That hasn’t changed – and I don’t think it ever will.

And while AI will change how we work, it won’t replace what matters most.

The first mile – starting a conversation, spotting an idea, being brave enough to reach out. And the final mile – building trust, relationships and follow‑through. That’s still human territory.

One final reflection: leadership only works if you stay close to the real work.

If you’re not spending time with the people doing the job, listening to what’s working and what isn’t, it’s very easy to slip into assumption rather than reality.

A big thank you to Jackson Parsons and Meagen Burnett, CFO at Schroders, for such an open and honest discussion – and to the Richmond L&D Forum for creating the space for these conversations.

Today, as we celebrate the progress women have made around the world for #IWD, I can’t help but think about the girls and women who are living through conflict, not on the margins of the story, but right at the centre of it. Across conflicts around the world, women are among those most affected by wars they did not choose.

A few grounding facts, hard to read, but important to face, drawn from the work of the UN and its humanitarian agencies:

• In Afghanistan, women are now excluded from almost every part of public life. Following new restrictions in late 2024, no girls are expected to be in secondary education, according to UN reporting, making Afghanistan the only country where this is the case.

• In Gaza, UN Women reports that more than a million women are facing catastrophic hunger, reflecting the devastating humanitarian impact these sorts of conflicts have on civilians.

• Across parts of West and Central Africa affected by violence and climate shocks, women and children make up around 80% of refugees and asylum seekers, according to UNHCR.

• In Ukraine, UN agencies report that nearly 6.7 million women need humanitarian assistance, gender‑based violence has increased significantly, and years of progress on equality have been rolled back by the war.

Behind every statistic is a human story, lives shaped by disrupted childhoods, lost education, forced displacement and the quiet, relentless work of holding families and communities together.

So today, alongside celebration, I’m asking us to pause and think of them. To notice. To care. And to stand with women who are still fighting for safety, dignity and opportunity.

Happy International Women's Day to all.

Be curious, a continuous learner. Lean into the discomfort, hone critical thinking and communication skills.

Over the last year it has been clear to me that these are some of the core capabilities needed to succeed as we become a more AI-enabled workforce. They are just as relevant as I think about my kids trying to get to grips with learning in the age of AI.

One critical need, which the ‘Count on It: AI, Numeracy and Social Mobiliy’ report conducted by @Policy Connect rightly calls out - is the need for numeracy.

It was terrific to participate in a panel in the House of Commons this week, as part of the National Numeracy Council’s discussion of the findings of the report, which include:

- Numeracy is a foundational condition for critical AI engagement - AI outputs are based on probabilistic reasoning and statistical patterns shape responses - this makes numeracy a core skill in the critical thinking needed to interpret outcomes.

💡Yet, only 25 % of respondents in the report recognised numeracy as a prerequisite for using AI effectively

- Risk of over reliance - 77% of respondents who used AI trust outputs to be accurate - without key numeracy and critical thinking skills outputs will be used in error. 

⚖️instead of levelling the playing field with its ability to significantly broaden access to information, guidance and opportunity, AI could serve to tilt it further.

In my role as Chair of the LSEG Foundation we see numeracy as a confidence issue as much as a capability issue - through our charity partners we hear how many young adults avoid maths-related tasks completely, and have ‘maths anxiety’.

What’s clear is that to make AI a genuine driver of social mobility, three things matter:

✔️access to the tools themselves
✔️Human not in the loop as much as ‘at the Helm’ : in identifying where to delegate to the AI and the confidence to apply it to value driving use cases
✔️the capability to apply critical thinking to use and challenge outcomes

If we don’t build those capabilities more broadly in our workplaces, schools and societies we will be reinforcing our existing inequalities.

Highly recommend a look at the report below ⬇️ and the five recommendations for employers, policy makers and educators.

Today is World Mental Health Day 🌎 . It’s a moment to pause and reflect on something that affects us all—our mental wellbeing.

This year’s theme, “Access to Services – Mental Health in Catastrophes and Emergencies”, reminds us that mental health support is not a luxury—it’s essential, especially in times of crisis.

The bombardment and mental toll of wars, natural disasters, personal loss, and the uncertainty and complexity of daily life are omnipresent.


Did you know?
1 in 8 people globally live with a mental health condition.
After major disasters, up to 30% of survivors may experience depression, anxiety, or PTSD.
At work, 51% of employees fear that speaking about mental health could harm their career.

But we also know—because research has shown—that every conversation, every act of kindness, every moment of listening can make a difference.
I want to help others regain their sparkle, feel safe to say “I’m not okay,” and find ways to access the support they need. This is what building a culture of care is all about.

Because behind every title, every frown, and every smile is a person who might just need an act of kindness and a moment of compassion.

If we all commit to checking in on one another, we’re more likely to catch each other when we fall.

#WorldMentalHealthDay #CompassGroup #MentalHealthMatters #KindnessIsStrength

Since my discussion at FT Live with Andrew Hill and Andrew Chin on AI and economic growth last month, I've been reflecting on five questions that I believe leaders should be asking as they navigate the next phase of AI adoption. 
  
Our conversation explored what it really means to reimagine work in the age of AI. 

For me, the opportunity is not technology for technology's sake. It is about how AI can help us rethink the way work gets done, how we develop skills, and how organisations create value in an increasingly AI-enabled world. 

That raises important questions for leaders. Are we redesigning how we work, or simply adding technology? Are we building the skills that will matter most? How does leadership change when teams include both people and AI agents? Are we creating AI-enabled teams, or AI-dependent ones? Will AI help create more opportunities, or just do the same work differently?  

These are some of the questions I've been reflecting on, and I'd be interested to hear your perspectives in the comments.

India’s GCC story is entering a new chapter — defined by greater innovation and enterprise impact. 

Last week I was delighted to join our Standard Chartered India team in Bengaluru for the India GCC Forum, which brought together policymakers, industry leaders and leaders in the GCC space to discuss what comes next. Having watched the GCC model evolve over the years, it is clear the shift is from scale, efficiency and execution to innovation, transformation and strategic business outcomes. Across the conversations, three forces stood out: technology, talent and collaboration.

AI is accelerating this evolution, but technology alone will not determine success. The differentiator will be the ability to combine technology with judgement, creativity, problem-solving and deep business understanding.

Two panels featuring Dr. Sumit Mitra, Sunil Rao, Sudish Lambodara Panicker, Reema Thakker Kaweeshwar, Sandip Patnaik, Jayashree Swaminathan and Sathiya Padmanaban explored how organisations can translate innovation into business impact and build the workforce needed to sustain it. The AI session focused on combining AI with human and commercial judgement, accelerating adoption at scale, and moving from experimentation to industrialisation with measurable outcomes at the centre. The talent and operating models discussion examined the capabilities required for future success, highlighting learning agility, employee acumen beyond cost and scale, and stronger collaboration between industry and academia to build both capability and character.

A very different, but equally engaging, conversation with Indian cricket legend Anil Kumble was a reminder that leadership, preparation, adaptability, resilience and bringing people with you remain universal fundamentals.

My key takeaway: the next generation of GCCs will be defined not just by scale or technology, but by the capabilities, leadership and judgement needed to create lasting value.

Thank you to Dr. Manjula N, IAS, Secretary, of IT BT Department, Karnataka for your time, and to P D Singh and the India team for convening such a thoughtful conversation, and to all the speakers and attendees who made the evening so insightful.

Being a judge for the Financial Times Business Book of the Year is fast becoming one of the most energizing engagements for me this year. 
  
As I am reviewing entries and reading books this summer, what’s struck me most is the sheer breadth of literature that the business world is consuming – learning from our history, and preparing for the future. This week, we got the global teams sitting in the GCOO organisation together to discuss 1H progress, ambitions for the second half and deep dive into interesting aspects of work.  One of the highlights for me was hearing colleagues share how they are leveraging Copilot to augment their capabilities and deliver greater impact. 
  
Each practical experience reinforced something I've been reflecting on for some time: as technology becomes more capable, human judgment becomes even more important. It was also a great reminder about the importance of humans augmenting AI rather than competing with it.
  
AI is making technical skills more accessible than ever before, opening possibilities that many of us may not have had access to in the past. But the real differentiator won't be our ability to access information. It will be our ability to ask the right questions, interpret what we see, challenge assumptions and make sound decisions. Those skills will become increasingly valuable in a world where information is easily accessible.
  
As leaders, that shift also changes what must focus on:
1️⃣ We need to look ahead and anticipate change. Information has become highly accessible, so the value of leadership comes from navigating uncertainty, understanding where disruption may come from, and helping others prepare for what's next.
2️⃣ We need to think in systems. As technology becomes more embedded in our work, the ability to connect different data points, understand context and see the bigger picture will be critical. Human judgment is often most valuable when applied across complex systems rather than individual tasks.
3️⃣ We must embrace adaptability. Future-ready leaders will focus less on owning information and more on using judgment, foresight and curiosity to help their teams learn, evolve and thrive.
  
As AI makes information and technical capabilities more accessible, the skills that will keep us ahead are deeply human ones: judgment, curiosity, creativity, adaptability and the ability to ask better questions.
  
That's what leaves me optimistic about the future of work. If we continue investing in both technology and people, I believe we can build organisations that are more innovative, more inclusive and better prepared for whatever comes next.

We were treated to a fascinating opening conversation with England cricketer and Former Captain Jos Buttler, expertly moderated by Gaurav Ahuja, who shared leadership lessons from his remarkable career. We also discussed how organisations need to prepare for a future where work becomes more fluid and technology increasingly complements human capability. Reflecting some of Jos’s earlier comments, we discussed the changing role of leaders, who are not just responsible for encouraging performance ‘here and now’ but also responsible for steering the course and helping their teams build longer term capabilities, particularly ones which will evolve alongside AI.

I recently had the opportunity to join Ray Abuelidam for a conversation on the Business, Belonging and Beyond podcast which focused on identity, ambition and the human side of leadership.

During our discussion, we explored what it takes to lead high-performing teams while creating an environment where people can do their best work. One theme that stayed with me is the importance of balancing accountability with empathy. Leadership often requires difficult decisions, but how we make those decisions and how people experience them matters just as much. We also spoke about shifting the focus from perfection to progress, and the role that energy, wellbeing and presence play in sustaining high performance over time.

In today’s macro-environment, sometimes staying ahead is not only about reacting faster but also understanding how the global economic system itself is changing.

This is a theme that keeps coming up in conversations with clients and colleagues, and it’s what inspired our Group Public and Regulatory Affairs team to produce its latest report on the Top Five Policy Issues shaping public policy in 2026.

We’re moving into a phase where change is no longer gradual. It's structural and it’s happening in real time. At the centre of this shift are five interconnected trends that are reshaping how organisations think about growth, resilience and long-term positioning:

➡️ The rebalancing of power as global relationships become more dynamic and less predictable
➡️ Technology adoption and integration as AI and digital assets move from optional tools to strategic priorities, with real value coming from how we build the skills to use them well
➡️ The race for resources as energy, critical minerals and infrastructure increasingly shape economic and security decisions
➡️ Societal divisions influencing policy direction and making long-term reform more complex
➡️ Global governance shifting from traditional frameworks to more issue-based approaches

These forces are not arriving sequentially, and they cannot be managed in silos. The organisations that lead through this period are those that understand these shifts not as a constraint to manage, but as a strategic input.

So the question for leaders is: how are you adapting your strategy when the system itself is evolving in real time? I would be very interested to hear how others are thinking about these changes. The full paper is linked in the comments if useful as you reflect on what comes next.

An exciting moment for us at Standard Chartered with the launch of our first Agentic AI colleague-facing solution, focused on new-hire onboarding. This marks an important milestone in how we are using AI to improve our colleague’s experience by fundamentally redesigning how work gets done. 
 
By embedding AI, we are simplifying a complex journey, improving the experience for new joiners, and reducing onboarding effort for hiring managers by an estimated 35% of the time they would otherwise spend on these tasks. Crucially, humans remain firmly in the loop — working in partnership with AI, which takes on the repetitive and administrative coordination so colleagues can focus on judgement, problem‑solving, and human connection.
 
This approach is a direct response to what we have learned through our work on workforce and operating-model redesign. When AI is layered onto existing processes without redesigning the work, 95% of organisations see zero ROI from AI investments. By contrast, leading AI organisations are twice as likely to redesign workflows to deliberately integrate human and machine capabilities. These insights shaped our decision to breakdown jobs into tasks, deciding what should be done by humans versus machines, and rebuilding the workflow around that split. 
 
This points to a broader shift - jobs matter less than tasks and skills. As agentic AI application increases, the most valuable skills will be those that sit alongside technology, such as digital fluency, human-AI collaboration, and the ability to interpret and improve outcomes. That is why we are linking this work to our focus on skills of the future and Global Learning Week (which starts today), building capacity as we redesign work. 
 
There is opportunity for leaders to move beyond experimenting with AI, and to redesign the workforce within organisations where people and machines work together intentionally - not by accident. 
 
#FutureOfWork #AgenticAI #WorkforceTransformation

Renminbi (RMB) usage is expanding across trade settlement, funding and capital markets, reshaping how corporates think about currency strategy. 

As a cross-border Bank, Standard Chartered sits at the intersection of where this shift is happening — across Greater China, ASEAN, the Middle East, Africa and beyond. We've been present on the ground in these markets for decades, building the relationships, the expertise and the infrastructure that allow us to connect clients to opportunity across the corridors that matter most.

That's why we've published Renminbi in Motion for Corporates — a report that moves beyond the macro narrative to where it really matters for our clients: funding flexibility, payments resilience, liquidity management, and FX alignment in an increasingly multipolar financial system.

Here's the context that makes it essential reading right now. China represents roughly 15% of global trade, yet the RMB accounts for less than 3.1% of global payments and just 1.9% of global reserves. That structural gap is narrowing, and the drivers this time are durable — rooted in real-economy demand rather than short-term policy cycles.

The infrastructure to support this is firmly in place, liquidity pools are deepening, and onshore and offshore markets are becoming increasingly connected. For corporates with China-linked exposure, this is no longer a theoretical conversation — your supply chains, procurement flows and revenue streams are already embedded in Asia-centred trade networks, whether or not your treasury framework has caught up.

Helping our clients navigate exactly that kind of complexity — with the expertise, the network and the long-term commitment to the markets where they operate — is what Standard Chartered is here to do.

I’ve been reflecting on how quickly geopolitical developments move from headlines to markets and real economic trade‑offs. In a recent conversation on our podcast, Standard Chartered's Eric Robertsen and Madhur Jha explored a key question - is the oil shock arising from the Middle East conflict more likely to fuel inflation pressures, or deepen growth concerns? They also unpacked how the Strait of Hormuz closure is affecting not just energy supplies, but other critical sectors, and what this means across regions, economies, and asset classes. 
 
What we’re seeing right now feels less like a single event and more like a multi‑step adjustment. Even if there is de‑escalation, it may not follow a smooth or predictable path. Ongoing uncertainty around key routes like the Strait of Hormuz matters, not just for oil prices, but for the wider global economy. 
 
A few patterns stand out. First, this is about more than energy prices. Oil and LNG are the most visible channels, but the Middle East is deeply embedded in global supply chains. Disruption can extend into petrochemicals, with knock‑on effects across multiple sectors. Where infrastructure has been damaged, especially LNG facilities, the economic impact can last for years. 
 
Second, markets are reacting through an inflation lens, but growth risks sit just behind it. Energy prices tend to hit inflation expectations quickly, and we’ve seen a shift away from expected rate cuts in some markets. History suggests that when price shocks persist, there is a bigger hit to growth that unfolds gradually over several quarters rather than all at once. 
 
Third, diversification is proving more challenging than expected.  Some traditional safe havens assets have not behaved as they typically do, which complicates risk management and portfolio construction. In this environment, liquidity and judgement matter as much as models. 
 
For me, the key takeaway is a familiar one. Periods like this reward clarity of thinking and patience. Not every signal deserves an immediate response. For businesses (and leaders), this is a reminder that steady long‑term thinking is a competitive advantage when uncertainty rises.

AI is reshaping business outcomes across the entire value chain – from customer services and marketing, to operations, finance and supply chains. Treasury management is no exception, though perhaps not in the way many expect.

I’ve been reflecting on how AI is showing up in day-to-day decision-making, not just in theory but in practice. This conversation with my colleague, Thomas Kikis, Head of Markets, US & Americas at Standard Chartered, offers a compelling window into that reality. 

In treasury management, AI is clearly improving cash flow forecasting, liquidity visibility, and the precision of hedging decisions - particularly in complex, data-fragmented environments like emerging markets. Yet what stood out to me most is a pattern we are seeing across the organisation: the constraint is rarely the technology itself. It is how we apply human judgement to the insights it generates. 

More data, more models, and more signals do not necessarily simplify decisions. In many ways, they increase the premium on human context, interpretation, and accountability.

It’s a reminder that transformation isn’t just about the “hardware” - the models, tools, and infrastructure - but the “software”: how we think, decide, and lead differently in response.

The real value of AI isn’t in replacing judgment, but in sharpening it. That balance between machine-led precision and human-led accountability is where the most meaningful transformation takes shape. 

The podcast is worth a listen for anyone thinking about how AI moves from capability to real-world impact.

This week marks Neurodiversity Awareness Week, a timely reminder of how important it is to recognise that we all work, think, learn, and process information in different ways. 
 
To mark the week, we gathered colleagues across our markets to discuss a fundamental truth: creating a culture where people of all abilities thrive shouldn’t be complex, and it doesn’t require each of us to become an expert in every type of disability – it simply requires us to be curious and open minded. 

As the Global Sponsor of the Standard Chartered Ability Colleague Community, I was thrilled to join Disha Mehta and Ollie Thorn alongside colleagues in London to discuss how the experience of visible and invisible disability can impact leadership. My key takeaways from our session:

​1️⃣ Stop fixing humans, start fixing environments - we spend too much time trying to make people fit a mold. Real change happens when we design environments that accommodate everyone from the start.

​2️⃣ The Power of Lived Experience - having the “ingredients” for a good culture isn't enough. We must amplify the voices of those with diverse lived experiences. Their stories are the catalysts for true transformation.

​3️⃣ Create Safe Spaces - when we build forums where people can share openly, we bridge the gap between "initiative" and "impact."

​4️⃣ The Long Game - we often overestimate what we can do in one year, but underestimate what we can accomplish in ten. Changing the world doesn't happen overnight, but it starts with the questions we ask today.

​Our discussion reinforced my view that inclusion isn't a box to check; it's a muscle we build every day by active listening and driving small impactful change with consistency.

#Inclusion

Sometimes the blazer just has to feel too big at first…

And it struck me that’s exactly how growth feels. Whether it’s starting a new role, taking on more responsibility, or stepping up as a leader, we rarely feel like the blazer fits on day one. It feels oversized, a little daunting, maybe even uncomfortable.

But over time, with encouragement, support and experience, we grow into it. Eventually, what once felt far too big becomes second nature.

At Man Group, we talk about high performance and culture but really, it’s about creating the kind of environment where people feel safe enough to try, supported enough to stumble, and encouraged enough to keep going until the blazer fits.

As leaders, our job isn’t to tailor the blazer to fit perfectly on day one. It’s to help people grow into it.

AI adoption isn't just about bringing new technology into the workplace. It's also about helping people understand how to use it and feel comfortable doing so. 

An article in Forbes got me thinking about the role leaders can play in that process. 

As AI becomes part of more of our day-to-day work, people need space to ask questions, try things out and learn what works for them. The starting point is creating an environment where people feel able to learn. 

Curiosity, communication, and critical thinking will all matter here. AI can help us process information, automate tasks and work in new ways, but we still need people to ask questions, challenge assumptions and use their judgement. 

For leaders, that means paying as much attention to how people are adapting to AI as to the technology itself.

As conversations about FY27 get underway at Sage, I’ve been thinking about the role leaders play in helping people prepare for what’s ahead. 

At this time of year, it’s easy to focus on priorities and performance. But some of the most valuable conversations aren’t just about what someone has achieved. They’re about how they get things done, how they are feeling about the year ahead, where they want to go next and what they need to get there. 

As AI continues to change the way we work, helping people hone their skills in curiosity, adaptability, critical thinking and communication is becoming increasingly important. These are the skills that help people navigate change, take on new opportunities and build confidence along the way. 

That’s why leadership is about more than managing performance. It’s about creating the space for people to learn, develop and think about what comes next. 

As we look ahead to the next financial year, it’s a good time to think about how we’re supporting our people not just to deliver today, but to be ready for tomorrow. 

What will you do differently to support your people’s development as the world of work continues to evolve?

The future of work debate often sounds like a choice between investing in technology or investing in people. I don't think it's either/or. 

AI and data can help organisations make better decisions and work in new ways, but the real value comes when that progress is matched by investment in people, skills and inclusive leadership. 

That's what makes this article worth sharing. Sakeena Adams, our Regional People Director for Africa and the Middle East, explores how organisations can balance technology and data-driven insights with the human side of work, building workplaces that are more resilient and ready for what's ahead. 

For leaders, that means thinking about how technology can create opportunities for people to learn, grow and do their best work, rather than simply changing how work gets done. 

It’s a conversation we need to keep having as the workplace continues to evolve 👉 https://lnkd.in/evaM56ym

Last week was Neurodiversity Week, and it sparked some great conversations across Sage about how we make space for different ways of thinking at work. 

Many organisations, often unintentionally, still reward a fairly narrow style of contribution: thinking quickly, speaking confidently, and aligning fast. It works… but it also means we can miss valuable perspectives that don’t show up in that same way. 

Some of the most valuable insights I’ve seen don’t happen in the moment. They come later, from people who’ve had time to reflect, connect the dots, and really think things through. And when we make space for that, the quality of decisions improves. 

So maybe the question is less about getting everyone to contribute in the same way, and more about how we create the conditions for different thinking to shape outcomes. 

In reality, that often comes down to small things: 
💠  Giving people time to think before and after discussions 
💠  Making space for written input, not just verbal 
💠 Noticing whose perspective we haven’t heard yet 

As we move beyond Neurodiversity Week, that feels like the opportunity,   not just recognising difference, but actually designing for it. 

Because better thinking leads to better decisions.

This week, I had the pleasure of hosting a dinner with Jayney Howson, Chief Learning Officer at ServiceNow University, and a group of thoughtful leaders ahead of Knowledge 2026 to talk about something that feels increasingly urgent: AI is no longer just a technology challenge. It’s a people one. While we started out with a point of view that CHROs and CLOs need to have strong partnerships with CTOs, we got personal.  

What made the conversation especially meaningful is that Jayney and I weren’t only speaking as leaders but speaking as parents, thinking about the future our kids will inherit as AI rapidly deploys across society.

A few reflections that stayed with me:
* The pace of AI is outstripping how quickly we can ready the workforce
Human skills. Learning to learn, adaptability, creativity are becoming more, not less, important.
* In a multi‑generational workforce, trust and confidence in AI look very different

One insight that really resonated came from ServiceNow’s Gen Z research: their biggest concern isn’t job loss, but cognitive decline like losing creativity, critical thinking, and human connection. It struck a personal chord, as I recently had a similar conversation with my daughter. Her generation doesn’t want to outsource their thinking to AI. They want to protect it.

That hit home. As leaders and as parents, we’re shaping not just organizations, but the society our children will grow up in.

Grateful to everyone who invested time and perspective with us over dinner. These are the conversations that matter.

3. Role modeling from the top. Culture elevates when leaders take ownership of their results and commit to raising the bar.
4. Make it everyday. Integrate engagement drivers into the flow of work not just once a year, but every day.

Across industries, organizations are moving beyond the initial excitement around AI and asking how to create sustainable adoption and business value. Transformation is no longer a sequence of initiatives – it is happening everywhere, all at once.

At the German-speaking SAP User Group (DSAG e.V.) Personaltage event in Heidelberg, discussions showed: the shift toward an #AutonomousEnterprise is not about automation in the traditional sense. It is about intelligent assistants and agents that can operate end-to-end; augmented, orchestrated, and always with humans in the loop.

Three core takeaways I shared with the audience:
➖ Rewiring the organization for an AI-native world
We are moving from vertical silos to horizontal, end-to-end value streams. Agents operate across domains, so organizations must follow. This requires new operating models, orchestration layers, and hybrid teams where humans and AI collaborate seamlessly.
➖ Skills as the foundation of adaptability
With skill half-lives shrinking to 6–18 months, organizations need to become truly skill-based. “Learn to unlearn,” continuous reskilling, and real-time skill intelligence are becoming core capabilities for staying relevant.
➖ Human leadership remains central
In an Autonomous Enterprise, humans stay in the driver’s seat. Judgment, empathy, and ethical guardrails matter more, not less. The real challenge is to create the conditions for people to adopt, trust, and effectively work with AI.
 
During our joint panel, Hermann-Josef Haag, Board Member at DSAG, moderator Juliane Krampe, and I debated the following:
➖ Transformation is less a technology challenge, but increasingly a people, prioritization, and leadership challenge
➖ Organizations are managing multiple shifts at once: AI, architecture changes, workforce transformation, and external pressures
➖ The biggest pain points we see across customers are strategic workforce planning, skills transparency, and connecting data across HR, finance, and processes
➖ Progress requires clear target states and pragmatic, phased execution
➖ And most importantly: no organization can navigate this alone. Ecosystems and exchange are critical
 
From a broader SAP perspective, this reinforces our direction: enabling customers to run end-to-end business processes with integrated AI, data, and applications, while embedding people, skills, and change deeply into our transformation journey. Because ultimately, becoming an Autonomous Enterprise is about building adaptive organizations and ensuring employees have the enablement, support, and confidence to thrive in this new reality.

The pace will not slow down. The differentiator will be how deliberately we combine technology and human potential to shape what comes next.

The hardest part of AI transformation is not the technology. It is changing how work actually gets done.

Research points in the same direction: only a small share of AI value comes from the algorithms themselves. The bigger shift happens through people, processes and leadership; when organizations rethink roles, build new skills, and redesign how work happens.
That was at the heart of our first People & Culture Manager Day and the 2026 P&C Kick-Off at SAP, where colleagues from Mannheim, Prague, Bangalore, Newtown Square, Manila and many other locations came together to discuss what this means for the business and for P&C in particular.

Several insights stood out for me:
➔ Futurrist Ian Beacraft challenged us to think beyond automation: AI is reshaping how work is designed, how decisions are made, and which human capabilities create the most value.
➔ Kathi Enderes reinforced that the biggest barriers to AI impact are rarely technical, but organizational: skills, leadership, and the ability to translate technology into new ways of working.
➔ And in our panel with Pinar Dolen, Marielle Ehrmann, Dr. Magdalena Masluk-Meller Eric Goldstein and Ian, one point became very clear: if AI is reshaping the business, then People & Culture must transform too.

For us, that means three things in particular: rethinking how work happens with AI at the core, building new skills while unlearning outdated limits, and connecting more effectively across roles and teams to create impact faster.

For People & Culture, this is a defining moment. We’re not watching work change - we’re making it happen: redesigning the operating model, building the skills, and shaping the culture that turns AI into impact.

AI investments are at an all-time high. But a central question for leaders across industries is no longer whether to adopt AI. It’s how to build the capabilities to work with it.

Research gives us some insights on what matters most: Only 10% of AI value comes from algorithms, 20% from technology and data. But 70% comes from people, processes, and leadership. AI transformation is also a leadership and organizational transformational story, not just technology.

This perspective came alive this week at the Münchner Management Kolloquium at Technical University of Munich, where executives, scientists, and founders gathered under the theme “Bold Moves: Managing with Courage” to discuss how Europe can remain competitive in a rapidly changing technological landscape. In our panel with Britta Seeger, Bettina Dietsche, and Dane Molter, moderated by Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus, we explored how AI at work is crafting tomorrow.

One thing became clear: When technology evolves every few months, value no longer comes from what we know, but from how fast we adapt. That is why SAP is moving toward a skills‑led organization. We are entering a world where the shelf life of skills is shrinking dramatically, sometimes to just months.  
Therefore, the real challenge is not introducing AI. It is redesigning work, processes, operating models and skills at the speed AI evolves.

This year’s #MMK26 showed that we are ready for these bold moves. When companies, universities, and communities work together to prepare people for a world where humans and AI collaborate, we are not just ready for the future – we're actively designing it.

Thank you to Ricarda Engelmeier, Prof. Dr. Dr. h. c. mult. Horst Wildemann and everyone who contributed to such a thoughtful discussion.

Europe is at an important crossroads. Turning the “Union of Skills” from an idea into real progress will shape how competitive we remain in an AI-driven world. 

Last week in Brussels at Digital Europe’s Roundtable, I continued my conversation with the European Commission’s Executive Vice-President Roxana Minzatu, following up on our exchange at the EU Skills Summit in April. Together with leaders from industry, education, and policy, we identified a set of practical, near-term actions, all anchored in the level of scale and pace needed to succeed: investing in upskilling and reskilling, strengthening STEM pathways, building stronger industry–public sector partnerships, and using AI to better understand future workforce needs. 
At SAP, we take this work to heart, and it underpins our commitment to becoming a skills-led organization by 2028. Skills truly are the foundation of growth and innovation in an AI-powered economy. That’s why we collaborate with 2,800+ universities and schools worldwide, educating over 1 million students per year on business applications and technologies to help expand access to AI, cybersecurity, and digital skills – and why we fully support the EU’s Union of Skills agenda. 

This focus on preparing people for the future also came through clearly at UniCredit’s “Future of HR” panel in Milan this week. Alongside Hubert Joly, David Bach, Tim Good, and Monica Rancati, we discussed how HR can guide meaningful transformation, use AI responsibly, and create a culture of continuous learning as work evolves across all sectors. 

These back-to-back conversations made one thing very clear: Europe’s competitiveness depends on people, skills, and the thoughtful use of AI – and it will take genuine collaboration between business, policymakers, and educators to get this right.

Die Bitkom #TRANSFORM26 in Berlin war für mich ein wertvoller Impulsgeber: Wenn es um Transformation geht, müssen Politik und Wirtschaft eng zusammenrücken.

Im Dialog mit Bundesministerin Karin Prien (BMBFSFJ) und Marcel Fratzscher, Leiter des DIW, stand die zentrale Frage im Raum: „Diversity, Equity, Irrelevance: Kann unsere Wirtschaft auf Vielfalt verzichten?“

Die Antwort ist klar: Gerade für die digitale Transformation und zur Sicherung unserer Wettbewerbsfähigkeit ist #Vielfalt unverzichtbar. Sie ist kein „Nice-to-have“, sondern – in all ihren Facetten – ein entscheidender Wettbewerbsvorteil und ein Motor für #Innovation. Mehr Vielfalt, auch und insbesondere durch mehr Frauen, ist für die Wirtschaft essenziell.

Und mit Blick auf die demografischen Veränderungen in Deutschland wird deutlich: Wir können es uns als Gesellschaft und Wirtschaftsstandort nicht leisten, auf Erfahrung, Kompetenz und Engagement von Frauen zu verzichten.

Um mehr Frauen in Beschäftigung zu bringen, braucht es die richtigen Rahmenbedingungen. Ein zentraler Hebel ist dabei mehr #Flexibilität in der Arbeitszeit. Starre Vorgaben, wann und wie gearbeitet wird, sind in Zeiten von KI und digitaler Arbeit nicht mehr zeitgemäß. Die Einführung einer Wochenarbeitszeit kann hier ein wirkungsvolles Instrument sein: Sie ermöglicht es vielen Menschen, ihre Arbeitszeit auszuweiten und gleichzeitig Beruf und Privatleben selbstbestimmter zu vereinbaren.

Als einer der größten Arbeitgeber in Deutschland schaffen wir bereits heute – im Rahmen der gesetzlichen Möglichkeiten – vielfältige Optionen, um genau das zu unterstützen.

Doch klar ist auch: Ohne mutige politische Rahmenbedingungen und ein gemeinsames Verständnis von moderner Arbeit werden wir das vorhandene Potenzial nicht heben. Wenn wir Transformation wirklich gestalten wollen, müssen wir Vielfalt konsequent fördern, Flexibilität ermöglichen und die Arbeitswelt an die Realität der Menschen anpassen.


Bundesministerium für Bildung, Familie, Senioren, Frauen und Jugend | DIW Berlin - German Institute for Economic Research

After Davos, action begins.

The conversations were valuable. Now comes the hard work of turning them into action.

In my latest article, I share a few reflections from the conversations I had with the people at Davos and what they signal for the road ahead.

I’d love to hear: what actions are you taking after #WEF26?

𝐈𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐀𝐈, 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐣𝐨𝐛, 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?

That question framed our panel hosted by KPMG at AI House Davos during World Economic Forum. Together with May Habib and Alessandro De Luca, and moderated by Ashish Madan, we explored how AI and agentic systems are changing the very nature of work and organizations.

👉 A few reflections I keep coming back to:

1️⃣ What still defines a #job? 
A job is, fundamentally, a bundle of tasks or activities performed to achieve a certain outcome. What changes with AI is how these tasks are bundled –through automation or augmentation – and by whom they are performed: humans, machines, and agents. From an economic perspective, jobs are outcome-driven, balancing input and output. And yet, for us humans, a job is more than that. It is also about connection, identity, and purpose.

2️⃣ Transformation stands and falls with #people.
We tend to over-index on tools and technology, but 80% of change is behavioral and cultural. People’s engagement, rooted in trust and psychological safety, determines how fast organizations can really move.

3️⃣ #Leadership faces a paradox: “everything changes – and nothing changes.”
In the age of AI, it is the role of leaders to decide what business they are in and what purpose guides it. And they need to stay in control of what matters most. Leaders remain accountable for business models, quality, ethical decision-making, etc. The fundamentals – trust, empowerment, psychological safety and a growth mindset – matter just as much in the age of AI, if not more.

4️⃣ Which #organizations are we ultimately building?
AI will not lead to radical change unless we rethink our processes and operating models. The real question is which organizations we are ultimately building. This is not about incremental change, but about redesigning systems and enabling new ways of working. We need to be deliberate about where we automate tasks and where we augment human capability. And we must always keep humans in the loop – or even in the lead – because this is where human skills – such as judgment, contextual understanding, and purpose – remain essential.

I remain positive – yet not naive about AI. It can be a powerful enabler, helping us rethink industry, address demographic challenges, democratize knowledge, and protect our planet. 

In the end, the answers often do not lie in the technology alone.
They lie in the choices we make – and in how consciously and purposefully we apply technology, together.

It was a joy and a privilege to talk Circularity at the One Young World Summit in Munich, looking out to a room full of brilliant young leaders. I had the opportunity to engage on a topic that holds immense relevance for us today: how can we learn from circularity in nature and marry those eons of „R&D“ with today’s technology to get back to balance.
 
Life on this planet has always been circular. The ancient rhythm of cycles turns fallen leaves into soil, and returns a river’s water back to the sky. Everything in nature is interconnected. Every end is a new beginning.
And for the longest time, mankind lived by the rules and rhythm of nature - and its resourcefulness.

Yet with industrialization and globalization, we replaced the circle with a straight line - Take. Make. Dispose. The linear model seemed like a promise of growth and prosperity - but not for everyone, and it stretches our planet’s limits.

Now it's time to rebalance. We must decouple growth from resource consumption and change the operating model of the world from linear back to circular.

In this transformation to „circular by design“, technology is our most potent ally. AI and digital twins are enablers of breakthrough innovation in the digital world - with positive impact in the real world. 

Our wonderful young leaders and changemakers will be architects of renewal. If they - we all - choose the circle over the straight line. 

 So, let’s make the circle whole again – together!

80% of companies struggle to capture returns from their Gen AI investments, according to a 2025 McKinsey survey.

So how can we translate #GenAI potential into real #productivity?

There’s no simple answer – but #experimentation brings us closer.

The new Harvard Business Review article captures an important truth: the path to productivity isn’t linear. It’s a “J-curve” that requires a learning mindset and the courage to test, adapt, and scale what really works.

I’m pleased to see this approach, which we embrace at Siemens, featured in the article. For us, it’s experimentation that puts people at the center. In 2024, we ran the first test of our #IndustrialCopilot – a GenAI-powered shop-floor assistant – at our factory in Erlangen. Our maintenance engineers found it saved them time. But the real surprise came from our technicians – especially the more junior and less experienced staff – who said it helped them tackle complex issues more confidently, particularly on night shifts when no engineers were around.

This is what we mean by #TechnologywithPurpose: empowering people, enabling continuous learning, and ensuring digitalization delivers real value for our workforce and customers.

496 Punkte. KI als Sparringspartner. Und 8,61 Euro in einem Briefumschlag.

Was das miteinander zu tun hat? Alles drei habe ich bei meinem X-Day in Dortmund erlebt – einem Tag, an dem ich meinen Schreibtisch gegen den Arbeitsalltag unserer Kolleginnen und Kollegen im Service getauscht habe. Ein Tag, der mir richtig viel Energie gegeben hat!

496 von 500 Punkten hat die Deutsche Telekom zuletzt im Connect Mobilfunktest erzielt: eine Spitzenleistung, auf der sich in Dortmund trotzdem niemand ausruht. Im Live-Kundengespräch habe ich erlebt, was das heißt. Da ging es von einem Kupferanschluss über Glasfaser bis zur MeinMagenta App – und am Ende das spontane Urteil der Kundin: „10 von 10 Punkten.“ So machen wir Kunden zu Fans. 😊

Und KI? Ist hier längst im Arbeitsalltag angekommen. Kolleginnen und Kollegen trainieren Kundengespräche mit KI und bekommen direkt Feedback. Beim Bauherren-Service, der Hausbauer rund um Anschlüsse und die Anbindung von Neubauten an unser Netz unterstützt, hilft zum Beispiel unser KI-Assistent askT, schneller das richtige Wissen für komplexe Kundenanliegen zu finden.

Und dann die 8,61 Euro: Ein Kunde hatte sie samt handschriftlicher Notiz in einen Briefumschlag gelegt, um eine Rechnung zu bezahlen. Unsere Kundenwelt ist eben nicht nur digital. Die eine erledigt alles per App und online. Der andere schreibt einen Brief und legt das Geld dazu. Unser Anspruch ist es, für beide da zu sein.

Besonders beeindruckt haben mich die Gespräche mit Talenten und Führungskräften. Wie entwickeln wir Menschen frühzeitig in Führungsverantwortung? Was kann nur in der Praxis erlernt werden und wo können wir durch Lernangebote zusätzlich unterstützen? Offen über diese Fragen zu diskutieren und dabei so viel Vertrauen, Engagement und Lernbereitschaft zu erleben, hat mir einmal mehr gezeigt: Technologie ist wichtig. Prozesse sind wichtig. Aber am Ende machen unsere Menschen bei der Telekom den Unterschied.

DANKE an alle Kolleginnen und Kollegen für die offenen Einblicke und Gespräche – und für diesen großartigen X-Day! Alexander Torrejon Mora, Anna Gempfer, Dirk Hermes, Gunnar Hempelmann, Samira El Hasbouni, Silke Brandt-Langhammer, Sascha Wollenberg
Wirklich ein toller Weg, der Mut macht, lieber Haritharan - Harry Gunapalasingam. Meine Stimme habe ich gerade für Dich abgegeben.

KI ist da. Jetzt muss sie wirken. 
 
Die Ergebnisse aus unserer Mitarbeitenden-Befragung zeigen: Die regelmäßige KI-Nutzung bei der Deutschen Telekom ist erneut gestiegen – auf 83 Prozent. 

Das ist ein starkes Signal. Und es freut mich sehr.  

Denn KI entfaltet ihren Wert nicht dadurch, dass KI-Tools verfügbar ist. Entscheidend ist, dass Mitarbeitende die KI auch nutzen. Und – noch wichtiger – dass wir echte Wirkung damit erzielen. Deshalb bringen wir jetzt Struktur rein. Klar, unsere Leute bekommen die passenden Tools an die Hand. Und die bauen wir systematisch in Arbeitsprozesse ein:  

➡️ Unsere T-Cars planen die Glasfasertrassen automatisiert – mit KI und moderner Sensorik. 
➡️ Bei T-Systems arbeiten bereits rund 4.000 Software-Ingenieure mit unserem AI Engineer. 
➡️ Mit "Nadia" machen wir KI-gestütztes Coaching für Führungskräfte skalierbar. 
 
Genauso wichtig ist: Wir nehmen unsere Kolleginnen und Kollegen mit. Mit AI Explorer Journeys, Creatathons und AI Wizards, die Teams in Sachen KI beraten, schaffen wir Räume zum Lernen und Anwenden. Nicht jede und jeder muss KI-Expertin oder AI-Engineer werden. Was wir brauchen, sind Menschen, die ihr Fachwissen mit KI verbinden können und gleichzeitig ihre Urteilsfähigkeit bewahren. 

Mehr Nutzung ist gut. Aber der eigentliche Maßstab ist Wirkung: Verbessern wir Qualität und Service für unsere Kunden? Macht KI unsere Arbeit einfacher? Werden wir schneller? Schaffen wir Freiraum für die Dinge, die wirklich zählen?
