Warum will niemand mehr Führungskraft werden?

Das wollte DER SPIEGEL von Heike Bruch wissen. Sie ist die Herausgeberin der St. Galler Jugendstudie, die drei Kipppunkte ausgemacht hat, wieso junge Menschen keine Lust mehr auf Führungspositionen haben.

Vorgesetzte wirken oft ausgebrannt und in einer Arbeitsmühle, die wenig erfüllend wirkt. Junge Menschen nehmen Strukturen als alt und starr wahr. Und: Führungskräfte spüren oft eine Überforderung oder das Gefühl, am Limit zu arbeiten, sodass sie ihre Führungsaufgaben am liebsten wieder abgeben möchten.

Die Quintessenz – und auch mein Erleben aus meinem beruflichen Alltag: Es fehlt dem Nachwuchs nicht an Ehrgeiz, sondern mitunter an Möglichkeiten, Verantwortung zu erproben, und auch an Vorbildern, die zeigen: So sieht gute Führung aus. So macht Führung Spaß.

Wir bei RWE sind uns unserer Verantwortung, Führungskräfte kontinuierlich auszubilden, bewusst. Zunächst einmal ist es sicherlich erfreulich, dass wir bei RWE keinen Mangel an Mitarbeitenden haben, die Führungsaufgaben übernehmen möchten. Nun liegt es an uns, eine Umgebung zu schaffen, die sich von der oben skizzierten deutlich unterscheidet. Dazu zählt, dass wir unsere Führungskräfte und Potenzialträger auf ihrer Reise begleiten und unterstützen.

Für den Gesamtkonzern haben wir unser Führungskräfteprogramm, unsere RWE Executive Journey, weiter geschärft. In Linie mit unserem Purpose, unseren Unternehmenswerten und unseren erfolgskritischen Verhaltensweisen haben wir ein gemeinsames Führungsverständnis definiert: Unsere RWE Leadership Principles. Diese Führungsprinzipien folgen klaren Standards und formulieren eine klare Erwartung, wie gute Führung bei RWE gelebt wird:

▪︎ Lead for Business Impact
▪︎ Lead to Deliver
▪︎ Lead for Team Success

Eine Umgebung zu schaffen, in der unsere Mitarbeitenden am besten wachsen und wirken können, liegt an uns. Wir begleiten unsere Führungskräfte auf jedem Schritt ihrer Reise und bereiten sie strukturiert auf ihre Rolle vor. Das gilt für das gesamte Spektrum von der ersten Führungsrolle, der Weiterentwicklung als Führungskraft oder einem Neueinstieg bis zum Gesellschaftswechsel.

Wichtig ist uns auch: Leadership ist nicht immer eine lineare Entwicklung, sondern hochindividuell: Es gibt auch Möglichkeiten zurück in Fachpositionen, geteilte Führungsrollen oder Sabbaticals als Möglichkeiten, neue Perspektiven kennenzulernen.

Unsere RWE Executive Journey unterstützt kontinuierlich, leitet an und ermutigt, den Schritt in die Führungsverantwortung zu gehen. Ein großer Dank an die vielen HR Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus dem gesamten Konzern, die gemeinsam RWEs Weg an dieser Stelle unterstützen.

Ich bin schon sehr gespannt, wie sich die Ergebnisse in unserem Unternehmen widerspiegeln werden. Denn ich bin überzeugt: Führung ist attraktiv!

What does leadership look like when the world feels unpredictable? 
 
That was the focus of our discussions at this year’s Global Women’s Network Conference #GWN, where I had the privilege of sharing the stage with our Offshore Wind CFO Gunhild Grieve. How urgent this question is, shows the current situation in the Middle East. Energy markets can shift in an instant while assets last for decades. Leading teams in this environment requires clear direction, curiosity, and teamwork. It also takes courage — the courage to be open, show vulnerability, and face uncertainty together. Listening to different perspectives and sharing my own, I reflected on the small actions that help people feel supported and confident even when everything else is in motion. 
 
During these moments in a BANI world, our values and Essential Behaviours provide anchors. Leadership is about conviction. Conviction means being stable in purpose but flexible in method. You adjust how you move, but not why you move. And that stability helps people feel grounded, especially when change is constant. 
 
Sharing stories and ideas in this space reminded me that leadership isn’t only about decisions. It’s about people, culture, and the everyday actions that help us navigate change together. Moments like these leave me grateful and excited to continue learning and growing alongside such an incredible network of colleagues.

Offshore wind technology delivers stunning images, astonishing figures and equally remarkable teamwork.
 
The latest example: the start of the turbine installation at our Thor offshore wind construction project in the Danish North Sea, which we are implementing together with our project partner Norges Bank Investment Management.
 
Last night, the first of 72 wind turbines was successfully installed. The approximately 80-strong crew of the installation vessel erected the nacelle and the 115-metre-long rotor blades at a hub height of approximately 148 metres. A job for real precision. A real job for #TeamRWE. Another 71 wind turbines will follow until the largest Danish offshore wind farm to date, with an installed capacity of 1.1 GW, is completed. My respect and many thanks to the Offshore Construction teams for your great work — Julian Garnsey, Günther Fenle and your respective teams.
 
And to put the many figures into perspective: Did you know that with the 4.8 GW of capacity that we currently have under construction with project partners plus our existing offshore wind fleet, we could theoretically cover almost the entire annual electricity demand of Denmark? I find that impressive.

21 % der Schülerinnen und Schüler in Deutschland leben in Armut oder sind armutsgefährdet. Fast eine halbe Million Schülerinnen und Schüler benötigen schulische Unterstützung, können sich diese aber nicht leisten. Wir helfen mit, dagegen zu steuern. Seit April 2025 unterstützt die RWE Foundation den Lern-Fair e.V durch ein Mitarbeiterpartizipationsprojekt. 
 
Lern-Fair ist eine Plattform, die Kindern, Jugendlichen und jungen Erwachsenen in Ausbildung aus herausfordernden Lebenslagen kostenlose digitale Lernunterstützung ermöglicht. Gleichzeitig ermöglicht Lern-Fair ein barrierearmes, flexibles Ehrenamt - ortsunabhängig und inklusiv - sodass auch Menschen mit Behinderung oder eingeschränkter Mobilität aktiv mitwirken können. Das Angebot geht von Hausaufgabenhilfe, über Prüfungsvorbereitung bis hin zu Kursen zur Förderung der ganzheitlichen Entwicklung. Ziel ist es, die schulischen Leistungen zu verbessern, damit die Chancen auf höhere Bildungsabschlüsse zu steigern und gleichzeitig das Selbstvertrauen und die Motivation der Kinder und Jugendlichen zu stärken. Wie das funktioniert, erklärt Clara Grabitz, Geschäftsführerin Lern-Fair e.V. RWE-Mitarbeiter Christopher Savage gibt im Video außerdem Einblicke, was ihn bewogen hat, als Tutor mitzuwirken. 
 
Soziales Engagement gehört bei RWE zur Unternehmenskultur. Mit dieser Partnerschaft wollen wir ganz konkret dazu beitragen, dass mehr Kinder und Jugendliche faire Bildungschancen bekommen. Und weil junge Menschen ihre Startbedingungen nicht beeinflussen können, sollten wir uns dafür einsetzen, allen eine faire Chance zu ermöglichen. Schlussendlich profitieren wir alle davon – als Gesellschaft, aber auch ganz persönlich. Unser RWE-Kollege Christopher Savage ist ein starkes Beispiel dafür, dass das Engagement für Lern-Fair nicht nur den Nachwuchs bereichert, sondern auch die Ehrenamtlichen selbst.
 
Ich bin stolz darauf, dass sich bereits so viele Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus dem #TeamRWE auf vielfältige Art und Weise sozial engagieren. Gemeinsam machen wir den Unterschied!

One of the most rewarding aspects of my role at RWE is hearing inspiring stories from our employees around the world, and Dilraj Singh and his daughter Gurnoor Sekhon‘s story is one that truly stands out. For me, this story across two generations underlines one of RWE’s core values: passion!

Multigenerational employment and careers from apprenticeship to retirement are no exception at RWE. This is a true treasure, and we cherish it, as it emphasises the strength of #TeamRWE. I am proud of that. And it’s great to have you on board Dilraj and Gurnoor.

Bleiben wir Anwender oder ist unser Anspruch bei KI ein anderer?
 
Unter anderem darum ging es bei „Allianz der Chancen trifft… Lars Klingbeil“ gestern in Berlin. Die Arbeitswelt geht in die nächste Phase über. Und die gelingt nur im Zusammenspiel zwischen echter und künstlicher Intelligenz. 
 
Im Fokus der Gespräche stand daher, wie eng Finanzpolitik, technologische Entwicklung und Beschäftigung miteinander verbunden sind. Investitionen in Infrastruktur – wie zuletzt in die KI-Fabrik in München – sind zweifelsohne eine wichtige Grundlage. Entscheidend ist jedoch, ob wir Anwender bleiben oder den Anspruch entwickeln, Weltmarktführer für KI-gestützte Geschäftsmodelle zu werden – und ob wir KI dabei konsequent menschenzentriert denken. 
 
Dafür braucht es die Mitarbeitenden aller Unternehmen, die sich in der Allianz der Chancen zusammengeschlossen haben. KI und Mensch müssen dabei Hand in Hand gehen. Auch in dem Bewusstsein, die richtige Tonalität zu treffen, um auf die Ängste vieler Menschen zu reagieren. Mein Eindruck ist, dass wir uns bei Unsicherheit oftmals wieder an alten Verhaltensmustern bedienen, die wir eigentlich schon geglaubt, überwunden zu haben. The way AI is shaped will shape the world!
 
The question therefore is: Do we want to remove biases or reinforce blind spots? One alarm signal for the latter is that various studies indicate only around 22-30% of global AI talent is female.
 
At RWE, however, we strive to do the former. We want AI in our organisation to reflect the perspectives, creativity, and empathy of everyone – not just a few. This week I had the pleasure of joining the launch event for our Women in AI network. The network brings together women from different functions across teams and countries, creating a space to connect, learn, and experiment. It’s about more than representation – it’s about enabling women to actively and responsibly shape AI in ethical, inclusive ways.
 
During the discussion I shared my view of AI as a key enabler of digital transformation and the energy transition. And about what is needed in terms of a strong foundation for AI to scale. It's what I call a golden triangle consisting of:
▪️HR – to bring purpose and heart
▪️IT – to drive innovation
▪️Security – to provide the trust that allows us to move fast without breaking things
 
Together, they form the foundation of an organisation where AI can act as a co-pilot, supporting employees and freeing up time for creative, strategic work by humans. This is where women make a real difference. Women often bring strong domain expertise, ethical awareness, and empathy. Diverse teams reduce blind spots and help build robust AI solutions that are fairer and more sustainable. 
 
This was a successful start to the network, and I am already very excited to see the first tangible results. Thanks to Thomas Denny and Marina Sverdel for the lively discussion on stage and huge congratulations to Gülnaz Öneş and the women on the AI core team for making this network possible.

“Turning points”
“Geopolitical storms”
Uncertainty is no longer the exception, it’s now part of leadership.
 
How do uncertainty and a rapidly changing world shape the way we lead? This was a topic in the panel discussion with Colette Rückert-Hennen we had at  The London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) German Symposium.
 
From my personal perspective – being responsible for HR, IT and Security – the challenge is even more fundamental: We are moving from an era of efficiency to an era of agency. The past decades, leadership was about managing “Human Resources”. Now, AI is finally taking the 'robot' out of the job. It is absorbing the management chores, the data-drudgery, and the administrative friction. This creates spaces. New possibilities. 

The big question for us on this panel is: What would be the wisest way to fill the newly created spaces? Our shared conviction: If we manage to fill it with Human Agency - transparency, radical vulnerability, and shared leadership - we turn uncertainty into our greatest competitive advantage. My goal is to use technology as a multiplier, not a replacer, so that our collective time becomes our company’s most valuable asset.

Are women better prepared for uncertain times, as there is something called the "female" leadership style? 

I try to avoid stereotypes, but research shows that in times of high stress, there is the temptation to revert to autocratic styles when the world feels 'Brittle' or 'Incomprehensible' (BANI). It feels safe to have one person 'set the course.' But I have to argue the opposite. Autocracy is a bottleneck. In an era where AI agents are processing data and making micro-decisions in milliseconds, an autocratic leader becomes the slowest part of the system. An autocratic leader who pretends to have all the answers creates a fragile organisation. A leader who shows vulnerability and transparency creates a resilient one. In a BANI world, collaboration is a survival skill, not a 'soft' skill. And so is Diversity!

Thanks to Hartmann Ilka for your moderation, and again to Colette Rückert-Hennen. It’s always a pleasure to share perspectives and the stage with you.
 
Actually, this thoroughly inspiring day began already in the morning with a meeting at the German Embassy in London where we had the opportunity to speak with the British Ambassador, H.E. Andrew Mitchell, and the German Ambassador, H.E. Susanne Baumann. This exchange provided valuable international perspectives on leadership as well. A day fully packed with great discussions.

Let's start the year with a view!
 
After taking you on a virtual tour of a wind turbine, today we're heading to the “heart” of the offshore wind farm: the substation.
 
What you see here is the offshore substation of our Kaskasi wind farm, 35 km off the coast of Heligoland. The substation is the central hub where electricity from all turbines comes together before heading to shore. From the outside, it might seem like just another platform at sea, but inside it’s a giant tangle of components and connections, all designed to make the flow of electricity reliable and continuous.
 
What kind of work goes into this heart of an offshore wind farm? Nothing less than an engineering masterpiece in manufacturing, heavy-lift vessels to transport the thousands of tonnes of topside components, and absolute precision during the “marriage” at sea – the installation of the topside onto the foundation. 
 
Once completed, the wind turbines turn, the generators produce electricity, and this is fed into the relevant grid connections via the substation. Sounds simple – but take a look for yourself! It’s easy to forget, from the outside, just how much care and coordination goes into making everything work. 
 
Looking ahead, RWE Offshore Wind will deliver four construction projects with a total capacity of 4.8 GW and continue providing clean, reliable electricity from our wind farms. Considering the dedication that goes into every detail, it’s clear that none of this would be possible without #TeamRWE.

Why the future of HR is built on “And” 🤝 
 
That was the question I explored with Rudi Bauer in a podium discussion on the stage of the WeAreDevelopers Congress. 
 
While today's societies - at least in some parts of the world - oftentimes tend to a more confrontational "either… or", my personal experience, both at Daimler Truck AG and beyond, is different.
 
I believe that technological breakthroughs, innovation and societal progress happen when we combine elements and move beyond binary thinking: It’s not humans "or" AI, performance "or" culture, speed "or" responsibility, employees "or" capital markets. It is "and" - always.
 
As leaders, both in business, politics and society more broadly, our job is to embrace complexity and turn "either… or" into "and", in order to find solutions that really work.
 
If you want to dive deeper into this topic, you can listen to a podcast I previously recorded and that is available on YouTube:
 
Rudi Bauer & Jürgen Hartwig - The Future of HR Lies in AND – Not in OR

The most important questions rarely have simple answers.
 
Palm oil is a good example. It is one of the most discussed raw materials in the world, yet the conversation is often framed as either good or bad. The reality is more nuanced.
 
Palm (kernel) oil is an important ingredient in many everyday products and its impact depends largely on how it is produced and sourced. At Henkel, we are committed to achieving zero net deforestation for palm (kernel) oil by 2030. Together with our suppliers and partners, we work to increase transparency and traceability across the supply chain, protect forests and natural ecosystems, and support the transition towards more sustainable production. This helps protect primary forests and improve the livelihoods of smallholder farmers.
 
The last aspect is often overlooked: understanding the people behind the supply chain, the challenges they face, and how responsible sourcing can improve their lives.
 
That’s why we have been partnering with Solidaridad Network since 2013 to support smallholder farmers through sustainable agricultural practices, certification processes and digital solutions that increase transparency.
 
Because meaningful progress happens when environmental and social considerations are addressed together.
 
#WeAreHenkel

2.    As leaders, we need to be ready to challenge established ways of working, rethink roles and responsibilities and compose future-ready teams.

No matter how much experience we have, leadership in the age of AI requires a sense of urgency – and a learner’s mindset.

You can only manage what you can measure, especially in sustainability.
 
Measuring environmental impact can be more complex than traditional business metrics, with incomplete data and evolving standards. That’s why at Henkel, we’ve spent years building a strong data foundation – which is the basis for the road ahead, with concrete sustainability targets coming soon.
 
Across our Henkel Consumer Brands portfolio, a three-year analysis now gives us clear insights into product carbon footprints, and where transformation is needed – what meets our sustainability criteria, what needs to be redesigned. 
 
In Henkel Adhesive Technologies, our HEART (Henkel Environmental Assessment Reporting) tool calculates the footprint of more than 70,000 products, creating transparency for our customers and helping us steer our portfolio toward lower-emission solutions. Why does this matter? For industries like automotive, where we contribute to Scope 3 emissions, reliable data is essential for our customers to meet their climate goals.
 
Building these data capabilities requires collaboration with suppliers worldwide. I’m not tired of saying this: we can only make real progress if we work hand in hand across the value chain. 
 
With thanks to Bertrand Conquéret, Ulla Hueppe and Agnès Thée for driving this work forward.

It doesn’t replace human judgment – it amplifies it. 
 
As a global company and employer, we have a big responsibility: to take our people with us on this fast-moving journey. Here’s how we approach it at Henkel: 
  
🔹 We build AI literacy at scale.
From company-wide learning programs to leadership training, we want everyone to understand how AI can support their work (not replace it).
 
 🔹 We encourage our teams to experiment.
Across HR and the business, teams are already exploring how AI can help them work differently and better. This bottom-up energy is powerful.
 
 🔹 We keep people at the center.
Critical thinking, creativity, and empathy remain uniquely human. AI amplifies these strengths.
 
The future of work will not be defined by technology alone. It will be defined by how we choose to use it. 
 
I’m curious – what role does AI already play in your own learning or growth journey?

Two years ago, we took a bold step at Henkel: introducing 8 weeks of fully paid parental leave for all new parents – regardless of gender, family constellation, or location – across all ~70 countries and for all 47,000 colleagues.

We knew it would be complex. But we knew it was the right thing to do – and that it would make us stronger, as a company, as a team.
 
Today, the results from last year speak for themselves. And honestly, they move me.
 
📈 +15% overall uptake vs. 2024
 👨‍👩‍👧 +35% more male colleagues taking parental leave

We are living in a time of profound change – technological, societal, and environmental. In moments like these, learning becomes more than acquiring new skills: it helps us stay curious instead of fearful, critical instead of polarized, and open instead of certain that we already have all the answers.
 
Education supports our ability to think critically, understand different perspectives, and engage in meaningful dialogue. These aspects are essential foundations for strong and democratic societies. Especially when the world feels complex or uncertain, lifelong learning allows people to stay connected, informed, and able to shape change responsibly.
 
What we should not forget: in some countries, education is not a given. It is a luxury that many cannot afford. I had the privilege of growing up in a country that guarantees free education, and this is what allowed me to be where I am today. And I experienced the opportunity to receive higher education as a life-changer.
 
It is our all responsibility to make sure that we take all people with us. That everyone has the chance to receive education and shape their own future.
 
Organizations also have a key role to play in this. Creating environments where upskilling and exchange are encouraged helps people grow, not only professionally, but also as active members of society. And by offering young people the opportunity to enter the job market – keeping on learning beyond.
 
At Henkel, we strive to make learning a natural part of everyday work, across generations, regions, roles, and stages of life.
 
I would like to thank everyone who learns, teaches, mentors, and shares knowledge, helping keep curiosity and dialogue alive.

134 years. That’s how long it could take to close the global gender gap at the current pace, according to the World Economic Forum.

At Beiersdorf, we made a conscious decision years ago: we want to be as diverse as the consumers and communities we serve.

Back then in 2017, women held only 28.8% of top management roles, and our Executive Board was entirely male. As a team, we listened carefully and challenged our assumptions to rethink what needs to be true to change that - and reach gender parity. 

Four levers became central to this journey
💙 ensuring fairness in how we hire and promote 
💙 strengthening our internal talent pipelines 
💙 fostering inclusive leadership globally
💙 and embedding flexibility into career paths – for example, through jobsharing (a game changer!)

The result: in 2023, we reached gender parity across all global management levels, including our Executive and Supervisory Boards. And we’ve sustained it since.

I’m very proud of our progress but we can only scale when we share and build on what works. That’s why exchange with others matters. And today I had one of these opportunities: a group of leaders from the “A Seat at the Table” initiative by manager magazin visited us to exchange about our gender parity journey.

Thank you to Simone, and to all participants, for the open dialogue. And to our colleagues Misel, Christina, Birte and Kibreab for bringing this topic to life by sharing your insights and jobsharing experiences.

My Daily Question: “Am I a Good Leader?”

Was I a good leader today?

Not perfect. Just present. 
Did I listen enough? 
Did I create clarity? 
Did I create an environment where others can thrive?
Did I make someone feel valued?

Other days, I see room to grow and to be very honest, I am not happy with myself. 
And that’s okay because leadership is a journey, not a destination.

You can’t force productivity. You build it through environments where people feel trusted, valued, and empowered.

During my keynote at Mercer’s Human Works Conference themed "All eyes on productivity", I shared how HR is taking the lead as a strategic co-pilot to create environments that help people thrive and, in turn, drive productivity. When designing the employee experience at Beiersdorf, I always return to three beliefs that anchor how we bring our purpose to life.

1️⃣ 𝗔𝘀 𝗱𝗶𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗲 𝗮𝘀 𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗲𝗿𝘀
To truly build an inclusive culture, you need both mindset and action: leaders who understand inclusion and systems that make it real. We reached global gender parity among our leaders in 2023, continue to advance disability inclusion through, for instance, our employee community “Ability” and have embarked on a major journey to upskill all 3,000+ people leaders through our three-month DEI Essentials program with around 70% already finished.

2️⃣ 𝗢𝘂𝘁𝗽𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲 𝗵𝗮𝗽𝗽𝗲𝗻𝘀 𝘄𝗵𝗲𝗻 𝗲𝗺𝗽𝗹𝗼𝘆𝗲𝗲𝘀 𝗰𝗮𝗻 𝗯𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗶𝗿 𝗯𝗲𝘀𝘁 𝘀𝗲𝗹𝗳
Enabling everyone to be their best self means giving people the flexibility and security they need to thrive at work and beyond. That’s why we offer flexible working models, including 42 job-sharing tandems (over half in leadership roles), and support our employees in the Moments that Matter through our Global Critical Illness Policy, which provides paid leave, job security, and care for those facing life’s toughest challenges, whether personally or as caregivers.

3️⃣ 𝗪𝗲 𝗯𝗲𝗹𝗶𝗲𝘃𝗲 𝗶𝗻 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝘄𝗲𝗿 𝗼𝗳 𝘄𝗲
One of the clearest examples of how care connects people, builds pride, and strengthens engagement across our company is our global Care Beyond Skin Day. Every year, more than 10,000 colleagues across 65 countries dedicate over 60,000 hours to local volunteering projects giving their time, skills, and heart. Our internal research confirms what we feel: 72% of participants say the experience makes them feel more engaged and connected to Beiersdorf

In the end, it’s simple: when people feel seen, valued, and empowered they bring their best selves to work and that’s what drives real productivity. Our role as senior leaders is getting the balance right between raising the bar for performance in an increasingly more difficult environment while strengthening a culture where everyone can thrive. If these two go together, we can unlock productivity.

The closer we stay to our people, the better we lead

Staying in touch with our people is one of the most important parts of my role. That’s why I make it a priority to be approachable and to regularly connect with colleagues across all levels – to listen, to learn, and to exchange perspectives. Our Lunch Connect format in HR is a wonderful opportunity to spend valuable time with colleagues across the organization.

Whether it’s a town hall, a team meeting, or just a chat in the coffee kitchen, every conversation helps me understand what matters most to our colleagues. It’s my daily dose of learning, inspiration, and connection.

Our recent HR Lunch Connect was another great example of how powerful these informal moments can be. We talked about career journeys, our own modernization, the importance of learning and what is next on the agenda.  Every time I walk away with new ideas and a deeper appreciation for the passion and purpose that drive our people.

A big thank you to Talita Queiroz Alves, Gloria S., Anna Nina Börner, and Elisa Maehl for such an open, inspiring conversation and for your honesty, passion, and great ideas! I learned a lot from you!

Day 87 of #100DaysWithTVS ➡️ 
🚨 Would I trust HDFC AMC’s management with another ₹1,000 crore?

To answer that, don’t just look at profit growth. 👇 

🤜 I looked at five years of capital allocation — FY21 to FY25.

1️⃣ Did management reinvest wisely?

HDFC AMC is an asset-light business, so it doesn’t need huge amounts of money for factories, inventory or heavy machinery.

Over FY21–FY25, PAT increased from ₹1,326 crore to ₹2,461 crore — an ~16.7% CAGR. Revenue rose from ₹1,853 crore to ₹3,498 crore. At the same time, the company continued investing in technology, distribution and newer businesses such as PMS/AIF.

In FY26, capex was only around ₹22.6 crore, showing that the business can grow without consuming massive amounts of capital.

2️⃣ Did management hoard cash? 💰

Yes — HDFC AMC has accumulated significant cash and investments.
But this isn’t automatically a negative.

For an AMC, maintaining a strong balance sheet provides flexibility and reduces financial risk.

The important question is whether excess cash is eventually returned to shareholders or deployed productively.

HDFC AMC has used a combination of dividends, investments and business expansion, rather than simply burning cash.

3️⃣ Did management dilute shareholders? 👇 

Over the period, there hasn't been a major equity dilution story where management repeatedly issued shares to fund growth.

That means existing shareholders have not been constantly asked to give up their ownership to finance expansion.

4️⃣ Did management overborrow? 👇 

The company has maintained a debt-free/very low-debt balance sheet, while generating strong operating cash flow.

That means growth has largely been funded internally rather than through aggressive borrowing.

🏆 My Verdict: YES — I would trust them with another ₹1,000 crore. 👇 

Why?
Because the last 5 years show a relatively disciplined capital-allocation approach:

🤑 Strong cash generation + low debt + limited dilution + selective reinvestment + shareholder distributions.

The biggest question going forward isn't whether management can generate cash.

👉 It's whether they can deploy the growing cash pile at attractive returns without overpaying for growth.

So I wouldn't give them ₹1,000 crore blindly.

👉 But based on their capital-allocation track record, I would trust management to handle it.

The Valuation School Parth Verma

Bhai, ₹15 lakh ka package mil gaya!

A young professional told me this recently.

The excitement was obvious.

And honestly, it reminded me of something I've seen happen far too often.

The CTC becomes the headline.
The number people proudly tell their parents.

The number they mention when friends ask, “Kitne ka package mila?”

₹8 lakh.
₹15 lakh.
₹25 lakh.

But a few months later, reality usually introduces itself through a salary slip.

Because CTC and in-hand salary are two very different conversations.

There's PF.
There's tax.
There are components that don't land in your bank account every month.

And suddenly, the ₹15 lakh you were celebrating starts looking very different when divided by 12.

I don't blame anyone for getting excited about a big CTC.

It's a big milestone.

But over the years, I've realised that one number alone rarely tells the full story.

Maybe before celebrating the package, we should start asking a more practical question:

“Month-end mein account mein kitna aayega?”

Because that's usually the number that tells you how much your new job will actually change your life.

5 habits that make me more productive.

1. Monthly reset ritual. Every 1st of the month, I spend 45 mins writing my vision and dream outcome for the month. Then write down what I’m actually gonna do every week. I use Matt Gray's Personal Board Meeting template. It removes the distractions and keeps me on what actually moves me forward.

2. Sweat at least 3-4 times per week. Gym, swim, dance or some kind of movement.

3. Sunsama. I was against productivity tools because you can waste a lot of time setting them up. I use it for one thing: the timer. Claude reviews my week and shows me where I underestimate time taken to do something so I can plan better in the future.

4. Write every day. I journal, and I also write for my newsletter and LinkedIn. Journaling removes cognitive load. Writing makes my thoughts sharper. Most of my ideas for solving other people's problems start there.

5. 8 hours of sleep. I’ve stopped trying to be an early riser lol. I just work better after 2pm. Every time I try to get up earlier I'm sluggish all day. This is still the habit I want to work on because I can really feel the difference.

Midweek reminder for anyone trying to figure out LinkedIn

You don’t need Premium to start building your personal brand here.

Seriously.

Before paying for more features, make sure you’re actually maximising the free ones.


Here’s where I’d start:

1️⃣ Make your headline searchable.

Don’t stop at “Executive at XYZ”.

Tell me what you do + your expertise + what you want to be found for.

Think: HR | Talent Development | Employee Engagement

Those are also the keywords people may search for.


2️⃣ Write your About section like YOU.

Please retire:

“Results-driven professional with a proven track record…”

😭

Tell people what you do, what you’re good at and what you’re building towards.


3️⃣ Don’t copy your job description.

Your Experience section should show what you actually did.

Projects. Results. Tools. Problems solved. Improvements made.


4️⃣ You don’t need to post every day.

Start with once a week.

Share something you learnt at work, an industry update, a mistake, a project or your perspective on something happening in your field.

You already have content. 
You probably just don’t call it content.


5️⃣ Stop commenting “Great post!”

Add an opinion. 
Ask a question. 
Share your experience.

Sometimes people discover you through somebody else’s comment section before they ever see your post.


6️⃣ Connect before you need something.

Industry peers. Recruiters. Alumni. Leaders. People you meet at events. People whose work you genuinely follow.

Networking gets very awkward when your first message is also your first request. 


7️⃣ Use AI, but don’t let AI invent you.

Use ChatGPT, Claude  or Gemini to clean up your headline, About section or content.

Give it your real experience first.

AI can package your value.
It cannot manufacture credibility.


Premium gives you more features.
It doesn’t give you a personal brand.


Start with the free version. 
Build your profile. 
Build your voice. 
Build relationships. 
Be searchable.

Then decide whether you actually need Premium.


That’s my midweek reminder for anyone quietly trying to figure this platform out.

"One merger, three companies, countless zeros added to shareholder value."

The smartest move Shriram Finance made in 5 years wasn’t a buyback or dividend—it was a merger.

Day 83 of 100.

Shriram Group merged Shriram Transport Finance, Shriram City Union Finance, and Shriram Capital into one company: Shriram Finance.

But the most interesting part is that after this merger the company got diversified and bigger and now it is one of India’s largest retail NBFCs, not just a truck-loan company.

Through this merger it became one strong entity that can borrow more easily and at lower cost, improving margins and ROE.

It's better for shareholders because everyone now owns a stake in a single, listed operating company with better liquidity and clearer valuation.

After the merger AUM crossed ₹3 lakh crore, profits jumped (Q4 FY26 PAT up ~41%), and the stock’s P/E rerated higher


This merger turned three good businesses into one much stronger, more valuable company—clearly a smart, value-creating decision.

In business, the smartest capital allocation decision can shape your future, or the worst can ruin it.

Two agriculture companies. Similar industry.
But investors are valuing them VERY differently. 👀

So I asked a simple question:

Why?

I compared Coromandel International and Godrej Agrovet on P/E, growth, margins, ROE, debt and overall business quality.

And the valuation gap starts making sense.

1. Growth is the biggest differentiator

Coromandel has been growing faster, with FY26 revenue up ~30% and EBITDA up ~23%.

Godrej Agrovet’s growth was more moderate.

Markets usually don't pay a premium for today's profits.

They pay for tomorrow's profits.

2. Balance sheet matters

Coromandel's debt/equity is around 0.12x, while Godrej Agrovet is around 0.73x.

Lower leverage gives Coromandel more room to invest and grow without putting as much pressure on the balance sheet.

 3. Business quality ≠ just ROE

Interestingly, Godrej Agrovet had a higher FY26 ROE of roughly 19%, compared with ~16% for Coromandel.

So why doesn't it command the higher valuation?

Because investors are looking beyond one metric.

Growth visibility + balance sheet strength + consistency are what can create a valuation premium.

And that's the interesting part about P/E.

A higher P/E doesn't automatically mean a stock is expensive.

A lower P/E doesn't automatically mean it's cheap.

The real question is:
“What am I getting in return for the price I'm paying?”

That's where valuation analysis gets interesting. 📊

Capital Allocation Audit: Would I Trust Management With Another ₹1,000 Crore?

​Headline: Would I hand Thyrocare Technologies another ₹1,000 crore to deploy? Here is the capital allocation verdict based on the last 5 years of cash flows. 

​In equity research, evaluating past capital allocation tells you if a management team acts as responsible stewards of shareholder capital or if they burn cash on empire-building.

​If I had to hand Thyrocare ₹1,000 crore today, here is the clear verdict based on the hard evidence:

🔍 The Hard Evidence

​1. Zero Financial Leverage (No Debt Burden):-

Unlike aggressive health-tech platforms that piled on high-interest debt, Thyrocare's management kept the core operating company 100% debt-free. They financed facility automation and regional hub upgrades purely through internal cash flows.

​2. Exceptional Cash Returned to Shareholders:-

Over the last 5 years, management consistently maintained a dividend payout ratio of >75% of operating cash flows. Instead of hoarding non-earning cash on the balance sheet, they returned excess profits straight to investors.

​3. Disciplined M&A over Ego Buyouts:-

Management avoided vanity, expensive mega-mergers. Instead, they deployed small, targeted cash bites into strategic bolt-on assets like Think Health (adding home-ECG capabilities) and Polo Labs to fill specific market gaps without overpaying.

​4. Resolution of Parent-Level Overhang:-

When parent entity API Holdings (PharmEasy) faced debt pressures, Thyrocare's cash generation remained insulated. With API Holdings completing its parent-level debt payoff, promoter-level pledged shares were fully released—clearing the major balance-sheet overhang without diluting minority shareholders.  

​💡 THE VERDICT: YES (With Strategic Guardrails)
​Yes, I would trust this management with capital—specifically for expanding execution.
​Thyrocare has proven that it does not empire-build, overborrow, or dilute shareholders. 

It operates as an ultra-efficient capital return machine: run low-cost operations, reinvest only what is needed for organic growth, and pass the rest to owners.

​As long as management maintains its strict dividend discipline and avoids large, unproven acquisitions, capital deployed here remains in safe hands.

Sometimes the reason your resume isn't working is that you haven't decided what job it's supposed to help you win.

That sounds obvious.
It becomes less obvious when your experience could credibly point in three different directions.
Imagine this:
You have experience in operations.
You also worked with clients.
You also  managed projects.
You have  also picked up some analytics skills.
So you apply for operations roles.
Then project roles.
Then business analyst roles.
Then you look at the resume and think: Maybe the formatting is the problem or need more refine it.
So you rewrite it.
Then now think,
Maybe I need more keywords. You add those too.But the deeper problem may still be there. The resume is accurate.
It just isn't making a clear case for where you fit next.
That distinction matters.
A strong career story usually has a sequence:
JOB TARGET: What role are you actually pursuing?
POSITIONING: Why should someone see you as relevant to that role?
RELEVANT EXPERIENCE: Which experience, skills and achievements support that positioning?
RESUME: Does the document make that experience easy to understand?
LINKEDIN: Does your professional profile reinforce the same direction?
INTERVIEW: Can you explain the same career story when someone asks Tell me about yourself?
Notice where the resume appears.
It is not first. It is  an expression of the positioning decision.
So before opening your resume, run this solving:
1. TARGET: Can I name the specific role or direction I'm pursuing?
2. NEED: What problem does that role need someone like me to solve?
3. EXPERIENCE: What have I actually done that demonstrates I can contribute to that problem?
4. EMPHASIS: Does my resume make that evidence more visible than less-relevant experience?
5. CONSISTENCY:  Would someone looking at my LinkedIn reach roughly the same conclusion about my professional direction?
If you struggle with the first two questions, rewriting your resume may be premature.
If you know the target but can't find convincing evidence, you may have an evidence or experience gap, not simply a resume problem.
If the evidence exists but is buried, that's when document optimization becomes much more useful.
That's the reframe:
Don't start by asking, How do I make my resume better?
Start by asking:
What do I want this resume to make someone understand about me?
Once that answer is clear, the editing becomes much easier to understand

Save this post  before your next resume rewrite.

More Practice Questions Do Not Automatically Produce Better BCBA Examination Performance

Repeatedly answering similar questions may improve familiarity without producing conceptual flexibility.

A candidate may memorize that deprivation is an establishing operation, yet still misclassify an antecedent when a scenario contains both a motivating operation and a discriminative stimulus. Knowing the label is not the same as analyzing the controlling relations.

Effective preparation requires candidates to:

* Explain why an answer is correct.
* Refute the competing alternatives.
* Identify missing information.
* Predict how the answer changes when the scenario changes.
* Apply the concept across unfamiliar examples.

That is why my Socratic teaching style consultation emphasizes depth rather than the mechanical completion of large question banks.

A scammer who almost looked like a perfect CEO
I want to share something that happened to me last month.
We received an email from someone introducing herself as Daniela Salvoni , founder of an Italian company.
At first, I checked her LinkedIn profile.
Everything looked almost too perfect — CEO & Founder, impressive background, very professional profile.
But somehow, the email didn't feel right.
It looked very much like a template used in scam emails.
So I decided to be careful.
I replied with some basic information about our company and products, and also sent her a LinkedIn connection request.
She never accepted it.
We continued exchanging emails for a while, including some technical discussions and drawings.
Then came the moment that really confirmed my suspicion.
When I asked for technical drawings, she started sending files with strange extensions.
Today, I received an HTML link.
That immediately reminded me of something my Amazon mentor told me on my very first day in international trade:
Never open an HTML link from an unknown email.
It could be used to steal company information or compromise your IT system.
He even told me how expensive the consequences could be if confidential company information was involved.
That number was big enough for me to remember this rule ever since.
I know this is a basic rule in the workplace.
But I still wanted to share it because scammers are getting much better at pretending to be real people.
A perfect LinkedIn profile doesn't necessarily mean a real person.
And this isn't just something I heard about.
At my previous company, a hacker once impersonated a colleague and communicated with a customer by email. The customer ended up transferring money to a different bank account.
Even the customer's finance team didn't notice that the sender's email domain had been slightly changed.
That experience taught me something simple:
In international business, trust is important.
But verification is even more important.
Sometimes, being cautious isn't being difficult.
It's just doing your job properly.

After a 40-year career in HR—and over five truly incredible years at Google —I have decided to retire at the end of Q2. My family all lives in Europe, and as my mum gets older, I want to prioritize spending quality time with them.

While I’m sharing this news externally today, this transition has been thoughtfully underway for several months. I recently first shared my plans internally at Google and with my People Operations organization back in March, and will be staying on for a short period to support the team’s transition. The company expects to name a new Chief People Officer sometime later this year.

When I look back over the last four decades, it is astonishing to see how much the HR profession has evolved. We've gone through periods where the function was heavily weighed down by process and administration, but today, we are on the cusp of something extraordinary.

Watching AI begin to fundamentally reshape how we work fills me with so much hope and excitement for the future of HR. Is it finally going to strip away the process work and allow teams to do what they do best: focus entirely on the human element? I truly hope so.

I’m so grateful to have worked with many amazing companies and my time at Google has undoubtedly been the highlight of my career. Leading this team and seeing the company transform through our hard work and change management has been the privilege of my life. Google is a remarkably special place, full of kind and brilliant people who are actively building the future and shaping the world as we lean into the age of AI.

Professionally, it is difficult to step away when things are this exciting, but personal and professional timelines rarely align perfectly. I am so proud of what the People Operations team has built together to set the foundations for this success—supporting Google and Googlers to get ready for this new era.

Rahul Jindal's latest paper on “Organizational Metabolism” is a masterclass in shifting our focus from AI adoption to AI absorption. His core thesis? The real differentiator in 2026 isn't your technology budget—it’s your "Metabolic Rate."
The framework’s biggest win is the concept of Workflow Debt. We are often layering AI on top of legacy processes instead of retiring them. As Rahul puts it: "Low-metabolism organizations accumulate experiments. High-metabolism organizations retire workflows."
The one piece I think we still need to solve for: The Emotional Metabolism.
While the structural roadmap is brilliant, we can’t ignore the "human immune system." Retiring a workflow can feel like retiring an identity. For an organization to truly become "Adaptive," we have to figure out how to build the psychological safety that allows teams to dismantle their own processes without fearing for their future.

January always sets the tone. It is a moment to define who we want to be in the year ahead – professionally and personally – and to anchor ourselves in purpose.
 
Attending the World Economic Forum Annual Meetings this year reminded me that progress is not about crossing items off a list. It is about expanding your mind while staying grounded in your values.
 
This year in Davos, AI was not just on the agenda – AI took center stage, and for good reason. Policymakers and business leaders across the globe are grappling with how AI is rewriting the rules of work, commerce, and daily life.
 
At Davos, Visa showed up in force. In every session, in every conversation, that sense of purpose resonated. Visa is contributing to shaping a human-centered, AI-powered future, where humans are in charge, and AI amplifies our potential. And, with our purpose always in sight, we are building the future of payments: uplifting economies, businesses, and communities and expanding the circle of opportunity.
 
Discussions on AI and the future of work, including with Judson Althoff and Carl Eschenbach, left me fired up and inspired. On The Female Quotient panel, I reaffirmed that people remain at the center of progress. At a PwC panel focusing on early career development, I underscored the extraordinary opportunity AI creates as a career accelerator. Strong leaders are those creating cultures where curiosity is encouraged, skills evolve continuously, and technology becomes a tool for amplifying human creativity and judgment.
 
Thank you to #WEF26 and our incredible Visa delegation for a powerful week of learning and connection. Our path forward is exciting and fueled, always, by purpose.

Yesterday, I had the honor of moderating an incredibly inspiring World Economic Forum session on AI and the future of work, with two visionary leaders Judson Althoff and Carl Eschenbach. Yesterday’s discussion made it clear that while AI continues to transform our world, it is our people – with their creativity, adaptability, and judgment – who are powering the future. 

We came away with three clear lessons leaders can use when empowering people to lead with AI:

1. Optimism over anxiety. The conversation is shifting, and employees are increasingly hopeful about what AI can do for them and their organizations. Success starts with leaders who champion and empower their teams to see challenges as opportunities. 

2. AI is for everyone. Universal adoption is key. AI should amplify every employee’s impact, regardless of their role. Commit to championing AI literacy in your organization, ensuring every person has the confidence and skills to thrive alongside AI tools. 

3. AI is the tool, but people are the power. Your people are the engine of transformation – fuel them. As leaders, we must invest in both cutting-edge tools and world-class training equally. When we do both, we do more than adopt AI – we lead the future.

Thank you to Judson and Carl for sharing your perspectives in such an insightful discussion. I look forward to helping shape the future of work we discussed – a future where AI amplifies and empowers what makes us uniquely human. #WEF26 Workday Microsoft

Today marks #WorldCancerDay, a day that hits close to home for me.

Cancer has affected my life in very personal ways—my dad fought prostate cancer for more than 17 years and my mom faced stage 3b breast cancer. And just last year, one of my routine screenings came back with an irregular result. Like so many people who face this type of unexpected news during their preventive screenings, my first reaction was fear. Thanks to Merck’s comprehensive benefits, I was able to quickly get follow-up testing and a biopsy — and fortunately, everything came back clear.

These tough moments remind me of how much access and support matter. That’s why I am so proud of the progress our company has made in support of cancer prevention and early detection. In under a year, we have expanded access to WHO-recommended screenings (breast, cervical, colorectal), HPV-related cancer vaccinations, and the time and flexibility to use these services—now reaching more than 96% of employees and their families across 71 countries. The team continues the hard work to extend these benefits where they are not yet available.  

I’m so grateful to everyone at Merck who made this possible and to all those working tirelessly to advance cancer prevention, early detection and care.

One of the most important questions in today’s world of work is: How do we help people keep growing when skills are changing faster than ever before?
 
Today marks a proud moment for SAP, and an important milestone in our journey to become a truly skills-led organization.
With the internal launch of the Growth Portfolio for approximately 84,000 employees so far, we are bringing skills, learning, and career opportunities together in one experience through SAP SuccessFactors and the HCM Talent Intelligence Hub.

This is more than the launch of a new experience. It is a meaningful step in transforming how we support employee development at SAP, making skills more visible, development more personalized, and growth opportunities easier to discover.

As AI reshapes the world of work, employees need clarity on their strengths, visibility into emerging and future-facing skills, and guidance on where to grow next.
 
Our Growth Portfolio helps make that possible by enabling employees to:
 
→ showcase their skills, strengths, and aspirations
→ better understand their current capabilities and future skill needs
→ discover adjacent and future-facing career opportunities
→ receive AI-powered recommendations for learning and development
→ understand skill gaps and how to close them
→ connect learning more directly to career growth and internal opportunities
→ gain greater visibility into the AI skills that will shape the future
→ take greater ownership of their personal growth journey

For leaders, it provides a more dynamic view of team capabilities and helps support stronger, future-focused employee development, so we can develop, mobilize, and grow skills where they matter most.

What makes me especially proud is that this milestone puts employees at the center of our skills-led transformation. By making skills more visible and development more personalized, we are helping our people navigate change with confidence, unlock new opportunities, and continue building the skills that will shape the future of SAP.

A heartfelt thank you to everyone who helped bring the Growth Portfolio to life. This is a moment to celebrate, and an exciting starting point for the next chapter of employee development at SAP.

I’m excited to see how our colleagues use the Growth Portfolio to build new skills, explore new opportunities, and shape their future at SAP.

Belonging does not happen by design alone. It is something we create, every day. 

As executive sponsor of Cultures@SAP, this is something I deeply care about. And as a half-Italian, I have always believed that some of the most important things in life can be expressed through food.

At the Multicultural Evening a few days ago, celebrating 20 years of this remarkable network, I shared a simple idea: belonging, too, follows a recipe. 

For me, that recipe has four essential ingredients:

First, culture. Recognizing that every colleague brings a unique perspective, history, and way of seeing the world. 
Second, curiosity. The willingness to ask, listen, and learn. It is one of the most practical and powerful forms of inclusion. 
Third, community. Built by people who invest time, energy, and passion. For two decades, volunteers have been the driving force behind Cultures@SAP, creating spaces where others feel seen and connected. 
And finally, sharing. Because like any good meal, culture only creates impact when it is experienced together and opened up to others. 

What matters to me is that this is not separate from business at SAP. Cultural intelligence strengthens collaboration, builds trust, and enables better decisions in a truly global company. 

Thank you to everyone who has contributed to Cultures@SAP over the past 20 years. You have turned diversity into connection — and connection into belonging.

Transformation is no longer a sequence of initiatives – it is happening everywhere, all at once.

At the German-speaking SAP User Group (DSAG e.V.) Personaltage event in Heidelberg, discussions showed: the shift toward an #AutonomousEnterprise is not about automation in the traditional sense. It is about intelligent assistants and agents that can operate end-to-end; augmented, orchestrated, and always with humans in the loop.

Three core takeaways I shared with the audience:
➖ Rewiring the organization for an AI-native world
We are moving from vertical silos to horizontal, end-to-end value streams. Agents operate across domains, so organizations must follow. This requires new operating models, orchestration layers, and hybrid teams where humans and AI collaborate seamlessly.
➖ Skills as the foundation of adaptability
With skill half-lives shrinking to 6–18 months, organizations need to become truly skill-based. “Learn to unlearn,” continuous reskilling, and real-time skill intelligence are becoming core capabilities for staying relevant.
➖ Human leadership remains central
In an Autonomous Enterprise, humans stay in the driver’s seat. Judgment, empathy, and ethical guardrails matter more, not less. The real challenge is to create the conditions for people to adopt, trust, and effectively work with AI.
 
During our joint panel, Hermann-Josef Haag, Board Member at DSAG, moderator Juliane Krampe, and I debated the following:
➖ Transformation is less a technology challenge, but increasingly a people, prioritization, and leadership challenge
➖ Organizations are managing multiple shifts at once: AI, architecture changes, workforce transformation, and external pressures
➖ The biggest pain points we see across customers are strategic workforce planning, skills transparency, and connecting data across HR, finance, and processes
➖ Progress requires clear target states and pragmatic, phased execution
➖ And most importantly: no organization can navigate this alone. Ecosystems and exchange are critical
 
From a broader SAP perspective, this reinforces our direction: enabling customers to run end-to-end business processes with integrated AI, data, and applications, while embedding people, skills, and change deeply into our transformation journey. Because ultimately, becoming an Autonomous Enterprise is about building adaptive organizations and ensuring employees have the enablement, support, and confidence to thrive in this new reality.

The pace will not slow down. The differentiator will be how deliberately we combine technology and human potential to shape what comes next.

That became very tangible for me last week across Singapore, Melbourne, and Sydney. I had the opportunity to speak and engage with customers, partners, employees, and early-career talent, and the core questions were remarkably consistent: How do we turn AI ambition into adoption? How do we redesign work, not just add tools? And how do we build the skills and leadership needed to make that transition real?

My conversations with customers and partners made one thing very clear: people strategy is business strategy. In CHRO roundtables, customer meetings, and partner exchanges, the focus was not only on technology, but on workforce transformation, skills, AI adoption, and performance culture. That is exactly where our People Agenda becomes a business agenda. 
The same was true in our global People & Culture Employee Meeting live from Singapore. One reason I valued the session with Alexandra Steiger so much is that it reinforced the outside-in perspective: strategy is important, but the real question is how credibly we translate it into organizational readiness, workforce capability, and measurable progress.
From a P&C perspective, helping build the #AutonomousEnterprise means enabling adoption, strengthening skills, supporting role and work redesign, and connecting our priorities much more tightly to business execution.

These candid conversations, hosted by LIHER URBIZU in Southeast Asia and by Tim Bryant, Debbie Rigger and Simon Morris, (CAHRI) in ANZ, created space for direct dialogue, honest questions, and real exchange. We need to bring the next generation in - but we also need to rethink early-career entry points, development paths, and learning experiences for a very different world of work. Critical thinking, judgment, and resilience will matter even more.

We clearly see the shift from AI as a productivity feature toward AI embedded into end-to-end business processes, grounded in trusted data, process expertise, and governance. A very different (but equally memorable) moment was the Celebrity Keynote with #RogerFederer in conversation with our CEO Christian Klein. What stayed with me most was not the trophies, but the mindset behind a decades‑long career at the very top.
From a people perspective, three themes really stood out: #discipline, #resilience and #continuousgrowth. Federer talked about staying “coachable” even when you are already successful, being willing to keep learning, and having “fire in your belly and ice in your veins” when the pressure is highest. Finally, his focus on character and how you treat people really resonated with me. Excellence is not just what you deliver, but how you show up for others – on the court, in the office, and in our communities. That is the kind of leadership mindset we want to develop and reward.
 
Roger Federer demonstrated adaptability and reinvention as the real edge.

During last week’s HANNOVER MESSE, one thing became very clear: AI is already embedded in real business processes – from the shop floor to supply chains and enterprise systems.
At the SAP booth, this became tangible through a simple but powerful example: the production of a ginger shot. From planning and mixing to packaging and delivery, AI connects the entire process – with agents monitoring production, robots inspecting quality, and AI copilots supporting decisions in real time. What used to be fragmented becomes one integrated flow.
 
This is a remarkable shift: AI is not just supporting tasks. It is orchestrating outcomes across systems, teams, and physical operations. A simple way to think about it: It’s Monday morning. You start your job – and your AI teammate is already at work. Analyzing data, simulating scenarios, preparing decisions. What changes is not just speed. What changes is how work itself is designed.
 
But technology alone does not create value. The real question is whether we are redesigning work fast enough to unlock its full potential.
Because this transformation changes the fundamentals: We go from executing tasks to orchestrating outcomes, from rigid roles to dynamic skills, and from isolated tools to integrated, AI-supported processes.
 
That was the focus of our engaging discussion on the Center Stage: Skills are becoming the new currency of work. In a world where capabilities evolve continuously, the differentiator is not what people know today, but how quickly they learn, adapt, and apply.
 
For companies, this means: AI transformation is not a technology program. It is a work redesign and leadership challenge. Technology creates potential, but organizations need to learn how to turn it into impact.

AI is already more powerful than what most organizations are able to realize today.

This idea kept coming up at Lake Como last week in conversations with business leaders. The challenge is turning that potential into new ways of working, new skills, and real business impact. That was the focus of the SAP Italy Executive Summit, where more than 100 leaders came together to discuss how to build future-ready organizations in an AI-driven world.

In my conversations with Lavinia Spingardi, Carla Masperi, and Augusta Spinelli, we explored why so many companies still struggle to unlock AI at scale: Many are still trying to layer AI onto fragmented data landscapes, siloed processes, and legacy operating models. As a result, AI remains isolated in use cases instead of transforming how work actually gets done.

Organizations that move ahead take a different approach: they redesign workflows end-to-end, integrate AI directly into core processes, and clearly state where decisions are augmented by AI, and where accountability remains human.

During an interview with Giulia Cimpanelli for La Repubblica, another dynamic became very clear: many organizations are currently in the productivity dip of AI transformation. That dip exists because work is being rebuilt while results are not yet visible. People are learning new skills, roles are shifting, and processes are being redesigned at the same time. The critical mistake is to interpret this phase as failure. In reality, it’s where the real work happens – rebuilding skills, processes, and ways of working.
This is exactly the moment where leadership matters most. Being clear about direction, transparent about what’s changing, and giving people the space to learn and adapt, even when things feel less efficient at first.

Grateful for the conversations, the openness, and the shared ambition to not just adopt AI, but to truly turn it into value for business and people.

The hardest part of AI transformation is not the technology. It is changing how work actually gets done.

Research points in the same direction: only a small share of AI value comes from the algorithms themselves. The bigger shift happens through people, processes and leadership; when organizations rethink roles, build new skills, and redesign how work happens.
That was at the heart of our first People & Culture Manager Day and the 2026 P&C Kick-Off at SAP, where colleagues from Mannheim, Prague, Bangalore, Newtown Square, Manila and many other locations came together to discuss what this means for the business and for P&C in particular.

Several insights stood out for me:
➔ Futurrist Ian Beacraft challenged us to think beyond automation: AI is reshaping how work is designed, how decisions are made, and which human capabilities create the most value.
➔ Kathi Enderes reinforced that the biggest barriers to AI impact are rarely technical, but organizational: skills, leadership, and the ability to translate technology into new ways of working.
➔ And in our panel with Pinar Dolen, Marielle Ehrmann, Dr. Magdalena Masluk-Meller Eric Goldstein and Ian, one point became very clear: if AI is reshaping the business, then People & Culture must transform too.

For us, that means three things in particular: rethinking how work happens with AI at the core, building new skills while unlearning outdated limits, and connecting more effectively across roles and teams to create impact faster.

For People & Culture, this is a defining moment. We’re not watching work change - we’re making it happen: redesigning the operating model, building the skills, and shaping the culture that turns AI into impact.

AI investments are at an all-time high. But a central question for leaders across industries is no longer whether to adopt AI. It’s how to build the capabilities to work with it.

Research gives us some insights on what matters most: Only 10% of AI value comes from algorithms, 20% from technology and data. But 70% comes from people, processes, and leadership. AI transformation is also a leadership and organizational transformational story, not just technology.

This perspective came alive this week at the Münchner Management Kolloquium at Technical University of Munich, where executives, scientists, and founders gathered under the theme “Bold Moves: Managing with Courage” to discuss how Europe can remain competitive in a rapidly changing technological landscape. In our panel with Britta Seeger, Bettina Dietsche, and Dane Molter, moderated by Prof. Dr. Claudia Peus, we explored how AI at work is crafting tomorrow.

One thing became clear: When technology evolves every few months, value no longer comes from what we know, but from how fast we adapt. That is why SAP is moving toward a skills‑led organization. We are entering a world where the shelf life of skills is shrinking dramatically, sometimes to just months.  
Therefore, the real challenge is not introducing AI. It is redesigning work, processes, operating models and skills at the speed AI evolves.

This year’s #MMK26 showed that we are ready for these bold moves. When companies, universities, and communities work together to prepare people for a world where humans and AI collaborate, we are not just ready for the future – we're actively designing it.

Thank you to Ricarda Engelmeier, Prof. Dr. Dr. h. c. mult. Horst Wildemann and everyone who contributed to such a thoughtful discussion.

Building Bridges, Shaping Futures: AFRIKA KOMMT! 

This week, I had the honor of celebrating the 13th cohort of AFRIKA KOMMT! at Schloss Bellevue in Berlin, hosted by President Frank-Walter Steinmeier. 

37 young, talented professionals from across Africa completed this one-year talent development program – and their energy, courage, and curiostiy were truly inspiring. 

AFRIKA KOMMT! has been building bridges since 2008. SAP, together with the former German President Horst Köhler and Tillmann Todenhöfer (Bosch), was among its founding partners. The vision is simple yet bold: connecting young African talent with German companies to learn, grow, and ultimately win as one. 

17 years on, that vision feels more relevant than ever. Actively engaging with the cohort – listening to their journeys, exchanging ideas, and learning from their hopes, challenges, and achievements has moved me deeply. It reaffirmed that cross-cultural collaboration isn’t just good for business; it’s essential for a peaceful future. 

As President Steinmeier put it: “Wir Deutsche wollen unsere Beziehungen zu afrikanischen Ländern nicht nur festigen und stabil halten, wir wollen sie ausbauen. ... Gerade jetzt, in dieser Zeit der Umbrüche, Kriege und Konflikte, gerade jetzt setzen wir Deutsche auf Weltoffenheit – auf Vernetzung statt auf Abschottung, auf Freihandel statt auf Protektionismus, auf mehr statt weniger Zusammenarbeit!”  

His call for openness, connectivity, and deeper collaboration is a clear compass for business – and it mirrors SAP’s commitment to partnership, innovation, and shared growth. 

To all participants of AFRIKA KOMMT! 13: thank you for your ideas, energy, and determination. Keep your networks alive, keep challenging assumptions, and keep paying it forward. 

We are proud to have been part of AFRIKA KOMMT! from day one, and we look forward to welcoming future cohorts to SAP to keep building bridges. The bridges we build today will become the paths others walk tomorrow – let’s keep building, together.

Die Bitkom #TRANSFORM26 in Berlin war für mich ein wertvoller Impulsgeber: Wenn es um Transformation geht, müssen Politik und Wirtschaft eng zusammenrücken.

Im Dialog mit Bundesministerin Karin Prien (BMBFSFJ) und Marcel Fratzscher, Leiter des DIW, stand die zentrale Frage im Raum: „Diversity, Equity, Irrelevance: Kann unsere Wirtschaft auf Vielfalt verzichten?“

Die Antwort ist klar: Gerade für die digitale Transformation und zur Sicherung unserer Wettbewerbsfähigkeit ist #Vielfalt unverzichtbar. Sie ist kein „Nice-to-have“, sondern – in all ihren Facetten – ein entscheidender Wettbewerbsvorteil und ein Motor für #Innovation. Mehr Vielfalt, auch und insbesondere durch mehr Frauen, ist für die Wirtschaft essenziell.

Und mit Blick auf die demografischen Veränderungen in Deutschland wird deutlich: Wir können es uns als Gesellschaft und Wirtschaftsstandort nicht leisten, auf Erfahrung, Kompetenz und Engagement von Frauen zu verzichten.

Um mehr Frauen in Beschäftigung zu bringen, braucht es die richtigen Rahmenbedingungen. Ein zentraler Hebel ist dabei mehr #Flexibilität in der Arbeitszeit. Starre Vorgaben, wann und wie gearbeitet wird, sind in Zeiten von KI und digitaler Arbeit nicht mehr zeitgemäß. Die Einführung einer Wochenarbeitszeit kann hier ein wirkungsvolles Instrument sein: Sie ermöglicht es vielen Menschen, ihre Arbeitszeit auszuweiten und gleichzeitig Beruf und Privatleben selbstbestimmter zu vereinbaren.

Als einer der größten Arbeitgeber in Deutschland schaffen wir bereits heute – im Rahmen der gesetzlichen Möglichkeiten – vielfältige Optionen, um genau das zu unterstützen.

Doch klar ist auch: Ohne mutige politische Rahmenbedingungen und ein gemeinsames Verständnis von moderner Arbeit werden wir das vorhandene Potenzial nicht heben. Wenn wir Transformation wirklich gestalten wollen, müssen wir Vielfalt konsequent fördern, Flexibilität ermöglichen und die Arbeitswelt an die Realität der Menschen anpassen.


Bundesministerium für Bildung, Familie, Senioren, Frauen und Jugend | DIW Berlin - German Institute for Economic Research

After Davos, action begins.

The conversations were valuable. Now comes the hard work of turning them into action.

In my latest article, I share a few reflections from the conversations I had with the people at Davos and what they signal for the road ahead.

I’d love to hear: what actions are you taking after #WEF26?

𝐈𝐧 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐚𝐠𝐞 𝐨𝐟 𝐚𝐠𝐞𝐧𝐭𝐢𝐜 𝐀𝐈, 𝐰𝐡𝐚𝐭 𝐢𝐬 𝐚 𝐣𝐨𝐛, 𝐫𝐞𝐚𝐥𝐥𝐲?

That question framed our panel hosted by KPMG at AI House Davos during World Economic Forum. Together with May Habib and Alessandro De Luca, and moderated by Ashish Madan, we explored how AI and agentic systems are changing the very nature of work and organizations.

👉 A few reflections I keep coming back to:

1️⃣ What still defines a #job? 
A job is, fundamentally, a bundle of tasks or activities performed to achieve a certain outcome. What changes with AI is how these tasks are bundled –through automation or augmentation – and by whom they are performed: humans, machines, and agents. From an economic perspective, jobs are outcome-driven, balancing input and output. And yet, for us humans, a job is more than that. It is also about connection, identity, and purpose.

2️⃣ Transformation stands and falls with #people.
We tend to over-index on tools and technology, but 80% of change is behavioral and cultural. People’s engagement, rooted in trust and psychological safety, determines how fast organizations can really move.

3️⃣ #Leadership faces a paradox: “everything changes – and nothing changes.”
In the age of AI, it is the role of leaders to decide what business they are in and what purpose guides it. And they need to stay in control of what matters most. Leaders remain accountable for business models, quality, ethical decision-making, etc. The fundamentals – trust, empowerment, psychological safety and a growth mindset – matter just as much in the age of AI, if not more.

4️⃣ Which #organizations are we ultimately building?
AI will not lead to radical change unless we rethink our processes and operating models. The real question is which organizations we are ultimately building. This is not about incremental change, but about redesigning systems and enabling new ways of working. We need to be deliberate about where we automate tasks and where we augment human capability. And we must always keep humans in the loop – or even in the lead – because this is where human skills – such as judgment, contextual understanding, and purpose – remain essential.

I remain positive – yet not naive about AI. It can be a powerful enabler, helping us rethink industry, address demographic challenges, democratize knowledge, and protect our planet. 

In the end, the answers often do not lie in the technology alone.
They lie in the choices we make – and in how consciously and purposefully we apply technology, together.

It was a joy and a privilege to talk Circularity at the One Young World Summit in Munich, looking out to a room full of brilliant young leaders. I had the opportunity to engage on a topic that holds immense relevance for us today: how can we learn from circularity in nature and marry those eons of „R&D“ with today’s technology to get back to balance.
 
Life on this planet has always been circular. The ancient rhythm of cycles turns fallen leaves into soil, and returns a river’s water back to the sky. Everything in nature is interconnected. Every end is a new beginning.
And for the longest time, mankind lived by the rules and rhythm of nature - and its resourcefulness.

Yet with industrialization and globalization, we replaced the circle with a straight line - Take. Make. Dispose. The linear model seemed like a promise of growth and prosperity - but not for everyone, and it stretches our planet’s limits.

Now it's time to rebalance. We must decouple growth from resource consumption and change the operating model of the world from linear back to circular.

In this transformation to „circular by design“, technology is our most potent ally. AI and digital twins are enablers of breakthrough innovation in the digital world - with positive impact in the real world. 

Our wonderful young leaders and changemakers will be architects of renewal. If they - we all - choose the circle over the straight line. 

 So, let’s make the circle whole again – together!

80% of companies struggle to capture returns from their Gen AI investments, according to a 2025 McKinsey survey.

So how can we translate #GenAI potential into real #productivity?

There’s no simple answer – but #experimentation brings us closer.

The new Harvard Business Review article captures an important truth: the path to productivity isn’t linear. It’s a “J-curve” that requires a learning mindset and the courage to test, adapt, and scale what really works.

I’m pleased to see this approach, which we embrace at Siemens, featured in the article. For us, it’s experimentation that puts people at the center. In 2024, we ran the first test of our #IndustrialCopilot – a GenAI-powered shop-floor assistant – at our factory in Erlangen. Our maintenance engineers found it saved them time. But the real surprise came from our technicians – especially the more junior and less experienced staff – who said it helped them tackle complex issues more confidently, particularly on night shifts when no engineers were around.

This is what we mean by #TechnologywithPurpose: empowering people, enabling continuous learning, and ensuring digitalization delivers real value for our workforce and customers.

Because an issue articulated – an issue spoken out loud – is an issue that we can address.

Let’s begin with a few simple words, and mean them: 
👉 “How are you?”
💭 “I have not been feeling myself lately…”
