Your career does not always follow the plan you made for it.

Last week at ESMT Berlin I said as much to over 130 graduates from 34 nations. A path that turns out differently does not mean your plan has failed. It means there is room for directions you could not have designed yourself.

I started my own career in 1991 as a Certified Public Accountant, fairly certain of where it would lead. I certainly did not expect to end up in the energy industry, in an Executive Board role at the intersection of HR and IT.

I left the graduates with one further thought: responsibility does not arrive with a title. It arrives much earlier, usually in a perfectly ordinary meeting, at the moment you notice something is not right and have to decide whether to say so out loud.

Thank you to ESMT and to Jörg Rocholl for the invitation, and congratulations to the classes of 2026.

Three years ago, I took on responsibility for both HR and IT on the Executive Board of RWE. A good opportunity to look back and reflect on what has really stayed with me.

I’m taking so much away from these past three years. Above all, a few key lessons stand out:

 ▪️ Developing an international company successfully starts and stands with talent.
 ▪️ Learning has become a core business capability.
 ▪️ The most important transformation happens where technology and people come together.

A few years ago, HR and IT was an unusual combination at board level. Today, I see more organisations moving in a similar direction. Looking back, I am convinced this convergence is no coincidence. Technology transformation and people transformation can no longer be separated.

The rise of AI has made this clearer than ever. Surprisingly, many organisations still approach AI primarily as a technology topic. In my experience, that is only half the story. The real challenge is not deploying the technology. It is enabling people to adopt it, trust it, learn with it and use it to transform the way they work. That is why the connection between HR and IT has moved from valuable to essential: AI has made the partnership between HR and IT a strategic necessity.

As RWE continues to grow internationally, one of our most important tasks is to create opportunities across borders, connect people globally and build career paths that span functions, businesses and countries. At the same time, in a world where skills evolve faster than job descriptions, continuous learning is essential for everyone: specialists, leaders, employees developing new capabilities, and yes, board members as well. What excites me most is seeing how our colleagues continue to embrace new technologies, develop new capabilities and help shape the future of our company.

I feel truly privileged to work at this significant intersection every day. Thank you to everyone across #TeamRWE who contributes to this journey every day.

Together, our energy has impact!

Are you an introvert or an extrovert? It is a question that has become more common. And it is equally relevant for the professional realm.
 
I'd say I’m somewhere between the two – an ambivert. Being with people, building trust and getting them excited about a shared direction brings me energy. On the other hand, there are also aspects of my role that can be draining.
 
Creating space for all perspectives – quiet or outspoken, reflective or spontaneous – is exactly what Carrie Jäger and her team from our Supply & Trading Business are exploring with the initiative "The Power of All Voices". When every voice gets the chance to be heard, we make better decisions together.
 
The initiative made me think of how I make sure that every voice in the room gets the chance to speak. I have two rules for meetings. When I'm leading the room, I stay quiet as long as I can – because I learned very early on that the moment a leader takes a position, the room tends to stop weighing options and starts agreeing with it. So I want other views on the table first. Among peers, I do the reverse. I speak early, knowing that the first voices in such discussions set their direction, whether they deserve to or not.
 
My message to the more reflective voices at RWE is simple: use yours. The outspoken are often heard by default. The more reflective voices need space to be invited in.
 
One habit that helps: bring your perspective into every meeting at least once. It gets easier every time. And more than once, I've watched a nearly unheard voice flip a decision, raising a point everyone else had missed.
 
What's your strategy for making sure everyone gets heard?

Geopolitics, economic volatility, shifting regulation, AI moving fast. Pressure is building on organisations from several directions at once. For HR, helping the business transform is one task. Transforming ourselves to manage these changes is where it gets real.

This task set the tone for our recent HR All Hands Offsite, where our global HR community focused on three areas: how we develop our leaders, how we work with AI, and how we run the function.

When used well, AI makes HR more human, not less. The move that matters is embedding it where the work already happens. As automations take on more of the complex, multi-step tasks, our people can spend more of their time on what technology cannot do: being present, building trust, and being a real human interface to the business.

That's why leadership itself sits at the centre. The job is no longer to keep things steady. It is to grow people who hold a clear direction while their surroundings shift, and to turn our executive programmes into everyday practice.

The same honesty has to apply to how we run the function. The real gain comes from doing things once and well, as one team, and that takes leaders willing to question how we work.

The strongest moments came from learning across the organisation. Our teams shared openly and built on each other. That is #TeamRWE at its best.

Thank you to everyone who contributed and continues to shape the future of HR at RWE.

My position as an Executive Board Member changes every conversation before a word is said. Something which is rarely discussed among top management is that truly honest feedback becomes scarce.

Dissent is phrased more cautiously, feedback loses its sharp edges, and much of what really needs to be expressed remains unsaid. Yet leaders have to be able to rely on people in their own circle who are trustworthy and unaffected by hierarchical differences. And these people, in turn, need an environment where they feel safe and valued.

I greatly value those around me who, despite my role, continue to treat me with clarity and honesty. Today, when I seek advice, I turn to colleagues who approach me with integrity and tell me what they think, regardless of whether or not it's pleasant for me personally. I also seek out conversations with those whose perspectives challenge me, sometimes from angles I wouldn't have considered on my own. They encourage me to re-examine my own take on things, even when I felt certain about it beforehand.

I wasn't born a board member. For most of my career, I sat on the other side of the table. And that’s why I know from personal experience the impact a leadership position can have on others. We must consistently act with courage, steadfastness, and clarity in our interactions with each other!

I am returning from my UK visit, which was all about our offshore wind operations and the people behind them.
 
It started at our Humber Gateway base, meeting the team before joining them on a Crew Transfer Vessel to the wind farm itself. It’s not often I get to see one of our offshore wind farms up so close, and the scale never fails to impress: 73 turbines, 219 megawatts, enough to power up to 199,000 homes.
 
The team's footprint goes well beyond the wind farm. They support local schools to help young people into technical careers – especially girls, half of their apprentices are female. And the proceeds of honey sales from the beehives on site go straight to local community projects.
 
Back onshore, five minutes down the road lies the Grimsby Hub – base to our Triton Knoll and Sofia offshore wind farms and their operating teams. From the control room there, eleven wind farms across the UK are monitored around the clock. Getting to know the teams during a town hall meeting or lunch together was a very insightful experience, until we then watched the Sofia installation crew head out for two weeks at sea – an immense 14 to 16 hours vessel trip to the construction site.
 
The UK is one of RWE's most important offshore wind markets. Our existing fleet, including Humber Gateway and Triton Knoll, delivers power today. What comes next? Earlier this year we secured Contracts for Difference for 6.9 gigawatts of new capacity in UK waters. I believe that people are keen to take on leadership roles if they know that an organisation is investing in them and their professional development. 
 
Many organisations are dealing with leadership fatigue. We don't see this to that extent at RWE. What we do see are leaders guiding their teams through a transformation of historic proportions – and they deserve the best possible preparation and support for the job. It's our commitment and a promise I stand by entirely. 
 
That's the thinking behind our RWE LEAD programme, which started with its first cohort this week. LEAD is part of our Executive Journey – the structured backbone we've built for how leaders grow at RWE, from the first leadership role all the way through to Board level. 
 
35 executives are with us this week – international, from various RWE operating companies, bringing the RWE world together from every angle. They're here to learn with each other and from one another, to challenge their assumptions, and to shape what our Leadership Principles mean in practice. In addition, every cohort meeting is accompanied by a member of our AG Board. Visible, approachable, sharing what they know and learning alongside the group. 
 
A heartfelt thank you to our LEAD participants for their energy and vision and to #TeamRWE behind the programme for getting us to this starting line. Now let’s keep going!

Current debate keeps asking whether AI is a job killer or an engine for growth. From where I sit, it is neither. It is a leadership and organisational stress test – and how we shape it is on us.
 
That was the question our panel at the Allianz der Chancen network meeting in Düsseldorf discussed. Together with representatives from research, business, the political sphere and unions, we looked at how AI is reshaping work, what it means for skills and continuous training, and how transitions can be designed in a socially sustainable way. The decisive variable is not the technology but rather how we lead.
 
One thing is clear: AI does not replace human judgement, it actually raises the need for it. The skills that are gaining in importance are the human ones – critical thinking, leadership and collaboration.
 
This is where business, unions and policy-makers must deliver together by creating room for experimentation, incentivising scaling, investing with focus, and enabling employee participation.
 
Thank you to Nina Weigel for guiding us through the discussion so well, to my fellow panellists Ronald Bachmann, Johannes Pöttering, Jochen Ott and Knut Giesler for the good discussion, and to Andreas Schmitz, Dr. Ariane Reinhart  and the team at Allianz der Chancen for hosting.

Leadership in times of permanent transformation only works when we know and trust each other and pull on the same threads. That was the measure of the last two days at the AG Directors' Leadership Conference. After Madrid and Berlin, this time we deliberately held the AG Board and Directors' meeting in RWE’s hometown of Essen.
 
One central topic was our new Leadership Principles framework. Lead for Business Impact, Lead to Deliver, Lead for Team Success are the three principles that translate our values and Essential Behaviours into clear expectations of how we lead at RWE. They are our Group-wide standard – the one we hold ourselves to and by which we develop the current and next generation of leaders.
 
In times of uncertainty, geopolitical crises and AI disruption, values and behaviours become even more important. Under pressure, there is always a risk of falling back into familiar patterns and unintentionally neglecting important facets of good leadership. That is why spaces like this offsite matter so much. They give us the opportunity to pause, reflect, recalibrate and learn from each other.
 
For me personally, Lead for Team Success is especially important. Business impact and delivery rely on people who feel seen, trusted and capable. Without that foundation, even the best strategy remains mere theory. Leading by example, fostering a sense of belonging, enabling everyone to do their best work is what culture is built upon.
 
My thanks go to our directors for the openness and energy they brought to the room. And to our colleagues from #TeamRWE behind the scenes who made this meeting yet another success.

Why do I keep going on pilgrimage year after year?
 
People walk the Camino de Santiago for many reasons. Some are fulfilling a lifelong dream, whilst others walk for spiritual reasons, to recover from an illness or to come to terms with the loss of a loved one.

For me, it is also an endeavour where the journey is the destination. It has become a personal tradition that during springtime I walk a stretch of it. This year I covered 175 kilometres from La Romieu to Argagnon in France on the Via Podiensis. I cherish these days of being in beautiful nature all day, without meetings nor screens, when my mind can settle, and my body finds the soothing rhythm of the trail.
 
What I find there is something that everyday life rarely affords me: genuine time to reflect, to recharge my batteries and to draw strength. The daily 5 to 7-hour walks carry an element of resilience too. Everyone walks at their own pace and meets their own personal limits. Nothing else allows me to do this in quite the same way.
 
I also cherish the exchange with like-minded pilgrims from all over the world, whom you meet on the trail or over dinner in the lodgings – this year Canadians, Australians, Scots, Israelis, Swiss and Dutch. Despite our different paths and backgrounds, we share the same beautiful experience and many a good conversation.
 
I'm returning to my desk with (let's be honest) slightly tired legs but energised with a fresh and clear mind. Whilst I'm already looking forward to next year's stage over the Pyrenees, the impressions of the last few days will stay with me for quite some time. 🥾

The recipe matters more than the kitchen.
 
That is the title and the central finding of the first paper published by our RWE Commercial AI Lab in Bellevue, Washington State. It argues that in AI weather prediction, how you train a model – the data it learns from, the methods used, what it is rewarded for getting right – matters at least as much as the design of the model itself.
 
The initial findings from our AI Lab are quite something, as they offer direct business value. Better weather prediction means sharper trading decisions, smarter dispatch of renewable assets, and stronger resilience when extremes hit the grid.
 
My sincere thanks to the four authors of the paper: Piyush Garg, Diana Gergel, and Galen Yacalis from our Commercial AI Lab, as well as Andrew Shao, PhD from Hewlett Packard Enterprise. You brought the recipe to the kitchen!
 
Why this matters beyond academia:
 
▪︎ NVIDIA Earth-2 Open Models (FCN3, Atlas) and ECMWF’s AIFS-Ens ranked higher than other models in the overall model assessment. However, no single model performed consistently across all the metrics, thus suggesting that the choice of training pipeline matters more than choosing the right architecture.
▪︎ The study's impact is already resonating within academic institutions and wider groups working on building AI weather models. NVIDIA teams have reached out directly.
▪︎ Using NVIDIA Earth2Studio – the open framework now standard for testing AI weather models – the team validated the results across ten architectures, thirty initialisation dates and four extreme events – the 2021 Pacific Northwest heat dome, the Texas freeze, Winter Storm Elliott and the 2023 heatwave in Europe.
 
What I find most compelling is how this work positions RWE and our research team at the AI Lab as a contributor to the science the AI field depends on. The energy transition runs on forecasts and some of the science behind them is now being shaped at RWE.

AI for value. Humans at the centre. Real impact only happens when AI is truly embedded into everyday work – not as a concept, but as part of how decisions are made, processes run, and teams collaborate.
 
Last week at the Government Innovation Board hosted by GovTech Deutschland, I shared how we at RWE are working with AI, particularly in the context of agentic AI.
 
Four key messages shaped my speech:
 
▪︎ The division of labour is shifting, but the human stays at the centre: Agentic systems prepare tasks, weigh up options and flag where action is needed – always within clear guardrails. Speed, structuring and pattern recognition move to the system. Judgement and decision-making authority remain with people.
▪︎ Real innovation happens in concrete workflows – where processes are genuinely understood and responsibility is lived.
▪︎ Governance builds trust and resilience: AI governance is not optional – it is the foundation for safe, transparent and responsible AI use at scale.
▪︎ AI challenges leadership: leaders must become role models in learning and using AI. Change management is crucial for a successful AI transformation.
 
One thing became clear once again: public administration and industry are working towards a shared agenda – building capabilities, strengthening trust, and scaling AI responsibly – even if at different stages.
 
Many thanks to Markus Richter and Achim Berg for the invitation and dialogue, and to Bernd Gemein for sharing the Deutsche Post perspective.

Leadership has never been about certainty; it has much rather been about helping others move forward without it.
 
End of last week, over 170 colleagues from near and far gathered in Copenhagen for our 7th RWE Group Leadership Meeting. What made this year’s meeting truly special to me was the collective energy in the room which was filled with a sense of purpose, determination and vision. 
 
This year’s theme: Living Leadership. This was chosen because we’re currently witnessing three profound shifts happening simultaneously:

▪︎ Speed and complexity: We are scaling our portfolio, our partnerships and our geographies at pace. Decisions must be driven by competitive outcomes, not by waiting for perfect information, which in the current environment is rarely available.
▪︎ Technology and AI: AI is transforming the tools available to us, creating new opportunities but also uncertainties around accountability, skills, and where human judgement ends and the algorithm begins. AI is not an IT initiative. It is a leadership topic that is relevant to every one of us.
▪︎ Permanent transformation: Change is no longer a phase. It is the operating condition. In this world, resilience is not a soft skill; it is an organisational capability. And the instinct to control complexity can become a liability. Leadership is about creating clarity and adaptability under pressure.

In practice, Living Leadership comes down to the following factors: being explicit about priorities and trade-offs; owning decisions even when AI has shaped the analysis; building teams that are empowered enough to act and where it is safe enough to speak up. But it is also our personal responsibility – leading others requires a strong self. We as leaders need to be fit for future, confident, curious, and capable of performing in this uncompromised environment.  

That is how resilience is built – not through comfort, but through capability.
 
Thank you to everyone involved for two days of clear thinking and meaningful conversations.

Industrial history and personal history are rarely far apart. That connection became very real when 91-year-old Paul Diestelhorst opened his photo albums and gave us a glimpse into a life shaped by the power station in Frimmersdorf. A rare and valuable insight.
 
The demolition of cooling tower Q at the end of February made the connection very tangible. The enormous steel and concrete chimney was built in the 1960s as part of what would become Europe's largest power station at that time. It is a significant part of our company's history and of the region's industrial identity.
 
At the age of 19, Paul came to Frimmersdorf in search of work. What followed was an entire working life with RWE – from power plant operator to control room operator to foreman. He knew every corner of tower Q. And at this advanced age, he witnessed the demolition of the very structure that he helped build and operate for decades.
 
Stories like Paul’s demonstrate to me what makes RWE stand out as an employer: the recognition of every single employee’s contribution. Day in, day out, shift after shift, on land and at sea.
 
With RWE’s accelerated phase-out of coal by 2030, a chapter of industrial history is coming to an end. And at the same time, our story continues. The Frimmersdorf site, for example, will be transformed into an innovative digital and transformation hub, and key parts of the power station will be preserved in the spirit of industrial heritage conservation. That is what RWE stands for: knowing and respecting our history yet always looking ahead and shaping the future.
 
Thank you, Paul, for everything you have achieved and given to #TeamRWE.

Kaum etwas prägt die Zukunft eines Unternehmens so sehr wie die Entscheidungen, die im Aufsichtsrat getroffen werden.
 
Die gestrige Wahl der Arbeitnehmervertreterinnen und -vertreter war daher ein wichtiger Moment für RWE. Die Botschaft meiner Rede war deshalb klar: Wir tragen gemeinsam Verantwortung - konstruktiv, wertegeleitet und auf Augenhöhe.
 
Dieser gemeinsame Ansatz hat in den vergangenen Jahren entscheidende Meilensteine ermöglicht. Der Atomausstieg mit all seiner betrieblichen und personellen Komplexität konnte nur gelingen, weil wir vertrauensvoll zusammengearbeitet haben. Auch die Transformation unseres Kohlegeschäfts und die strategische Ausrichtung von RWE auf erneuerbare Energien wurden maßgeblich durch die konstruktive Zusammenarbeit zwischen Aufsichtsrat und Vorstand geprägt. Deshalb treiben wir den Ausbau von Wind- und Solarenergie weiter voran, entwickeln Batteriespeichertechnologien und stärken unsere Position in wichtigen Wachstumsmärkten.
 
Ich danke allen, die diese Verantwortung bisher mit großem Engagement getragen haben, und wünsche den gestern Gewählten viel Erfolg in ihren neuen Aufgaben.
 
Auch künftig setzen wir auf einen Aufsichtsrat, der unabhängig, mit kritischem Urteilsvermögen und langfristiger Perspektive agiert. Eine enge Zusammenarbeit zwischen Vorstand und Aufsichtsrat bleibt entscheidend für die Zukunft unseres Unternehmens – und für die mehr als 20.000 Menschen im #TeamRWE, die RWE ausmachen.

Selbst gesteckte Ziele sind das Eine, die externe Bestätigung das Andere. 

Wir sind stolz darauf, dass unsere Vielfalts- und Inklusionsvorhaben erneut ausgezeichnet wurden – abermals mit einem Platz auf dem Treppchen.

Die FKi Inclusion for Excellence-Platzierung ist für uns keine Trophäe, sie bestätigt uns in unserer Überzeugung, dass eine Kultur, in der alle Mitarbeitenden die gleichen Chancen zur beruflichen Weiterentwicklung und Entfaltung haben, Grundlage für unser Wirtschaften und unseren Erfolg ist.

Jede und jeder bringt etwas Neues und Eigenes ein – unterschiedliche berufliche Hintergründe, Lebenserfahrungen und kulturelle Perspektiven. Wir bei RWE haben Mitarbeitende aus über 80 Ländern. Und unser Arbeitsumfeld fördert den Austausch und die Zusammenarbeit über gesellschaftliche und geografische Grenzen hinweg. 

Das Fundament dafür ist eine Kultur des Vertrauens, die den Raum bietet, offen die eigene Meinung zu sagen, um Hilfe zu bitten und ehrliches Feedback zu geben. 

Mein Dank gilt allen Kolleginnen und Kollegen, die diese Kultur tagtäglich leben und prägen. Stellvertretend danke ich Rachel Disney und ihrem Team, die Chancengerechtigkeit strukturell verankern und messbar machen.

Ich bin stolz darauf, Teil eines Unternehmens zu sein, in dem viele Stimmen nicht nur vorhanden sind, sondern tatsächlich gehört werden.

Cybersecurity is a top priority for RWE. After all, cyberattacks on critical infrastructure are no longer the exception – they are part of our everyday reality.

Yesterday, I spoke about precisely this topic at the Digitalk meets ZACTALK event (Digitale Stadt Düsseldorf e.V.) at XPONENTIAL Europe and highlighted three key perspectives:

▪︎ Cybersecurity is a key factor in building trust: for our employees, for our partners and for society, which relies on a reliable energy supply at all times.
▪︎ Cybersecurity as a strategic issue: cybersecurity is managed just like any other key management and risk issue: transparently, taking a risk-aware approach and an integrated view of resilience.
▪︎ The corporate culture dimension: sustainable cybersecurity is effective not only in systems, but also in day-to-day actions and through mindset. It requires informed, attentive, and empowered employees and managers who actively exemplify security. At RWE, we bring this to life through a variety of formats – from web-based trainings and phishing simulations to live hacking sessions and escape rooms.

AI is a particular focus. It is fundamentally changing the risk landscape, including in the field of cybercrime. Precisely because AI-powered cyberattacks specifically target the human factor, human judgement becomes more important – not less so.

For RWE, this means that cybersecurity does not end with prevention. Strong detection and response capabilities, clear responsibilities and a security culture that is put into practice form the foundation for a secure energy transition without disruption.

It is not every day that industry, law enforcement and the military sit down together to discuss security and economic policy perspectives. Thank you for this enriching discussion Manfred Boudreaux-Dehmer, Markus Hartmann, Jens Elstermeier and Stephan Schneider for chairing.

The energy transition is powered by people!
 
And that is why we want to give our apprentices, in particular, the opportunity to gain work experience across different RWE operating companies wherever possible. On an exchange programme between RWE Power and RWE Renewables, six of our apprentices spent two weeks working alongside our operations teams in the field. They looked at how maintenance projects work, supported troubleshooting activities, and gained hands-on insight into the technical heart of modern wind turbines. Just as important, they experienced what strong teamwork, trust and safety culture truly mean in practice.
 
When speaking with the apprentices afterwards, one thing became very clear: experiences like these change perspectives. Renewable energy becomes tangible. It becomes personal. And for many, it opens up new ideas about their future. Running for its third consecutive year, this program does more than offer practical experience – it builds bridges between teams, nurtures curiosity, and helps the next generation understand the vital role of our Onshore Wind and Solar PV business in Europe and Australia.
 
Creating these opportunities across business units is essential for us. Development happens when curiosity meets real responsibility. And transformation succeeds when people are given the space to explore, learn and grow.

Because in the end, the energy transition is powered by people.

This morning, we presented RWE’s results for fiscal year 2025 and our strategy for the coming years. First of all, I would like to take this opportunity to express my sincere thanks to the entire #TeamRWE for your high engagement, motivation and professionalism. This is our shared success!
 
We achieved a strong financial performance and are on track for exceptional earnings growth through 2031.

Let’s take a closer look at the numbers:
▪︎ Adjusted EBITDA reached €5.1 billion and adjusted net income amounted to €1.8 billion, the upper end of our earnings guidance.
▪︎ We commissioned new plants with a total combined capacity of 2.8 gigawatts.
▪︎ Between 2026 and 2031, we are planning €35 billion in net investments to expand our generation portfolio to 65 GW, including flexible generation in the United States.
▪︎ Our adjusted earnings per share to rise from €2.48 today to €4.40 by 2031.
▪︎ Our shareholders will benefit more than before from earnings growth – our dividend is set to grow by 10% per year.

But numbers alone do not tell the full story. Behind these results is the work of many teams across the company. The dedication and expertise of our people, across countries, technologies and disciplines, makes these achievements possible. In a dynamic and often challenging environment, adaptability and a strong sense of teamwork enable RWE to keep delivering results and continue building the energy system of the future.

Warum will niemand mehr Führungskraft werden?

Das wollte DER SPIEGEL von Heike Bruch wissen. Sie ist die Herausgeberin der St. Galler Jugendstudie, die drei Kipppunkte ausgemacht hat, wieso junge Menschen keine Lust mehr auf Führungspositionen haben.

Vorgesetzte wirken oft ausgebrannt und in einer Arbeitsmühle, die wenig erfüllend wirkt. Junge Menschen nehmen Strukturen als alt und starr wahr. Und: Führungskräfte spüren oft eine Überforderung oder das Gefühl, am Limit zu arbeiten, sodass sie ihre Führungsaufgaben am liebsten wieder abgeben möchten.

Die Quintessenz – und auch mein Erleben aus meinem beruflichen Alltag: Es fehlt dem Nachwuchs nicht an Ehrgeiz, sondern mitunter an Möglichkeiten, Verantwortung zu erproben, und auch an Vorbildern, die zeigen: So sieht gute Führung aus. So macht Führung Spaß.

Wir bei RWE sind uns unserer Verantwortung, Führungskräfte kontinuierlich auszubilden, bewusst. Zunächst einmal ist es sicherlich erfreulich, dass wir bei RWE keinen Mangel an Mitarbeitenden haben, die Führungsaufgaben übernehmen möchten. Nun liegt es an uns, eine Umgebung zu schaffen, die sich von der oben skizzierten deutlich unterscheidet. Dazu zählt, dass wir unsere Führungskräfte und Potenzialträger auf ihrer Reise begleiten und unterstützen.

Für den Gesamtkonzern haben wir unser Führungskräfteprogramm, unsere RWE Executive Journey, weiter geschärft. In Linie mit unserem Purpose, unseren Unternehmenswerten und unseren erfolgskritischen Verhaltensweisen haben wir ein gemeinsames Führungsverständnis definiert: Unsere RWE Leadership Principles. Diese Führungsprinzipien folgen klaren Standards und formulieren eine klare Erwartung, wie gute Führung bei RWE gelebt wird:

▪︎ Lead for Business Impact
▪︎ Lead to Deliver
▪︎ Lead for Team Success

Eine Umgebung zu schaffen, in der unsere Mitarbeitenden am besten wachsen und wirken können, liegt an uns. Wir begleiten unsere Führungskräfte auf jedem Schritt ihrer Reise und bereiten sie strukturiert auf ihre Rolle vor. Das gilt für das gesamte Spektrum von der ersten Führungsrolle, der Weiterentwicklung als Führungskraft oder einem Neueinstieg bis zum Gesellschaftswechsel.

Wichtig ist uns auch: Leadership ist nicht immer eine lineare Entwicklung, sondern hochindividuell: Es gibt auch Möglichkeiten zurück in Fachpositionen, geteilte Führungsrollen oder Sabbaticals als Möglichkeiten, neue Perspektiven kennenzulernen.

Unsere RWE Executive Journey unterstützt kontinuierlich, leitet an und ermutigt, den Schritt in die Führungsverantwortung zu gehen. Ein großer Dank an die vielen HR Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus dem gesamten Konzern, die gemeinsam RWEs Weg an dieser Stelle unterstützen.

Ich bin schon sehr gespannt, wie sich die Ergebnisse in unserem Unternehmen widerspiegeln werden. Denn ich bin überzeugt: Führung ist attraktiv!

What does leadership look like when the world feels unpredictable? 
 
That was the focus of our discussions at this year’s Global Women’s Network Conference #GWN, where I had the privilege of sharing the stage with our Offshore Wind CFO Gunhild Grieve. How urgent this question is, shows the current situation in the Middle East. Energy markets can shift in an instant while assets last for decades. Leading teams in this environment requires clear direction, curiosity, and teamwork. It also takes courage — the courage to be open, show vulnerability, and face uncertainty together. Listening to different perspectives and sharing my own, I reflected on the small actions that help people feel supported and confident even when everything else is in motion. 
 
During these moments in a BANI world, our values and Essential Behaviours provide anchors. Leadership is about conviction. Conviction means being stable in purpose but flexible in method. You adjust how you move, but not why you move. And that stability helps people feel grounded, especially when change is constant. 
 
Sharing stories and ideas in this space reminded me that leadership isn’t only about decisions. It’s about people, culture, and the everyday actions that help us navigate change together. Moments like these leave me grateful and excited to continue learning and growing alongside such an incredible network of colleagues.

Offshore wind technology delivers stunning images, astonishing figures and equally remarkable teamwork.
 
The latest example: the start of the turbine installation at our Thor offshore wind construction project in the Danish North Sea, which we are implementing together with our project partner Norges Bank Investment Management.
 
Last night, the first of 72 wind turbines was successfully installed. The approximately 80-strong crew of the installation vessel erected the nacelle and the 115-metre-long rotor blades at a hub height of approximately 148 metres. A job for real precision. A real job for #TeamRWE. Another 71 wind turbines will follow until the largest Danish offshore wind farm to date, with an installed capacity of 1.1 GW, is completed. My respect and many thanks to the Offshore Construction teams for your great work — Julian Garnsey, Günther Fenle and your respective teams.
 
And to put the many figures into perspective: Did you know that with the 4.8 GW of capacity that we currently have under construction with project partners plus our existing offshore wind fleet, we could theoretically cover almost the entire annual electricity demand of Denmark? I find that impressive.

21 % der Schülerinnen und Schüler in Deutschland leben in Armut oder sind armutsgefährdet. Fast eine halbe Million Schülerinnen und Schüler benötigen schulische Unterstützung, können sich diese aber nicht leisten. Wir helfen mit, dagegen zu steuern. Seit April 2025 unterstützt die RWE Foundation den Lern-Fair e.V durch ein Mitarbeiterpartizipationsprojekt. 
 
Lern-Fair ist eine Plattform, die Kindern, Jugendlichen und jungen Erwachsenen in Ausbildung aus herausfordernden Lebenslagen kostenlose digitale Lernunterstützung ermöglicht. Gleichzeitig ermöglicht Lern-Fair ein barrierearmes, flexibles Ehrenamt - ortsunabhängig und inklusiv - sodass auch Menschen mit Behinderung oder eingeschränkter Mobilität aktiv mitwirken können. Das Angebot geht von Hausaufgabenhilfe, über Prüfungsvorbereitung bis hin zu Kursen zur Förderung der ganzheitlichen Entwicklung. Ziel ist es, die schulischen Leistungen zu verbessern, damit die Chancen auf höhere Bildungsabschlüsse zu steigern und gleichzeitig das Selbstvertrauen und die Motivation der Kinder und Jugendlichen zu stärken. Wie das funktioniert, erklärt Clara Grabitz, Geschäftsführerin Lern-Fair e.V. RWE-Mitarbeiter Christopher Savage gibt im Video außerdem Einblicke, was ihn bewogen hat, als Tutor mitzuwirken. 
 
Soziales Engagement gehört bei RWE zur Unternehmenskultur. Mit dieser Partnerschaft wollen wir ganz konkret dazu beitragen, dass mehr Kinder und Jugendliche faire Bildungschancen bekommen. Und weil junge Menschen ihre Startbedingungen nicht beeinflussen können, sollten wir uns dafür einsetzen, allen eine faire Chance zu ermöglichen. Schlussendlich profitieren wir alle davon – als Gesellschaft, aber auch ganz persönlich. Unser RWE-Kollege Christopher Savage ist ein starkes Beispiel dafür, dass das Engagement für Lern-Fair nicht nur den Nachwuchs bereichert, sondern auch die Ehrenamtlichen selbst.
 
Ich bin stolz darauf, dass sich bereits so viele Kolleginnen und Kollegen aus dem #TeamRWE auf vielfältige Art und Weise sozial engagieren. Gemeinsam machen wir den Unterschied!

Bleiben wir Anwender oder ist unser Anspruch bei KI ein anderer?
 
Unter anderem darum ging es bei „Allianz der Chancen trifft… Lars Klingbeil“ gestern in Berlin. Die Arbeitswelt geht in die nächste Phase über. Und die gelingt nur im Zusammenspiel zwischen echter und künstlicher Intelligenz. 
 
Im Fokus der Gespräche stand daher, wie eng Finanzpolitik, technologische Entwicklung und Beschäftigung miteinander verbunden sind. Investitionen in Infrastruktur – wie zuletzt in die KI-Fabrik in München – sind zweifelsohne eine wichtige Grundlage. Entscheidend ist jedoch, ob wir Anwender bleiben oder den Anspruch entwickeln, Weltmarktführer für KI-gestützte Geschäftsmodelle zu werden – und ob wir KI dabei konsequent menschenzentriert denken. 
 
Dafür braucht es die Mitarbeitenden aller Unternehmen, die sich in der Allianz der Chancen zusammengeschlossen haben. KI und Mensch müssen dabei Hand in Hand gehen. Auch in dem Bewusstsein, die richtige Tonalität zu treffen, um auf die Ängste vieler Menschen zu reagieren. Mein Eindruck ist, dass wir uns bei Unsicherheit oftmals wieder an alten Verhaltensmustern bedienen, die wir eigentlich schon geglaubt, überwunden zu haben. Hier wünsche ich mir ein gemeinsames Narrativ, eine gemeinsame Strategie aus Politik und Wirtschaft. 
  
Ein herzliches Dankeschön an Ulrike Zeiler für die Gastfreundschaft im Allianz-Forum, an Vizekanzler und Bundesminister Lars Klingbeil für den Impuls, an Dr. Ariane Reinhart für die Moderation und an alle Teilnehmenden für den offenen Austausch und die inspirierenden Perspektiven. So leisten Formate wie die Allianz der Chancen einen wichtigen Beitrag für die Arbeitswelt von morgen.

The way AI is shaped will shape the world!
 
The question therefore is: Do we want to remove biases or reinforce blind spots? One alarm signal for the latter is that various studies indicate only around 22-30% of global AI talent is female.
 
At RWE, however, we strive to do the former. We want AI in our organisation to reflect the perspectives, creativity, and empathy of everyone – not just a few. This week I had the pleasure of joining the launch event for our Women in AI network. The network brings together women from different functions across teams and countries, creating a space to connect, learn, and experiment. It’s about more than representation – it’s about enabling women to actively and responsibly shape AI in ethical, inclusive ways.
 
During the discussion I shared my view of AI as a key enabler of digital transformation and the energy transition. And about what is needed in terms of a strong foundation for AI to scale. It's what I call a golden triangle consisting of:
▪️HR – to bring purpose and heart
▪️IT – to drive innovation
▪️Security – to provide the trust that allows us to move fast without breaking things
 
Together, they form the foundation of an organisation where AI can act as a co-pilot, supporting employees and freeing up time for creative, strategic work by humans. This is where women make a real difference. Women often bring strong domain expertise, ethical awareness, and empathy. Diverse teams reduce blind spots and help build robust AI solutions that are fairer and more sustainable. 
 
This was a successful start to the network, and I am already very excited to see the first tangible results. Thanks to Thomas Denny and Marina Sverdel for the lively discussion on stage and huge congratulations to Gülnaz Öneş and the women on the AI core team for making this network possible.

“Turning points”
“Geopolitical storms”
Uncertainty is no longer the exception, it’s now part of leadership.
 
How do uncertainty and a rapidly changing world shape the way we lead? This was a topic in the panel discussion with Colette Rückert-Hennen we had at  The London School of Economics and Political Science (LSE) German Symposium.
 
From my personal perspective – being responsible for HR, IT and Security – the challenge is even more fundamental: We are moving from an era of efficiency to an era of agency. The past decades, leadership was about managing “Human Resources”. Now, AI is finally taking the 'robot' out of the job. It is absorbing the management chores, the data-drudgery, and the administrative friction. This creates spaces. New possibilities. 

The big question for us on this panel is: What would be the wisest way to fill the newly created spaces? Our shared conviction: If we manage to fill it with Human Agency - transparency, radical vulnerability, and shared leadership - we turn uncertainty into our greatest competitive advantage. My goal is to use technology as a multiplier, not a replacer, so that our collective time becomes our company’s most valuable asset.

Are women better prepared for uncertain times, as there is something called the "female" leadership style? 

I try to avoid stereotypes, but research shows that in times of high stress, there is the temptation to revert to autocratic styles when the world feels 'Brittle' or 'Incomprehensible' (BANI). It feels safe to have one person 'set the course.' But I have to argue the opposite. Autocracy is a bottleneck. In an era where AI agents are processing data and making micro-decisions in milliseconds, an autocratic leader becomes the slowest part of the system. An autocratic leader who pretends to have all the answers creates a fragile organisation. A leader who shows vulnerability and transparency creates a resilient one. In a BANI world, collaboration is a survival skill, not a 'soft' skill. And so is Diversity!

Thanks to Hartmann Ilka for your moderation, and again to Colette Rückert-Hennen. It’s always a pleasure to share perspectives and the stage with you.
 
Actually, this thoroughly inspiring day began already in the morning with a meeting at the German Embassy in London where we had the opportunity to speak with the British Ambassador, H.E. Andrew Mitchell, and the German Ambassador, H.E. Susanne Baumann. This exchange provided valuable international perspectives on leadership as well. A day fully packed with great discussions.

My first business trip this year, and I'm returning with a lot of insights and impressions.

The last days in Vietnam were dense and fully packed. Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City: Two site visits with our partner FPT Software, where parts of our IT services are delivered and where we are currently further exploring our Best Shoring Model. Every conversation focused on capability, reliability, and long-term performance rather than short-term optimisation. 

The same mindset was apparent at FPT University. A very holistic view on education: Computer science is central, of course, but every student is required to also study English, practises Vietnamese martial arts, and learns to play a traditional musical instrument. Performance, they showed me, grows not from technical skills alone, but from discipline, balance, and cultural grounding. That combination is remarkable. 

This perspective carried into a panel on Women in Tech and Energy, which I opened with a speech while wearing a beautiful traditional Vietnamese dress. We spoke about technology, but the deeper question was how to prepare people for what comes next. At RWE, a human-first approach means using AI to support people: to simplify work, increase efficiency, and create space for strategic thinking, creativity, and developing new capabilities.

I see women playing a dedicated role in the AI transformation. We must lean in when AI models and LLMs are trained, ensuring that the future AI world is at least as diverse as today's. And this commitment comes to life in the field, as we noticed during our visits to Offshore Delivery Centres and the AI Campus in Saigon, where we saw AI already processing vast data sets in real time and accelerating development cycles from months to days, all underpinned by a performance culture built on clarity, ownership, and ambition. 

I leave Vietnam with gratitude for the openness and generosity of everyone who shared their insights – especially Chu Thi Thanh Ha and all colleagues at FPT Software. 

Happy Lunar New Year next month to everyone celebrating.

Let's start the year with a view!
 
After taking you on a virtual tour of a wind turbine, today we're heading to the “heart” of the offshore wind farm: the substation.
 
What you see here is the offshore substation of our Kaskasi wind farm, 35 km off the coast of Heligoland. The substation is the central hub where electricity from all turbines comes together before heading to shore. From the outside, it might seem like just another platform at sea, but inside it’s a giant tangle of components and connections, all designed to make the flow of electricity reliable and continuous.
 
What kind of work goes into this heart of an offshore wind farm? Nothing less than an engineering masterpiece in manufacturing, heavy-lift vessels to transport the thousands of tonnes of topside components, and absolute precision during the “marriage” at sea – the installation of the topside onto the foundation. 
 
Once completed, the wind turbines turn, the generators produce electricity, and this is fed into the relevant grid connections via the substation. Sounds simple – but take a look for yourself! It’s easy to forget, from the outside, just how much care and coordination goes into making everything work. 
 
Looking ahead, RWE Offshore Wind will deliver four construction projects with a total capacity of 4.8 GW and continue providing clean, reliable electricity from our wind farms. Considering the dedication that goes into every detail, it’s clear that none of this would be possible without #TeamRWE.

AI transformation is a journey. That's true for us at RWE, too. 
 
For me, the goal of the journey is clear: We want to become a best-in-class company that seamlessly integrates human expertise with agentic capabilities! The areas of application are diverse, ranging for example from process improvements to site layouts for offshore wind farms or weather models for our trading business.
 
What vehicles are we using to embark on this journey? A very important one is the Promptathon. It brings users and technology together, in a kind of laboratory environment where employees can bring specific concerns and then experiment with them. The impact is proven: we know from past projects that we can go from an idea to a prototype within a day. I find that remarkable and I am confident and excited about the future.
 
Many thanks to Dr. Max Schumm and Scott-Oliver Luehrs for your commitment in preparing and running the Promptathons and for the insights into the status quo of our journey.

My personal AI vision for RWE: We will become a best-in-class company that seamlessly integrates human expertise with agentic capabilities!
 
After a week on the US west coast, one thing is clear: AI is everywhere. From the Microsoft Ignite Conference to our very own AI Lab in Seattle – it was the predominant subject. Together with our CIO Gülnaz Öneş, the first item on the agenda was the Microsoft Ignite Conference in San Francisco. My highlights:

•   A use case for AI in the energy sector
•   Playbooks from manufacturing companies
•   Future possibilities of agents and targeted hands-on prompting
 
The inspiration continued at RWE's own Commercial AI Research Lab. Founded in mid-2023, around 15 employees are now working intensively on probabilistic AI weather forecasts, scientific research into weather and climate, and commercial weather models. They are working on coding complex and chaotic interactions across multiple domains to maximise the value of weather data. Accurate weather forecasts are particularly important for our power plants and renewable energy facilities, as electricity production and trading are heavily based on data analysis.
 
What else remains from a week full of AI? Personal, human interaction remains the most enjoyable aspect, whether in the office or with family and friends. With this in mind, I would like to wish all our American colleagues a Happy Thanksgiving.
